PROCEEDINGS OP THE

next two years, he was elected Senior Grand Warden and Deputy
Grand Master.
The 1955 Communication of this Grand Lodge was held during the
fourth week of October. It was at this Communication that Brother
Stewart was elected and installed as Grand Master. The Communication over which he presided terminated in the third week of September,
1956. This added to Ned's several distinctions that of having served the
shortest term as Grand Master (eleven months) in any recent year.
The shortness of his occupancy of the position did not in any way detract
from the scope of his effectiveness or from the competency with which
he discharged all of the responsibilities and functions of that office.
One of the many compliments accorded our Grand Master during
his year came to him in connection with the Annual Conference of Grand
Masters. With characteristic modesty, Ned refers to the event as
planned to extend honor to this Grand Jurisdiction. He so refers to it
in his published Message. However, his statement conveys but part of
the story. Elected to preside as Chairman of the Conference, and given
the distinction of acting as Master of Ceremonies at \ts annual banquet
afforded him an opportunity to demonstrate that his abilities were fully
commensurate with the dignity and prestige of the Jurisdiction which
had been honored. Ned fully measured up to the highest standard of
his predecessors.
In addition to his activities in the Grand Lodge of California,
Brother Stewart has been an active member of the Los Angeles Bodies
of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite since 1926. His work there
earned for him the honor of being coroneted with the 33rd Degree in
1943. Currently, he is serving as Junior Warden of the Lodge of Perfection and Director of the Work. He also holds membership in Al
Malaikah Temple, Ancient Arabic Order of the Nobles of the Mystic
Shrine.
In business life, this Brother has successfully established and operated a general insurance agency. The full measure of the development
which has resulted from Ned's administration is emphasized by the
manner in which his organization continues to effectively function even
though the "boss" absents himself a large part of the time in fulfilling
his Masonic responsibilities.
Other organizations with which Brother Stewart ·h as shared his time
and ability include the Los Angeles Chapter of Chartered Life Underwriters, the Los Angeles Athletic Club, Town Hall, and Midnight Mission. He is now serving the last named as Vice-President of its Board
of Directors.
His activities with the First Church of Christ, Scientist, Beverly
Hills, included membership on the Board of Directors from 1941 to 1943.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

3

During the latter year, he served as President of the Board. He is now
serving as a Director of the Southern California Foundation, Inc.
The most effective way to realize the type of administration which
Ned gave to this Grand Lodge is to read his Annual Message as it
appears in these Proceedings. The manifold activities to which he gave
minute attention and capable direction, the extent to which he favored
all parts of the Jurisdiction and all types of activity with his presence are
detailed in the comprehensive summary which he presented. This reflects his interest, his understanding, and his constructive suggestions.
It demonstrates why all who have the privilege of. associating with him
soon acquire an affection and admiring regard for him. His officers
esteem the privilege of having served under his direction. All will continue to be inspired by the devotion and effectiveness of his leadership.

1260 Officers and representatives from 627 Chartered Lodges and

the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge was opened in ample form, following which the Flag of Our Country was received.

11

Most Worshipful Sir,
Members of the Grand Lodge of California,
Delegates to the 107th Annual Convention of the
Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California,
Visiting Brethren of Districts,
One would be inhuman indeed who did not feel humble in ·standing
before .you in the opening hours ·of this Grand Lodge, representing as
you do, 230,000 Masons. In a sense you also represent a like number of
Masons who reside in this State but have their membership elsewhere.
The importance of this Grand Lodge because of its glorious history and
the size of its membership is an impressive fact that should cause pride
among all of us. As a Grand Lodge officer one could only dream of the
ultimate power of Masonry as one experienced during the past year
new members, new lodges, and new buildings from the North to the
South of this favored state.
During my tenure as Grand Chaplain, however, I had a rude awakening: After living for 46 years in the Western World with its JudeoChristian background, I ventured into another world-Russia-with its
39 year old campaign against all of the spiritual values for which our
lodge stands. It defies and attacks the great spiritual truths which have
been tried and tested against the experiences of man, not for one century, but many centuries. It was in this kind of a setting that I reflected
upon the many things which I so often take for granted. I determined
one night in a Moscow hotel never again to take so casually the spiritual
realities of life. In a land now trying to build upon dialectic materialism,
and teaching science biased toward atheistic assumption, matters of the
spirit suddenly became more alive to me in a strange way. Masonry
now means more to me because of this experience.
The ·spiritual potential of our craft defies the imagination. Time and
time again it has come to me in one of the •parables of the greatest
teacher of all who is reported in Matthew Chapter 13, verse 33, to have
said, "the kingdom of heaven is like leaven which •a woman took and
hid in three measures of meal, till it was all leavened."
The parables are a ipart of our rich heritage coming from Jewish
background. They are effective and were used particularly by Jesus because they were simple and easily understood by all. They carried a
" 1homey" quality. No one could miss a truth as fitly pictured in one of
them.
The parable of the leaven has particular significance for Masonry.
Let us delineate its importance.
Leaven as used by the housewife, it is written, is a means by which

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

become parts of the pattern by which the lives of others are tailored.
You do not have to be an "important" person ·to have your influence
count. Thomas Carlyle once wrote, "The work an unknown good
man has done is like a vein of water Bowing hidden undergroun d, secretly making the ground green. Whether you realize it or not you exert
a very definite influence. Be sure it is the kind you wouldn't be ashamed
to claim."
Soon after Matthew Simpson had delivered 'his inaugural address as
president of DePaw University he went about Indiana delivering the
same address in various Indiana towns and cities. The address dealt
with the need for institutions o.f higher learning. and in the course of his
speech he noted that it was actually easier to start an institution of
higher learning in a relatively new territory than in the older, more
settled areas of the country. A young doctor, John Evans, heard this
address in Attica, Indiana. Some years later Dr. Evans, realizing that
there was no college in Chicago and none nearer than Galesb~rg. I.llinois, together with a small group founded Northweste rn University.
A -few years later Dr. Evans was appointed by his friend, Preside~t
Abraham Lincoln, as the second territorial governor of Colorado. Still
rooalling the address by Matthew Simpson, he with a few oth~rs,
founded the University of Denver, the first institution of higher learning
in Colorado even though there were very few people in the entire territory at the time, and the Civil War was in progress. The leaven working from that original talk was and still is permeating the whole!
Harry Emerson Fosdick relates that:
"At one stage in his career William Wilberforce was so downcast
about the British Empire and the world at large that he hesitated to
marry and have children and so give hostages to fortune in so dreadful
a world. He was as low in his mind as that. Morever, he was not unjustified in being discouraged about social evil in general and the slave
trade in particular. Was not the slave trade a cruel and towering fact?
Had it not existed throug'h all history so that the memory of man went
not back to the time when it ~ad not cursed the race? Did not the world's
wisest statesman say that they foresaw slavery's indefinite continuance?
Even Edmund Burke said that. With the existant facts, the inveterate
history and the cynicism of the worldly wise on the side of slavery's
continuance, what was there to give a ·man hope? Nothing much. Only
an idea, which spread like fire from mind to mind. that slavery was
wrong, that it never could be harmonized with the principles of Christ,
that it was, as well, economically self-defeating. that it was as degrading
to the masters and as impoverishing to the wage-earne rs as it was brutal
to the slaves-an idea which kept using more and more people, with
Wilberforce pre-eminent among them. until before he died he was
assured of the abolition of the British slave trade. Once more in history

the statement was vindicated: There is nothing so powerful in this
world-not existent facts, nor the reluctance of apathetic governmen ts-nothing so powerful as an idea whose dawn has dawned."
The idea that slavery was wrong was the leaven that permeated the
whole until it all was leavened and slavery was abolished not only in the
British Empire, but in the United States as well.
Coming closer to home I am reminded of a former student of the
College of the Pacific, Mary Glide, who developed an interest in astronomy looking into the heavens through the six inch telescope which we
have on the campus. Her interest in this area never diminished and
some years later as she was walking with her husband in Golden Gate
Park s·h e remarked that there should be located in this place of beauty a
planetarium and that they should start the movement for it with the
initial gift. This offer was at first rejected but later accepted, and as
the idea kept growing and multiplying among many people the fund for
a planetarium grew larger and larger. The happy result is the Morrison
Planetarium in this city, one of the finest to be found anywhere in the
world. A small piece of leaven changed the whole and thousands have
and will be benefited.
Let me mention a brother Mason in Sacramento , Mr. Charles M.
Goethe. While in Europe the idea came to him that ihe should be instrumental in establishing naturalists in our famed National Park System.
Through letters, pamphlets, speeches, and other devices, park naturalists
ultimately became associated with our national parks and later became
an official segment of that operation. Each year millions see and hear
the wonders of nature unfolded by the men who are there now because
a Mason had an "idea whose day had dawned."
A supreme example is found in Past Grand Master Charles Albert
Adams. Masons have always believed in the free public school in California and have opposed everything they honestly thought was to its
detriment. Sensing the crisis in public education through the lack of
competent teachers, the closing of schools, and particularly the apathy
of the people to initiate remedial measures, Adams as Grand Master in
1920 proclaimed Public Schools Week in the Masonic Lodges of California. At a designated week during the year a meeting was to be held
in every Masonic Lodge, open to the public at which conditions affecting
the public schools should be discussed by qualified speakers. Meetings
were under way, speakers cooperated, school officials aided in every way
possible. Literature was published and newspapers gave space. Later a
constitutional amendment was adopted by the people which established
a fixed contribution of State funds for the public schools and placed
California in a enviable position in the educational world. This annual
observance is now not only Masonic but has become a community affair,
and in many areas the observance extends over the entire week with the

1

16

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

schools holding open ·house. The idea is each year becoming more
widely accepted, has more people. participating. broadens its scope of
activities, and bids well for a glorious future. Could anyone deny that
this is an excellent example of the leaven at work? The idea started
from the center in the mind of a man, and is working its way through the
whole.
It is obvious that it has been my purpose to present the biblical background of one of the most important parables of all time and then use
examples of how the leaven has worked in life situations. But the point
I want to emphasize is that there are John Evanses, William Wilberforces, Mary Glides, Charles M. Goethes and Charles Adamses in the
Grand Lodge today if they will only allow their lives to be used. The
world is waiting for the changing force of the leaven in every branch of
our common life. One might ask, who other than a Mason with the long
history of our craft and the high ideals which have sustained it is any
better suited to do this? We believe that God is a loving God and that
He wants to cooperate. It could be that possibly you are the one He
desires to speak through next. Heed the call and you will be the personal
exemplification of Matthew 13, verse 33: "The Kin~dom of Heaven is
like leaven which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, till
it was all leavened."

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California.
It is with a feeling of gratitude and appreciation to this Grand Lodge
for the privilege of presenting my second annual report as your Grand
Treasurer for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1956.
The individual printed reports of the auditors containing detailed
financial statements of the Grand Lodge F. & A. M .. the Masonic Homes
of California, including the permanent Endowment Fund and the California Masonic Memorial Temple, are available to all the brethren here
represented. Heretofore the Grand Treasurer's report has been included

made available which was actually Thursday, September 13, 1956.

accomplishing so much in such a short period of time.

and expense disbursements as shown in the Grand Treasurer's report

Again may I emphasize that members of Grand Lodge should study
and review the several printed reports. This is your Grand Lodge. This
is your business. It is your responsibility as an officer of your lodge to
take these reports back to your membership.
The auditing firm of Skinner & Hammond have spent many hours
examining the various accounts in order to prepare these statements for
your study and review.
For those whose interest in analyzing balance sheets and income
statements is limited, I strongly recommend that you at least read the
auditor's certificate at the front of each report. Here you will generally
find in editorial comment what the figures represent to those experienced
in accounting procedures.
It is deeply regretted that this report showing a comparative summary of receipts and disbursements for the Grand Lodge of California
and certain of its affiliated organizations, are not ready for distribution
at this time as has already been indicated. This was a physical impossibility. It is recommended, however, that it be printed and mailed to all
those who receive printed reports by mail.
Respectfully submitted,
EDWARD H. SIEMS,
Grand Treasurer

SEVENTY-FIVE YEAR BUTTON
At the last Communica tion a resolution was introduced providing
for a Veteran Button to be presented to members who had attained
75 years membership. The Grand Secretary was instructed and empowered to design and produce such a Button. This has been done, and
a photograph of the Button is reproduced herewith.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
I have the honor to present to you herewith my Fifteenth Annual
Report as your Grand Secretary.
UNDER DISPENSATION
Lakeside Lodge U.D., Josiah W. Roller Lodge U.D., Coastside
Lodge U.D., Arabic Lodge U .D., Heritage Lodge U.D., Dana Weller
Lodge U.D., William Rhodes Hervey Lodge U.D. and James H. Kew
Lodge U.D. were instituted shortly before the close of the fiscal year.
Each of these Lodges collected only an equal or a less amount of
dues than the per capita tax, and in accord with precedent the Grand
Master, at my suggestion, directed that they be not required to pay that
per capita tax. It is respectfully requested that this be approved.

CHANGE OP MEETING PLACE
Artesia Lodge No. 377 has removed its meeting place from Norwalk
to Artesia, and Seafaring Lodge No. 708 has removed its meeting place
from Costa Mesa to Newport Beach. These have been officially
approved, under the authority of the Grand Master, and the Grand
Secretary now requests authority to properly endorse their charters.
In Alameda County a number of Communities and small towns have
been consolidated into a new city known as Fremont. Alameda Lodge
No. 167 was chartered to meet at Centerville, a part of the new incorporation. Authority is, therefore, requested to properly endorse their
charter.

the close of World War II and 1954 and 1955 are the first full years
following the end of the Korean conflict.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER

conduct of installation ceremonies in certain cases in a more or less undignified manner. The adopted installation service is required to be
adhered to, without additions or subtractions, and all proceedings before, during and after the ceremony should be conducted with dignity
and without embarrassment to anyone. The Inspectors have ample
power to control this situation.
In past years, the Grand Lodge has expressly prohibited the use of
slides, maps, charts or pictures of any nature showing in whole or in
part the secret work of Masonry, and has prohibited even the possession
of such material. We have recently had occasion to call the attention of
the Inspectors to tihe fact that this prohibition would also include certain
carvings or pictures of vessels, even though in our opinion they have
little or no symbolic significance. I may say rhat the Masters of the
lodges have generally cooperated to secure conformity to the regulation.
Under the provisions of section 24 7 of the Ordinances, six lodges
were permitted to continue to perform long-established ritualistic work
differing from the uniform ritual of this jurisdiction, "so far as the same
may not be disapproved by the Grand Master and the Grand Lecturer".
T·hree of the lodges have a ritual of a single degree differing from tihe
uniform ritual, and two of these have the remainder of the uniform
work in a foreign translation. Three others have what is supposedly a
translation of the uniform work. These are thus ·five lodges working in
a foreign language, each having an Inspector of its own.
It is obvious that this does not permit of conformity to our law,
requiring all Inspectors to be qualified by the Assistant Grand Lecturer or the Grand Lecturer, and requiring the Assistant Grand Lecturers to be qualified by tihe Gand Lecturer.
Practically all candidates of these language lodges speak English,
and the reason for work in a foreign language differing from the uniform ritual has almost ceased to exist. It is our hope that these lodges
will yield to voluntary persuasion to turn to the uniform work in English,
and that it will not become necessary at some future time to exercise the
discretion reserved in section 247 to require conformi-ty to the uniform
ritual.
In closing this report, I wish to express my personal appreciation to
the Grand Master for his unfailing courtesy and help, and to the Grand
Secretary and Assistant Grand Secretary for their assistance to me at
all times. Again I express my thanks to you bretihren for permitting me
to serve you.
Respectfully submitted,

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
This is my fourth annual report covering the activities of the Grand
Lecturer ·and of tlhe Committee on Ritual.
The customary Spring Conferences of Inspectors were conducted by
the Assistant Grand Lecturers, as follows:
Divisions 1 and 2, iat Bijou, Lake Tahoe, June 15-17, 1956, conducted
by Worshipful Clare B. Campbell and Worshipful Ralph M. Foote:
Division 3, at Guerneville, May 17-19, 1956, conducted by Worshipful Arthur J. Kahn;
Division 4, at Yosemite Valley, June 1-3, 1956, conducted by Worshipful Raymond G. Taylor:
Division 5, at Ojai, April 20-22, 1956, conducted by Worshipful
Donald G. Campbell;
Division 6, at Riverside, March 23-25, 1956, conducted by Worshipful Clark H. Shaw.
I was present at each of these Conferences and observed the work,
whkh was well done by Inspectors of the respective divisions.
At each Conference, the Inspectors were addressed by the Grand
Master, or in his absence by the Deputy Grand Master, and they were
also addressed by the Grand Secretary. Each of them discussed matters
of interest and importance to the Inspectors.
A special meeting of the Ritual Committee was held at each Conference to consider matters of ritual. A special meeting of the Committee
was also held on December 3rd and 4th, 1955, at San Francisco, with
all members of the Committee present, at which meeting the entire work
of the three degrees was reviewed and actually performed by the Assistant Grand Lecturers under the supervision of the Grand Lecturer.
The reports required by section 53 of the Ordinances have been
received from the Inspectors. The reports disclose a general good condition of our lodges, so far as ritual is concerned, and it is apparent that
uniformity of ritual is gradually being achieved throughout the jurisdiction. Tihese reports further reveal the considerable amount of work
which is done by our lnspectoral Corps. I want to express my appreciation for the devoted service of these men, and also for the excellent
work of the six men who serve you as Assistant Grand Lecturers.
The increased number of Inspectors reflects the constant and rapid
growth of the lodges in our jurisdiction. W hen I first became a member
of the Ritual Committee as Assistant Grand Lecturer in 1949, there
were 123 Inspectors. Today, only seven years later, we have 166 lnspectoral Districts, representing an increase of one-third in the number
of Inspectors.

REPORT OF INVESTMENT COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Another year goes into history, and the Investment Committee begins
its seventh year of activity this August 1, 1956. It seems appropriate
that each year's Investment Committee report give a certain amount of
historical background and basic information regarding its purposes and
principles. inasmuch as a large number of members present are attending Grand Lodge for the first time. We hope such information will be
helpful to those who wish to avail themselves of it.
The Prudent Man Rule in modified form was adopted by Grand
Lodge at its 1950 Communication. For the Constituent Lodges the same
Prudent Man Rule was adopted in 1951.
The Investment Committee of Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California
was formed for the purpose of administering the investable funds of
Grand Lodge, the Masonic Homes of California, and the Masonic
Homes Endowment Fund. The Committee does not supervise the investments of Constituent Lodges. Grand Lodge makes the services of its
investment advisor available to the Lodges. The investment advisor
keeps the Committee informed as to the use of su(jh services by the
Lodges. Inasmuch as the Lodges are making use of this service, the
Investment Committee feels that the expenditure is justified.
The Investment Committee of Grand Lodge is composed of the
Grand Treasurer, the Assistant Grand Treasurer, the Chairman of the
Finance Committee, the President of the Masonic Homes Board of
Trustees or a Trustee of that Board designated by him, and the Chairman of the Masonic Homes Endowment Board or a member of that
Board designated by him. The President of the Masonic Homes Board
of Trustees has designated Brother Past Master Ralph H. Head and
the Chairman of the Endowment Board has designated Brother Past
Master John W. Davey, as members of the Committee.
By Ordinance, under Section 86 with respect to investment of Grand
Lodge funds, and Section 152.1 respecting investments by Constituent
Lodges, the following •provisions were promulgated:
GROUP I. At least 40% of the funds available for investment
must be in:
A). Cash and/or bank accounts.
B ) Obligations of the United States.
C) Obligations of the State of California and its political
subdivisions.
D) Such other securities as are legal investments for California
savings banks.
GROUP II. Up to 20% may be invested in:
A) Other evidences of indebtedness, which are or will be fully

B)

43

listed and registered on an exchange registered with the
Securities and Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange. By amendment, 1955, the listing requirement will not apply to railroad equipment trust bonds.
Preferred stocks, which are or will be fully listed and registered on an exchange registered with the Securities and
Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange.

GROUP UI. Up to 40% may be invested in:
A) Common stocks, which must be fully listed and registered
on an exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange
Commission as a National Securities Exchange, except
that this listing requirement shall not apply to bank and
insurance stocks.
B) Shares of Investment Trusts.
With respect to the authority to invest in Groups II and III, die
Ordinance reads as follows: "No such investments, however, shall be
made which at the time of purchase will result in the total market value
of the securities referred to in this section exceeding twenty per cent
(or forty percent) of the total market value of all the cash, bank
accounts and securities held"-the controlling point being that there
cannot be more than 20% or 40% invested in Groups II and III,
respectively, at the time of purchase.
Since its formation the Investment Committee has met regularly
every three months. Between quarterly meetings, the business of the
Committee is handled by correspondence or telephone. This procedure
has proven satlsfactory.
We have just completed six years of operation. The following is

The following comment was also made by Moody's Investors Service
with respect to Constitu ent Lodges:
"The policy is not to increase Group III at this time unless there are
no Group III common stock at all, in which case some investment quality
income issues may be recommended. But if there is a fair represen tation
of commons, whether the per cent be only 10% or somewhat higher
(25% to 30% about present limit), no addition s are recommended.
"Group II preferred s are being suggeste d for income up to between
10% to 15% (maximum 20%). Most reviews of portfolios have concentrated on this aspect."
The Grand Secretar y will gladly furnish a copy of the procedur e
Ordinan ces respecting investments to any inquiring Lodge.
The Investment Committee recommends an amendmen~ to Sec. 86
and Sec. 152.1 relating to investments.
Proposed amendm ent to Sec. 86, Subsection 2 B, and Sec. 152.1,
Subsection 2 B: At the present time these Sections read as follows:
Investme nt may be made in "B) Preferre d stocks, which are or will be
fully listed and registered on an exchang e registere d with the Securities
and Exchang e Commission as a National Securities Ex~hange." To this
we ask for the following amendment by way of addition : " ... except
that the full listing and registrat ion of preferred stocks will not be
required wheneve r the common stock of the corporat ion issuing such
preferred stock is fully listed and registered on an exchang e registere d
with the Securities and Exchang e Commission as a National Securities
Exchang e, and provided further that such preferred stock is traded on an
exchang e registered with the Securities and Exchang e Commission as a
National Securities Exchang e."
There is no relaxing of our original concept that such "Preferr ed

Stocks" should be fully listed because. when the common stoc~ of a corporation is fully listed, all necessary information is disclosed m accordance with Securities and Exchang e Commission requirements. Therefore, when the common stock of a corporat ion is fully listed and the
preferred stock is traded on a National Securities Exchang e we have all
the necessary protection regardin g listing.
In closing, we wish to report that the !~vestment Committee continues to pursue a conservative policy, as will be seen by the amounts
invested in the three categories, namely Groups I, II, and III.
Our thanks to the Grand Secretary, the Assistan t Grand Secretar y,
and to the members of the Investment Committee for their wholehearted and generous support at all times.

tendency. After several months the Board of Trustees finally called to
the position Brother Jam es R. Eubanks, a Past Master of San Mateo
Lodge No. 226, F.&A.M. and a former Superintendent of the Home for
the Aged of San Mateo County. Brother _Eubanks stepped into the very
difficult position of succeecldng a beloved Superintendent and he succeeded even beyond the best hopes of those who had engaged him. Taking office in the middle Spring of 1941, he has served continuously until
February 1, 1956, when he requested a leave of absence from the Board
of Trustees for a period of six months and with the option of retiring at
the end of that time. Brother Eubanks having passed the age of retirement and feeling that he did not desire to continue in the Superintendency, retired as of July 31, 1956.
It would not be possible for any Superintendent to give a greater
percentage of his time to the administration of the Home at Decato than
"Jim" did. He lived on the property and was available twenty-four hours
a day. He did not take the time away from the Home on vacations which
he was entitled to and whic'h the Board felt he should have taken. His
devotion to the task has been outstanding and his ability has been recognized not only by our Board of Trustees but by the National Association
of Masonic Homes Executives of which he served as President just
a few years ago.
The Board has expressed its appreciation to Brother Eubanks for
the service which he has rendered and they hope for him many long
years of !happy retirement.

'J'ihis study is continuing and it is hoped that it will result in a five-year
analysis when the time comes.
No essential change in the medical program has taken place during
the past year. Home members have expressed their satisfaction and
happiness in having readily available the entire specialty staff at the
Palo Alto Medical Clinic. Hospitalization, primarily for surgery, has
been carried out through the Palo Alto Hospital.
The Clinic has been high in its praise of the diet provided for the
residents and t·he preparation thereof.
A start has been made on a rehabilitation organization at the Home
where directed physiotherapy and rehabilitation measures are carried
out under the supervision of the nursing staff. We hope that this department will be further expanded in the months to come.

GAIL H. DAVID

Brother Gail H. David, Junior Warden of Piedmont Lodge No. 521,
F.&A.M. was selected by Superintendent Eubanks, with the approval
of the Board, as the Assistant Superintendent of the Decato Home and
when Superintendent Eubanks took his leave of absence Brother David
was promoted to the position of Acting Superintendent. He has served
well in that capacity and. proven his worth and at the General Meeting
of the Board the latter part of July, prior to the actual retirement of
Superintendent Eubanks on July 31, 1956, Brother David was unanimously elected Superintendent of the Decato Home. The Board feels
that he is qualified for this important position and of course every assistance will be given 'him in the administration of the Home for the Aged.
MEDICAL CARE AT THE DECOTO HOME

It has been reported that there is a wide national interest in the
· medical care program at Decato as it is being instrumented through the
Palo Alto Medical Clinic. This interest has been expressed in communications and numerous conversations since the published report "Cost
of Medical Care of the Aged," which was a statistical analy!?iS of the
cooperative work of the Palo Alto Medical Oinic and the Decato Home.

SCHOLARSHIP

A number of years ago a gift was made to the Masonic Homes of
California by George F. and Laura E. Brigham for the purpose of establishing a Scholarship Fund. As may be seen in the audit the total Scholarship Fund today amounts to $48,942.59. To the original grant have been
added small sums from various sources from time to time and the Fund
has been drawn upon to assist many deserving graduates of our Covina
Home. Many have gone on to become fine professional men, others in
the business world and a number of the girls have become teachers,
nurses, etc. The Universities which are presently being attended by
these recipients of scholarship awards are:
Brigham Young University, Provo
Cali(ornia Institute of Technology, Pasadena
College of the Pacific, Stockton
I. B. M. School, Los Angeles
University of California, Riverside
FINANCE

Over tlhe past ten years substantial building improvements have been
made and our properties in Decato and Covina have been completely
rehabilitated. A full and all inclusive medical arrangement has been made
for our Decato residents. In addition, a retirement and pension program
for Home employees has been inaugurated with all of the money necessary for funding .past service deposited. Without cutting down on any
necessary .functions or facility, we have been able to set aside a modest
building fund to take care of future requirements at both locations.
Likewise, scholarship grants and loans are being made to worthy Covina
graduates. The Board has also allocated to the Endowment Fund
$100,000.00 from the Unappropriated Reserve Fund.
All of this has been made possible by generous gifts from our mem..
bership and friends through bequests and legacies and by means of con..
tributions to our growing Endowment Fund.

52

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Great praise is due our Investment Committee for the skillful handling of our security portfolio since the adoption of the Prudent Man
Investment rule. The increased income from this source has been a great
factor in enabling the Trustees to reduce the per capita tax from $1.00
in 1952 to the present 50 cent levy.
We had hoped to make a further reduction this year. However,
current labor problems and economic conditions indicate that we will
have another wave of inflation in wages and operating costs. A number
of well known institutions beset by rising costs have had to merge or
abandon certain activities due to union demands and rising operating
expenses.
Because of this uncertainty and with the knowledge that our brethren
are willing to give full support to this worthy cause, we request .that the
present per capita tax of 50 cents per member be levied in the 1957-8
budget for the benefit of the Masonic Homes of California.

REPORT OF SUPERINTENDENT-DECOTO HOME
To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
Brethren: It is with great pleasure and gratitude that I present my
first annual report as Superintendent of the Masonic Home at Decato
for the year ending July 31, 1956.
It is a pleasure to report that conditions are most satisfactory, the
morale of all the members is quite high, and they are very cooperative
in all respects.
At the beginning of the fiscal year there was a total of 340 members
in the Home, consisting of 128 men and 212 women. During the year
29 women, average age 79.69 years, and 39 men, average age 77.38 years
were admitted to the Home. There were 32 women, average age 83.62
years, and 29 men, average age 80.71 years, who passed away. 5 men
and 4 women were withdrawn. The total population on August 1, 1956
was 338, consisting of 133 men and 205 women, including 13 married
couples.

There are 78 members in our 'hospital, of which 68 are considered
permanent, and there are 22 men and 34 women in the ma.in building
who require semi-care. However, the majority of the members are enjoying fairly good health. Our hospital is supervised by Miss Bess L. Payne
and her very competent staff, who render to the ·patients the most excellent care in a very kindly and efficient manner.
The doctors from the Palo Alto Clinic visit our hospital five days
each week. They see the members from the Home in our clinic, and visit
the sick in our 1hospital. If further ex·amination is required, the members
are taken to the Palo Alto Clinic.
Dr. William O'Connor, of Hayward, visits our dental clinic every
Wednesday morning and perfol'!Dls the duties of his profession most
satisfactorily.
The members of the Home all seem quite pleased with the services
of both the Palo Alto Clinic and Dr. O'Connor.
On Feb. 1st, this year, Mrs. Sara Paris assumed the responsible
duties of Matron. During ·her brief time with the Home, she has been
most successful in coordinating the various departments in her charge.
Her love and sympathetic understanding for the members, and her untiring efforts in promoting a harmonious atmosphere are rapidly gaining
the admiration of all the members.

To The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
It is a privilege and a pleasure to present to you my eighth annual
report as Superintendent of the Masonic Home for Children at Covina,
for the year ending July 31, 1956.
HOME MEMBERSHIP

The population of our Covina Home Family for the year ending
July 31, 1956, numbered sixty-eight children, thirty-nine boys and
twenty-nine girls. During the fiscal year of 1955-1956 three boys have
been admitted to the Home. Six girls and three boys left the Home
during the year; three girls by graduation; six who returned to re-established homes of their parents. One graduate, Mary Darling. will enter
the University of California at Riverside in September. Lindy Deemer,
another graduate and Past Honored Queen of Bethel 98, International
Order of Job's Daughters, will continue her education at Santa Monica
Junior College. The third graduate, Cherie Larsen, has completed an
IBM training course in Los Angeles and is employed by a Los Angeles
Department store. Four boys and ·t hree girls were graduated from
Charter Oak Grammar School and will enter Covina High School at
the beginning of the fall term.

Family relationships in the Home consist of the following: One
family of five children each; seven families of three children each; nine
families of two children each; twenty-four families of one child each:
fifteen children, representing nine families, are in the Home under the
membership of the grandparent. One of the sixty-eight children, twentyone attend ·high school and forty-six are enrolled in the elementary
school. and we have one pre-school boy. Total number of Masonic
Lodges having wards in the Home, forty-one from forty-one families.
Our youngest member is five years of age and our oldest is seventeen
years of age.
HoME, ScHOOL AND COMMUNITY ACTIVITIES

The children attend the church of their choice and are encouraged
to participate in the church activities. The children are encouraged to
take an active part in all school activities as well as the Home activities.
They are encouraged to have their friends visit on week-ends and attend our movies, go swimming or just enjoy their dormitory life. Many
of our youngsters are in turn invited to attend parties of their classmates

SUMMER PROGRAM

Under the supervision of a trained staff all of our children have
enjoyed two weeks of Recreation and Camping at Pacific Beach on
Mission Bay in San Diego County. They enjoyed swimming, fishing,
boating, handicraft, trips on submarines, campfires, barbecues and the
usual song period around tlhe fire at night before retiring. Many interesting activities during the "Fiesta del Pacifico" celebration were
enjoyed including attendance of the play, "The California Story".
HEALTH AND WELFARE PROGRAM

We are again fortunate to be able to report a very successful year
for the children's health and physical welfare. Under the guidance and
supervision of Dr. W. P. Magan, Sr., and his Associates, and the excellent care given by our Home's Nurse, health and sound bodies are
very much in evidence among our young people. Complete physical
examinations are given at regular intervals during the year. Dr. Elmer
King, an alumnus of the Covina Home, examines the children's teeth
periodically and administers the necessary care and treatment. Ors.
Paul and Teal take care of the orthodontia treatments. At the present

58

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

time sixteen children are receiving this corrective treatment either for
functional or esthetic values so necessary for a growing child. Dr.
Wayne D. Kuettell, Covina, continued to supervise the childrens' optometry and visual needs as part of our health plan.
MASONIC PIONEERS 4-H CLUB

Mr. Val Dauc!hy continues to guide our children in their 4-H projects.
This is the seventh year that the Home's 4-H Club has received its
Charter and Achievement Seal. Each year the childrens' projects are
shown at the Annual San Gabriel 4-H Fair at Pomona and at the Los
Angeles County Fair in September. The Masonic Pioneers 4-H Club
maintains a herd of Registered Hereford breeding stock, as well as steer
projects for future shows and consumption. In addition the Club has
an outstanding herd of Registered Duroc Swine. The Club produced
and the Home consumed 3887 pounds of beef and 9058 pounds of pork
this past year.
VISITATIONS

During the past fiscal year over four thousand visitors were welcomed
to our Home. 'fihe many donations received this past year are greatly
appreciated and have brought additional happiness and enjoyment to
the children. The Lodges have responded very well in cooperating with
the Home's visitation program. Lodge or group visitations are the third
Sunday of each month. Reservations are taken for a maximum of four
hundred persons on this visitation Sunday, and Lodges may hold their
group visitation not oftener than once every two years. Picnic accommodations are available as well as guided tours by the children. Reservations must be made in advance and are taken in the order of their
receipt.
ALUMNI OF THE COVINA HOME

The second Sunday in September is dedicated to the observance of
of Covina Alumni Home Coming Day. All through the year the Alumni
visit the Home with their families reliving their younger days. The last
Alumni Reunion at Covina was one of the best attended. The Alumni
Dinner in San Francisco is always well attended with many from Southern California Alumni making special effort to attend. Invitations are
mailed to every Alumnus for whom we have an active address. Early in
January a copy of the Masonic Home Newsletter is mailed to each
Alumni, and to each Lodge sponsoring a child in the Home as well as to
Grand Lodge Officers.
In concluding this report I should like to express my sincere appreciation to the members of the Board of Trustees for their continued
guidance and counsel and to the Masonic Fraternity for this opportunity
of association with the fine young boys and girls who indeed are a source
of pride to the staff of your Covina Home Family.
Respectfully submitted.
ROBERT M. HENRY, Superintendent.

REPORT OF THE MASONIC HOMES
ENDOWMENT BOARD
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
It is a genuine pleasure to submit, herewith, the 24th Annual Report
of the Masonic Homes Endowment Board, covering the period from
August 1, 1955 to July 31, 1956 inclusive.
THE FOUNDATION

No building can be expected to be strong and stand throughout the
years without a firm foundation. It is our belief that your Masonic Homes
Endowment Fund has had a firm foundation. While the fund was created
by Grand Lodge in 1910, the Cornerstone, the establishment of the
Endowment Board, was not until 1933. Then by Constitutional Amendment, The Board was created ·and ·was charged with the responsibility of
dissemin'ating information about our Two Homes with the purpose in
mind that a fund of substantial amount should be builded to protect the
economics of these two great Masonic institutions, one for the children
at Covina, the other for older folk at Decoto.
In reviewing a 1933 report of the Most Worshipful Grand Master,
Frank W. Mixter, we note: "'It is my earnest hope that the Board shall
receive the active and hearty cooperation of all concerned to the end
that there shall eventually be brought up an Endowment Fund of truly
substantial proportions." Such was the hope and prophecy of this great
man. and such has been the realization. The Board as constituted consists of fifteen m~ers, five appointed each year for a period of three
years. The present board is constituted as follows:

Terms expiring 1956

1957

1958

The craft have given the Board marvelous support, and it is true
that a substantial amount of money has been builded into this fund.

60

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

It was no easy matter for that flrst Board under the leadership of that
great Mason, Brother W. P. Jeffries, to launch out into this new
endeavor. They had a purpose and a determination of accomplishment.
And so the pro!'.fram was launched in a splendid fashion. The next chairman, the Most Worshipful Past Grand Master, Frank M. Smith, carried
on in a magnifkant fashion. He rendered invaluable assistance to the
program and carried on for many years.
ERECTING OUR STRUCTURE

The Board has a wide distribution, so with this in mind, for the
last several years assignment of districts have been made to individual
Board members. They have served as liason officers to these particular
districts or areas and 'have worked with the Inspector, his duly representatives and others who have been particularly interested in the Endowment Fund program. We have found by placing such responsibility and
opportunities to individual Board members, our work has been much
more effective.
Since it was the responsibility of the Board to educate the craft,
the job was started and continued as a truly educational program. Outstanding representatives of the craft have given us their conception of
the Endowment Fund, the Homes. the opportunities and the responsibilities. These have been placed in pamphlet form and have been distributed in mass throughout the jurisdiction. They are concise, brief. easy
to read and have had a very wide distribution. Other methods have been
utilized for education regarding the homes, namely. 35mm. Kodochrome
slides covering the story and life at the two institutions. Our 16mm.
colored sound picture "The Extended Compass" has been well received
and given tremendous circulation. Its usefulness is not exhausted. New
members are coming into the craft, old members enjoy seeing it again,
allied organizations have been most interested and helpful in our program. The newly established Research Lodges have given great aid to
our program. We are deeply indebted for this assistance. In addition,
we have had a group of well informed speakers available for lodge meetings, not only our own Board members, but many others have rallied to
our aid. We are grateful for all of this help. The Most Worshipful Grand
Master, Edgar V. Stewart, Jr. has proven an invaluable cohert. He has
reminded the brethren of their opportunity and privilege to help in the
support of their homes. Your Board wishes to personally acknowledge
his complete cooperation. In addition, the hard working Inspectors have
had time to give us invaluable •assistance. To them. to the Master, to the
Chairman of the Endowment Fund Committees and to all others who
have assisted, we wish to personally acknowledge our grateful appreciation.
Your Board has seriously endeavored to follow the program as out-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

61

lined for them by Constitutional Amendment. We have endeavored to
individually and collectively tell the story and the privilege that is given
to members of the craft. It has been our purpose to use no coercion or in
any way exert a pressure program. Our work this year has been materially lessened by the helpful cooperation from the Secretaries. They
have mailed our very popular .. Stop/ Think/ and Consolidate/ notices to
the extent of some 75,000. Many like to send one check covering dues
and also their contribution to the Endowment Fund. By this method,
time, effort and money have been saved. We cannot over-estimate its
importance. We have diligently endeavored to keep our correspondence
up-to-date, acknowledge the many contributions, and the substantial
unusual contributions made by organizations and allied groups. We are
endeavoring to utilize a few pictures or graphs illustrating the important
features of the Endowment Fund. The old adage of one picture worth
a thousand words is particularly appropriate. We trust you will carefully
study these graphs as well as notating the important figures relative to
t!he fund. Our work has been a great pleasure, first because of the high
and lofty purpose, second, the unselfish devotion by so many members
of the craft cooperating with the Board throughout the year, and lastly.
the satisfaction that progress is being made and that we can hopefully
look forward to the realization as set forth when our course was chartered; our structure erected: and our progress noted throughout the years.
Cordially and sincerely,
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
ERNEST G. BASHOR, Chairman

72

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

APPOINTMENTS
The Grand Master announced the following appointments effective
for this Annual Communication:
Wm. C. Brouillard as Assistant Grand Lecturer in the absence of
Clare B. Campbell.
Emil W. Trefts to the Committee on Credentials in the absence of
Carroll A. Trefts.
Jesse M. Few to the Committee on Credentials in the absence of C.
Stanley Chapman.
Past Grand Master Arthur M. Warren to the Committee on Policy
and General Purposes.

RESOLUTIONS
Resolutions received at different times during the communication are
listed here for convenience of reference.
The Grand Secretary read the following resolutions which were
ref erred by the Grand Master to the Committees as noted:

ENTRANCE OF CANDIDATES
A resolution was presented by Santa Paula Lodge No. 291 with
reference to the ritualistic ,procedure in connection with the Entrance of
a Candidate.
The resolution was referred to the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes.

DISASTER RELIEF
To the Grand Lodge of California F.&A.M.
WHEREAS, the three principle tenets of Masonry: Brotherly Love, Relief
and Truth are universally recognized by Masons who strive
to uphold them, and
WHEREAS, we as Masons extend generous aid and relief to the mem~
hers, widows and orphans within our local Lodge jurisdictions
who are victims of poverty and distress, and,
WHEREAS, the Most Worshipful Grand Master has ruled that under
Sections 126 and 261 of our Ordinances, a local Lodge can~
not solicit its membership for the relief of members of neigh~
boring Lodges even in times of disaster, and
WHEREAS, that during the past year, within our jurisdiction, disastrous
floods have taken place causing great damage and loss of
life to many of our members and such events may happen
again,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

73

THEREFORE, be it Resolved that our Ordinances be amended so that
in times of major disaster when so declared by the National
or State Government or by the American Red Cross, Lodges

To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Whereas for more than thirty-five years. there have been in this
jurisdiction "Low Twelve Clubs" or "Widows and Orphans Funds,"
composed of Master Masons, organized to provide funds for the widows
a?d members of the families of Master Masons in good standing who
die, and
Whereas, the membership of these organization s involves several
t!h~usand Master Masons. and many Lodges under the jurisdiction of
this G~and Lodge, and they possess very sizeable trust funds and very
extensive moral obligations. and
Whereas, the Most Worshipful Edgar V. Stewart, Jr.• Grand Master of Masons in California, declared in 1his edict of December 30 1955
that "all Widows and Orphans Funds or Low-Twelv e Clubs or benefit
assessment organization s under any other name are without the bounds
of Masonic Law and must be discontinued and dissolved" and in his
~diet of March 2. 1956, extended the date af final dissolution thereof to
November 30, 1956, and
.Whe.reas, we are sensible botlh of the possibilities of abuse and harm
which 1lllght come ·from such benefit assessment organization s as well as
the great benefits to Masonry arising from them when conducted in
accordance with tlhe tenets of Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth.
Now, Therefore, Be It Resolved that the date of dissolution of such
benefit assessment organization s be extended to November 30, 1957, and
. ~e I.t Further Resolved that a Special Committee be appointed to
mquire into such benefit assessment organization s and to report to the
One. Hundred Eig~fh Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge concerning such bodies, and the financing, organization and regulation
thereof, and to recommend to said One Hundred Eighth Annual Communication the action to be taken thereon by this Grand Lodge.

To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California:
The undersigned respectfully submit the following Resolution:
That whereas we believe there is a sincere desire on the part of the
membership of our fraternity to participate in the relief accomplishe d
through the Widows and OrIYhans Funds, and/or Associations , and
Whereas these Association s have been functioning many years with
admittedly gratifying results, and
Whereas regardless of well laid plans, there comes the time in our
lives when we must leave all future family responsibilit ies and circumstances in the hands of those left behind, and
Whereas too often at this critical time sufficient and ready funds
are not available to take care of immediate needs, and
Whereas we believe that in the confines of the Grand Lodge members·hip there is the necessary ability and wisdom to bring forth workable
plans that will permit the functioning of Widows and Orphans Associations under reasonable regulations and rules,
Be it therefore resolved that Article 912 of the Edicts and Resolutions be amended to exclude references to Widows and Orphans Funds,
and that a committee be appointed to present a new amendment to our
By-Laws favorable to the operation of a regulated Widows and Orphans Fund, and/or Association within Masonic circles as a practical
application of our three great tenets: Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth.

W'hereas: Since 1922 it ,has been the proclamation of Grand Lodge,
that the members of the fraternity ·a re requested to lend their moral
and personal support to any chapter of the Order of DeMolay ... as a
method of carrying out the ideals embodied in teachings of the order."
(Sec. 520, Ross Digest); and
Whereas: In order to support the activities of DeMolay chapters,
Masons must be informed of the meetings of sueh chapters; and
Whereas: On the basis of Sec. 636, R.D., several Lodges have been
ordered to cease printing information in their trestleboards regarding
activities of the Order of DeMolay and other Masonic affiliated youth
organizations; therefore
Be It Resolved: That Sec. 636, R.D. be amended by the addition of
the sentence: "Nothing in this section shall be interpreted as preventing
such Lodges or concordant bodies from printing, for the benefit of tlheir
own members only, information regarding the leaders. meetings and
activities of the Order of DeMolay and similar Masonic affiliated organizations for girls."

PRAYER AT INSTALLATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of Calif omia.
We, the undersigned, members of Grand Lodge, respectfully present
the following resolution:
WHEREAS: One of the first lessons we are taught in Masonry
is that before entering upon any great or important undertaking, we
should first invoke the blessing of God. Certainly the installation of
officers of a constituent Lodge is a great and important undertaking.
WHEREAS: A prayer, delivered by a Brother, asking the Supreme
Architect of the Universe for guidance of these brethren during their
term of office, is bound to add solemnity to the occasion, and to inspire
these brethren to discharge their duties with fidelity and honor.
WHEREAS: This resolution is not inconsistent with the ceremonies used by our Grand Lodge, such as the Laying of Cornerstones,
Constitution of Newly Chartered Lodges, Dedication of Masonic
Halls, etc.
WHEREAS: This resolution is also consistent with the trend of
our whole United States of America, as we are constantly urged to
turn to prayer in our everyday life.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED: That the Installation
Services for Constituent Lodges be amended to include an appropriate

HAWAIIAN REPRESENTATIVE OF GRAND MASTER
The Grand Lodge of California first entered the Hawaiian Islands
in 1852 when it chartered Hawaiian Lodge No. 21. From that date,
Masonry in the Hawaiian Islands has gradually come under the influence of the Grand Lodge of California. The last Lodge to transfer to
California was Lodge Maui No. 472 in 1918. In 1924, the last of the
present existing Lodges in the Hawaiian Islands to be chartered by the
Grand Lodge in California was Pearl Harbor Lodge No. 598 in October 1924. There are now eight constituent Lodges located on the four
major Islands as follows: Oahu has at the present time, five Lodges and
the sixth Lodge is now in the process of being formed. Kauai has one
Lodge which is situated at Lihue, Kauai. Maui has one Lodge located
in Kahului, Maui and Hawaii has one Lodge, namely Kilauea Lodge,
located in the City of Hilo, Hawaii. Due to the distance of these Islands
from the seat of government of the Grand Lodge of California and the
geographical location of these Lodges and distance from each other,
separated by water, it •h as been impractical to have any uniformity in
ritual and administrative affairs, ·a nd
WHEREAS: The Lodges on the neighbor Islands being confronted by the fact that they do not receive proper and regular ritualistic instruction save only by the yearly visit of the Inspector and
WHEREAS: It would create greater unity in Hawaiian Masonry,
if the following resolution was adopted.
RESOLVED: That the present inspectoral Districts be abolished
and that an Assistant Grand Lecturer be appointed with jurisdiction
over all the eight Lodges, which together with an Officer's coach in eac'h
Lodge would have complete charge of all the esoteric work and
WHEREAS: T;h e representatives from the eight Lodges in the
Hawaiian group who are in attendance at Grand Lodge ea·ch Annual
Communication, in consideration of the distance that they travel. be

given by the Grand Lecturer each year with the understandi ng that they

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVE D: That a new section be added
to our organic laws which would enable the Grand Master, by virtue
of his authority to create the office of a District Deputy Grand Master

GRAN D MAST ER'S MESSA GE
EDGAR V. STEWART , JR., Grand Master

Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
Probably every man who is privileged to stand where I am standing
today does so with mixed emotions. There is a prayer in his heart that
his acts may be met with approbat ion by the brethren and that the
fraternit y might at least in some small measure have benefited from his
service. There is a ·fervent wish that the year had not gone quite so fast
that more might have been accomplished, but at the same time, a welcome anticipation of having the heavy mantle of responsibility soon to
be lifted from his shoulders. Then, too, he humbly recognizes what
a small cog he is after all in this mighty mac:hine and how importan t
every other cog is to the smooth operation of our Craft. To the many
hundred s of brethren who continue year after year to support and
sustain the Grand Master with their encourag ement and with their
friendship. ihe is anxious indeed to express his fervent thanks, well
realizing that his words are inadequa te to voice properly the innermost
feeling of his heart.
This •past Grand Lodge year, by reason of the fact that we met two
weeks late last year and three weeks early this year, is probably the
shortest Grand Lodge Year on record, consisting of exactly forty-seven
weeks, or almost ten per cent shorter than the normal year. By maintaining an increased tempo however, I believe the record will indicate
that there has been no sloughin g of the usual and customa ry activities
of the Grand Master or his official family, and it is indeed our heartfelt
hope that the record of this year's accomplishments here presente d,
may measure up to the highest ideals of the Craft.
SPECIAL CoMMUN ICATION s OP GR.l\ND LoDGE

During this Grand Lodge Year, it has been necessar y to open
Grand Lodge in Special Communications on forty-one different occasions.
The seventeen Lodges granted charters at our 1955 Communication
were duly constitut ed within five weeks from the close of our session,
each with its own individual ceremony. Two of these Lodges, I believe,
are worthy of special mention. Opportu nity Lodge No. 740 in Hawthorne is a daylight Lodge, the second one in the metropolitan Los
Angeles area. Claude H. Morrison Lodge No. 747 in San Diego was,
of course, named for our much loved Grand Master of 1943.
Grand Lodge was opened seventeen times for the laying of cornerstones for nine Lodge halls and eight schools, and seven additiona l
times for the dedication of newly completed Lodge halls.
On Saturday , May 5, 1956, I was schedule d to lay the cornersto ne
for the new Lodge hall in the town of Livingston in the San Joaquin

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

91

Valley. This is a six or seven hour drive from my home in Los Angeles
and I intended to get an early morning start for an early afternoo n
opening of Grand Lodge. To my constern ation however, I found that
during the night my car had been stolen from its garage stall and by the
time it was recovered just a few blocks away with the front end smashed ,
and all the necessar y police reports were made, it was evident I could
not make the cornersto ne ceremony in time. This was, I believe, the one
cornersto ne ceremony during the year when I was to be the only elected
Grand Lodge officer •present. It was also the only one I was unable to
make. I. therefore , called upon the ranking Grand Lodge officer, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Raymon d G. Taylor, to officiate for me on this
occasion, and by reason of this, waived the formality of opening Grand
Lodge. This makes the eighteen th cornersto ne ceremony however.
A chronological list of the openings of Grand Lodge with the occasions and the dates is shown in Exhibit "A".
NEW LoDGES

It is most gratifyin g indeed, and a source of much inspiration to note
the continual activity of the brethren in our jurisdiction in the formation of new Lodges. For the first six months of this Masonic year, no
requests for dispensations for new Lodges were received. Then, however, they came in rapid succession and between May 9th and this date,
eleven Lodges have been duly instituted.
In order not to delay the institution ceremonies any longer than
necessar y after granting the dispensations, I called upon Right Worshipful L. Harold Anderso n, Deputy Grand Master, to perform three
of them.
Two additional groups also have been granted dispensations but
so recently that time did not permit the institutio n ceremonies. In all,
therefore, thirteen new Lodges were formed this year. Two addition al
groups have been certified to me by the Grand Secretar y's office within
the past few days as being ready for consider ation of a dispensation, but
time has permitted no action to be taken prior to this Communication.
The names, locations and dates of the new Lodges as well as those
granted dispensations and awaiting institution are shown in Exhibit "B".
Two of the Lodges instituted have taken the names of Past Grand
Masters of California, Dana R. Weller Lodge in Gardena and William
Rhodes Hervey Lodge in Los Angeles. Inasmuch as your Grand Master
had many years of close Masonic association with these two distinguished brothers, it was no small thrill to authorize, and participa te in,
the ceremonies which should immortalize their names.
Despite the fact that this has been the second best of recent years
for the formation of new Lodges, you will be intereste d in knowing that
there are still nineteen groups througho ut the state working with assigned Inspectors toward the creation of new Lodges, eight such assignments having been made this year.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

An additional request recently received for permission to form a new
Lodge necessarily had to be handled quite differently from the usual, due
to the fact that it came from a group of regular Mexican Masons in Los
Angeles, who are asking for a charter for the establishment of a Spanish
speaking Lodge. This has been referred to the Committee on Policy
and General Purposes for their report.
DEDICATIONS

In addition to the dedication ceremonies of seven recently completed
Masonic Temples, Grand Lodge also was invited to dedicate three elementary schools and one junior high school.
On February 10th, Nelson Avenue School in Thermolito was dedicated by Right Worshipful L. Harold Anderson, Deputy Grand Master
and on April 27th, he performed the ceremony again for the Las Juntas
School in the Vine Hill area near Martinez. On April 23rd, I dedicated
the Ralph Smedley Junior High School in Santa Ana, and on April
27th, the dedication of the Orosi Elementary School in Orosi was in
charge of Right Worshipful Phil N. Myers, Junior Grand Warden.
These, together with the eight school cornerstones laid this year, g,ive'
ample evidence of our friendly relations with our public school authorities, and indeed, it is hoped that this activity will ever expand as our
Public Schools Committee still more firmly cements the cordial ties which
should ever exist between our fraternity and free public education.
On two occasions this year, Grand Lodge was asked to conduct a
dedication ceremony for a burial plot within a cemetery, for which we
have a brief but very beautiful ritual. This was performed for Valhalla
Cemetery in the San Fernando Valley on a beautiful sunshiny morning
on the 4th of February, with a most satisfactory crowd in attendance.
It was repeated on an equally nice afternoon on August 22nd, for the
Eternal Hills Cemetery in Oceanside.
On Saturday morning, April 14th, I was invited to be the speaker of
the morning at a most unusual dedication ceremony. On that day, the
Sacramento City Historic Landmarks Commission unveiled a plaque
at the corner of Fifth and "J" Streets in that city, marking the Pioneer
Masonic Site, the location of the formation of the Grand Lodge of California in 1850. Our own Past Grand Master, Leslie E. Wood, a former
Mayor of the City of Sacramento and now a City Councilman, was introduced. by the Historic Landmarks Commission who, in tum, presented the Mayor of the City and the Grand Master. It was a cold,
damp, threatening day which, undoubtedly, held the crowd to a minimum; but those who were there, and particularly our brethren, I am
certain, received the same thrill as did the Grand Master in having this
location marked for all to see, as the spot where the representatives of
a handful of Lodges in 1850 gave birth to what has now become one of
the great Masonic Jurisdictions of the world.

RECEPTIONS

While I was yet Deputy Grand Master I let it be known that should
I be elected to the office of Grand Master, I would not accept invitations
for receptions from individual Lodges except in Hawaii, but that I would
accept all the invitations to receptions that I possibly could coming from
Districts or groups of Districts. I also let it be known that I would not
accept invitations from concordant or appendant bodies, having a very
strong conviction that a Grand Master's time and efforts should be
devoted to Blue Lodge Masonry. My only exception to this was my
a-cceptance of a reception by my own Scottish Rite Bodies just ten
days ago.
I am happy to say that I have been able to accept all invitations
tendered to me from Districts and groups of Districts and out of tlhe
one hundred and sixty-six Ins.pectoral Divisions now in our jurisdiction,
I figure that my activities and travels this year have broug ht me in
contact with one hundred and forty of them or approximately eightyfour per cent of the total. Including the Lodgeroom receptions and the
District breakfasts, I have been received on fifty-two separate occasions,
not counting centennials or institutions, which have been enumerated
separately. At these affairs for the most part, I gave what I called a
workshop type of talk, which the brethren seemed hungry to receive,
telling of the plans, the hopes, the aspirations of Grand Lodge with its
various activities. These affairs without exception were marked by a
thrilling display of friendship and loyalty which this Grand Master will
dever forget. Gi'fts too, were showered upon him with such generosity
that it was almost embarrassing and to the many groups whioh received
no formal thank you letters from the Grand Master by reason of a lack
of time, I now extend my warmest appreciation for your many gestures
of friendship and assure you they will never be forgotten.
Appended as Exhibit "C" is a chronological list of the receptions
and breakfasts referred to.

HAWAIIAN VISITATION

After a welcome, restful five days aboard the Lurline in July, I paid
my visit to the eight most westerly Lodges in our jurisdiction, spending
fifteen days in all on four of the Hawaiian Islands. An official reception
was given me on each of the Islands and in that cordial fashion for
which they are justly famous. Much has been written by my predecessors
concerning not only the beauty of the Islands themselves but also the
hospitality of its people and I am indeed happy to say that none of it
has been exaggerated. Everywhere I went, the brethren outdid themselves, taking time off from their work to assist in sightseeing even to
the extent of several days trips at times. I was given a Luau or native
feast in magnificent style including native musicians and hula girls.
Thanks to many of our brethren in Pearl Harbor, the Navy too,
played host to me one morning and in addition to showing me many in-

PROCEEDINGS OP TH:a

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

teresting insta1lations, gave me a very fine tour of the harbor aboard
a Navy craft and permitted me and my party to alight on the platform
built over the sunken battleship Arizona where, on behalf of the fraternity, I laid an orchid wreath at the base of the monument there in
memory of the more than one thousand of our service men entombed
in this once proud giant of our fleet.
The Inspectors. our Junior Grand Steward, Milton E. Ba1lengee, and
the officers of the Lodges were most generous in their invitations to
their homes where I had the opportunity in an informal way of becoming better acquainted with that comparatively sma11 group of men
who are carrying more than their share of the burden of our fraternity
in the paradise islands of the Pacific. Needless to say, I sha11 never
forget the kindness shown me far beyond the call of duty and the many
friendships cemented during that visit.

CENTENNIALS

· Eight Lodges in the jurisdiction this year celebrated their centennials. By pre-arrangement I was able to attend each ci;lebration. In many
instances, of course, they were sma11 Lodges in remote areas which in
some cases had not had a visit from the Grand Master in years. Without
exception, these centennials were we11 attended, with visitors coming
from miles around. On some occasions they were community affairs with
historical displays open to the public and with the evening meeting free
to all who cared to come. The feeling prevailed that much good in the
way of public relations resulted from these anniversaries and surely it
was a gala :homecoming day for many oldtimers.
I was continually impressed by the fine caliber of young men found
to be officers of even the most out of the way of these one hundred
year old Lodges.
I also attended a most unusual affair which I believe deserves special
mention. It might well be termed the centennial of an extinct Lodge. You
will recall that last year, Forest Lodge No. 66 in Allegheny found it
necessary to surrender its charter in the one hundredth year of its
existence and to consolidate with Gravel Range Lodge No. 59 in Camptonville. Had it been able to continue its individual existence, it would,
of course, have celebrated its one hundredth anniversary. The brethren
of Gravel Range Lodge however, having already held their centennial.
in a truly Masonic spirit held a celebration this year which they called
the centennial of Forest Lodge and invited the Grand Master. He
happily accepted to lend ' the weight of his office to what he considered
a most thoughtful and brotherly act. We now have a Lodge in our
jurisdiction concerning which it can be said that it has held two centennial celebrations.
A list of these one hundredth anniversaries is appended as Exhibit

As is customary each February, the Conference of Grand Masters
of North America and the Conference of Grand Secretaries was held in
Washington, D. C. during the week of Washington's Birthday. California was represented by four delegates: Past Grand Master Arthur
M. Warren, who has been serving for several years as a member of the
Committee on Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges and who subsequently was elected Chairman of this important activity; our Grand
Secretary, Past Grand Master Lloyd E. Wilson; our Deputy Grand
Master, L. Harold Anderson (as the Deputies are also invited and
expected to attend) and your Grand Master.
California was honored by having its Grand Master elected Chairman of the Conference for the year 1956-57. Our Grand Lodge had not
been so honored since 1925, when our then Grand Master Randolph V.
Whiting, served in a similar capacity. Needless to say, it was a great
thrill for me to preside over such a distinguished group, as well as to
act as Master of Ceremonies at the annual formal banquet when all of
the Grand Masters invite their Masonic great with their ladies. Practically every man in the crowd of seven hundred and fifty would be a
proper head table guest at any civic or Masonic gathering any place
at any time, for in addition to the Masonic celebrities, we had present
many United States Senators, Congressmen, Supreme Court Justices
and Cabinet Members. California was proud to introduce as its guests,
the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, our own Past Grand Master
Earl Warren, our two United States Senators, William E. Knowland
and Thomas H. Kuchel, and the then Assistant Attorney General of the
United States, Stanley N. Barnes.
Our entire delegation also attended the annual meeting of the George
Washington Masonic Memorial Association in Alexandria, Virginia,
on February 22nd. The Grand Lodge of California at that time delivered
its check for $8,624 to be placed in the Endowment Fund. This represented the one dollar per capita on each new -applicant for the degrees
during the ·previous year. We are happy to report that the affairs of this
Association seem to be in better shape and under more competent and
active management than at any time in the past, and the final completion
of the project and its Endowment seem to be within sight. Every Mason
owes it to himself to visit this magnificent structure built to perpetuate
the memory of one who was indeed illustrious in Masonic as well as in
American history.

vthery gratef1,1l for the opportunity of attending the Communications of
e Grand Lodges of Washington and Colorado, the Centennial of the

Grand Lodge of Kansas, and the One Hundred and Seventy-Fifth
