have represented it in the past. An inter-jurisdictional visit is inevitably
an inspirational experience for one who bears the California credentials.
CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE

Probably no other project of Grand Lodge during this last year has
demanded more time and attention than the California Masonic Memorial Temple. Whereas, last year we reported that the plans were being
completed as rapidly as possible so that they could be put out to bid,
this year we can report that construction is well under way, and of
course, as you all know, the cornerstone of this magnificent structure
will be laid on Wednesday of this week in accordance with my proclamation of September 19th.
The Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple Corporation will make a report later in this Communication giving you t!he details of their very busy year's activity. These brethren have given hours
of their time and talents for your benefit and mine, for which we will
always owe them our sincere thanks. There are, of course, a multitude
of problems and responsibilities in connection with the erection of a
building costing in excess of $5,000,000 and we should be grateful indeed, that we have willing workers in our midst capable of properly
administering such an undertaking.
The continual outpouring of contributions from the brethren
throughout the jurisdiction has been a source of much satisfaction to
your Grand Officers as well as to the Memorial Temple Trustees. I
know that they are anticipating giving you the details in their report
and adding their appreciation to mine for your generous support of this
once-in-a-lifetime project which will further establish the leadershiip of
California Masonry.
RESEARCH COMMITTEE

For many years Grand Lodge has had a Committee on MasOnic Education. Because education seems to be a term from which some of the
. brethren shy, in more recent years this committee has been called the
Committee on Masonic Information. With whatever title t'hey may

97

have operated or wihatever size their budget, their efforts seemed to go
unrewarded as regards the gaining of the cooperation and enthusiasm
of the brethren.
As a result of the ardent labors of Grand Master Arthur Paulsen in
1950 and 1951 in promoting the idea of Research Lodges, Grand Master
Louis C. Drapeau the following year instituted the Northern California
Research Lodge and the Southern California Research Lodge, the first
such Lodges in California's history. T1his year those Lodges celebrated
their fifth birthday and while reports of their activities were most satisfactory and gratifying, I felt that with five years of experience behind
them, they could be of still more value to the membership as a whole, by
sharing with the entire jurisdiction the result of their years of study.
In lieu therefor, of continuing a Masonic Information Committee,
I replaced it with what I chose to call a Committee on Researdi. The
Committee is made up, and I should like to see succeeding Grand Masters follow the practice, of the Masters and Wardens of our two
Research Lodges, under the Chairmanship of a Past Master of one of
them, Brother Everett Houser of Long Beach.
Under his very vigorous and capable chairmanship, a research committeeman ihas been appointed in each Lodge, and each District has
committed itself for a minimum of one research program during the year.
The results of this activity have been nothing short of phenomenal
and as the Grand Master has traveled from one corner of the state to
the other, he has heard nothing but high praise for the brethren who
are engaged in this work and expressions of gratitude for the establishment of ways and means whereby all can know more of the history,
philosophy and symbolism of our Ancient Order.
This Committee on Research has arranged, and I might say with the
enthusiastic approval of the Grand Master, a program for this week,
which I hope will launch a new epoch in our research activity and indeed
become an annual 1feature of Grand Lodge. At the Masonic Temple at
25 Van Ness Avenue tomorrow night, over a three hour period, there
will be eighteen meetings which will be called "classes", under competent instructors. covering many phases of Masonic information and
education. This Research Seminar, for that is what it is called, will
enable every delegate to Grand Lodge to take back to his constituent
Lodge many new ideas as to the subject matter and method of presentation of a research program. Judging from the interest and enthusiasm
shown to date. I expect that this innovation Tuesday night will be one
of the greatest forward steps yet devised to bring to our brethren in a
practical manner the ty;pe of Masonic education and information which
~many ~ave been wanting. Yes, and these meetings will be your meetmgs. Questions will be invited and your participation welcomed.
I earnestly bespeak for my successors a continuation of tihe research

program, being fully convinced that as it becomes better established and
even more smoothly functioning, that we will have within our organiza~
tion a method of bringing to the membership at large the educational
background for which we have so long sought. My thanks to the many
members of the Research Committee and the Research Lodges who
through great sacrifices of time and effort on their part, have given a
mighty stimulus to the earnest brethren of our Craft who realize that
our ritual but scratches the surface and that there is much for us all to
learn about this time honored fraternity of ours.
GRAND LoDGE LIBRARY

Shortly after last year's annual Communication of Grand Lodge, I
was approached by the History Committee for permission to undertake
a task just a bit out of its line, but in which it was tremendously inter~
ested. I was reminded that the job might be done within the present
budget of the History Committee, being a very nominal one indeed, so
I gave them permission to proceed.

•

Their proposition was to index and catalog the books in our present
Grand Lodge Library. The History Committee, in the compilation of
its One Hundred Years of Masonry in California, became familiar with
the fact that we had quite an assortment of books on our shelves, some
of which were likely to be quite valuable. They also recognized the fact
that these volumes would be of far greater use to Masons at large if
they were properly catalogued and indexed. With permission granted
them to proceed, they have completed the task for which we are all duly
grateful. They have exceeded their budget by a few dollars, but I can
think of no better place to authorize an additional appropriation.
The approval of the Grand Master for this undertaking was given
readily because our research program this year has pointed up so clearly
the need for a Grand Lodge Library on Masonic and allied subjects.
Then, too, the Trustees of the Masonic Memorial Temple Corporation
have indicated the possibility of alloting certain unallocated space in our
new Masonic Memorial Temple for the use of a library.
In March, a very startling offer came in the form of a letter from
the Masonic Library of Southern California, Incorporated. This group
for more than sixty years has been maintaining a Masonic Library in
the City of Los Angeles. They are now however, formally offering to
Grand Lodge their entire library of several thousand volumes on the
following conditions:
"l. That the library remain permanently in Southern California and
open to all qualified Master Masons;
"2. That Grand Lodge obtain an adequate and convenient location
for the library in Los Angeles;

99

"3. That Grand Lodge assume the responsibility for compensating a
full time librarian and make a reasonable fund available for staff
assistance and maintenance;
"4. That the Masonic Library of Southern California be relieved of
all costs incidental to the acceptance of this offer."
My first inclination of course, was to accept this generous offer with
grateful thanks, knowing the crying need for a Grand Lodge Library in
Southern California to supplement the library in the north. On mature
deliberation however, it was recognized that certain costs and responsi~
bilities were involved, and I felt that Grand Lodge should be called upon
to decide whether or not it wanted to enter into a comprehensive library
program.
Brother John Bond, President of the Hollywood Masonic Temple
Association, in whose Temple the Southern California Research Lodge
meets, immediately came forth with an offer to provide proper housing
space in the Hollywood Masonic Temple, with no rental for the space
involved .
The Chairman of the Grand Lodge Committee on Research, Brother
Everett Houser, in a letter says that they "have been besieged with
requests for books and research material." They are, of course, intensely
interested in furthering the establishment of a Grand Lodge Library
within the state, to say nothing about the possibility of having two, one
in the north and one in the south.
It goes without saying I am sure, that the need for library facilities
has become more apparent with the advent of our active research pro~
gram. A library is practically a necessity if we expect to reach the
heights to which our present research program can carry us if properly
supplemented with library facilities.
The Masonic Library of Southern California is, of course, anxious
to receive, and is entitled to, an answer as to whether or not we will
accept their proposition made last March. Your Grand Master is of the
opinion that this is a golden opportunity for Grand Lodge to inaugurate
a library program consisting at the moment of two locations, one in
Los Angeles and one in San Francisco, where our Research Lodges are
located. I, therefore, recommend that my successor in office appoint a
Board of Library Commissioners, five in number, authorized and em~
J>owered to accept from the Masonic Library of Southern California,
on terms mutually agreed upon, their entire library, to become a part of
the library of the Grand Lodge of California, and that they be charged
with the responsibility of doing everything necessary to move, index
and catalog the library, place it in a proper location and operate it on a
ICale acceptable to the Grand Master, and for this activity, there be ap~
propriated from the fonds of Grand Lodge, the sum of $8,000 to cover
the necessary expenses involved. Further, that this Board work with the

REVISION OP Ross DIGEST

In 1953, Grand Master Arthur M. Warren appointed a Commission
on the Revision of Ross Digest. At the Grand Lodge Communication of
that year, the Commission made its first report in which are to be found
the following statements: "All law is in a constant state of change and
the books that record it must keep pace with these changes so that they
may be found and understood by those who need them. New questions
arise that bring forth amendments and new problems result in far
reaching decisions and interpretations, and this is as true of Masonic
Law and Masonic Law Books as of all others. No law book is of enduring
value unless it is revised from time to time and adapted to existing needs.
The ipresent Digest has served its purposes during a period when the
State has doubled in population and when Masonry has developed at a
corresponding .pace". "We should, to the extent possible, have a law
book written for laymen rather than for lawyers."
After several years of consecrated work, the Commission made a
very complete and detailed report at the 1955 Communication, and made
the recommendation that Grand Lodge authorize the publishing of the
new California Masonic Code Annotated, upon the approval of the
Grand Master, the Judge Advocate and the Chairman of the Jurisprudence Committee.
I am happy to report that the new book is in type and that we have
galley proofs of its contents, which are being carefully checked and rechecked by proper, competent persons. We have deliberately held up
the publication of the much needed volume so that we could incorporate
in it at the last minute any changes in our law that might develop during
this session.
This project has been no small task, brethren, and to Brother William Nankervis, Jr. and his righthand man, Brother Everett Houser, who
between them carried the lion's share of the responsibility, and to the
other members of the Commission, we owe a tremendous vote of appreciation. Our thanks should also extend to our Judge Advocate, Henry C.
Clausen, and to all the members of the Jurisprudence Committee for their
invaluable assistance and advice.
It is recommended that Grand Lodge authorize the publication of the
California Masonic Code Annotated.
SUPPLEMENTAL APPROPRIATIONS

Each year the Grand Master is called upon to approve extraordinary
expenditures as well as those in excess of budgeted appropriations. This
year, of course, has been no exception and I have approved payments
in excess of the budget for the History Committee (for their library
work), Ross Digest Revision Commission and the Memorial Temple
Committee. The costs of our Ground Breaking Ceremony also had to be
paid and then there were items of publicity for Grand Lodge events,

additional costs of the 1955 Grand Lodge Communication, a modest and
long overdue increase in the Grand Tiler's remuneration additional
insurance premiums and excess payments for printing, ~ostage and

knowledge and consent of the Finance Committee.
. I~ is m~st gratifyi?g to note that most of the committees operated well
withm their appropriations and that for the most part the budget prepared by the Finance Committee was extremely realistic.
Pursuant to a r~solution passed in Grand Lodge in 1952, a grant of
$10,000 wa~ n:iade m March of 1953 to both Tehachapi and Maricopa
Lodges to aid m the reconstruction of their Temples destroyed by earthquake.
.In October of 1953, Tehachapi Lodge requested additional financial
assi~tance and Grand Lodge passed a resolution providing that the incoming Grand Master, the Chairman of the Committee on Finance and
the Chairman of the Committee on Lodge Financing, be authorized to
extend ~uch ~ssis~a~ce to ~he brethren of Tehachapi and Maricopa
Lodges m their bmldmg pro1ects as it may in their judgment be decided

In December of 1955, Maricopa Lodge also requested an additional
$~.000 to be used toward completing their Temple. After consulting
with. the two Grand Lodge Committee chairmen whose approval was
requi~ed an~ after personally inspecting the building project, we were
unanimous m approving the additional grant of $5,000, as it appeared
that the intent o.f Grand Lodge was to treat these two groups equa11y.
On November 7, 1955, a communication was received from the Grand
Lodge of Tamaulipas, Mexico pleading for financial assistance for the
brethren there, due to the devastation of the city of Tampico by a hurricane in September. The appeal apparently was sent to all of the Grand
Lodges in the United States and probably was heeded by them all. The
Grand Lodge of California, ever mindful of the distresses of the less
fortunate, immediately forwarded $1,000 to our stricken Latin-American
brethren upon the authorization of the Grand Master and the Grand
T~easurer for which we have received a most cordial letter of appreciation.
INSURANCE COMMITTEE

For years the Grand Secretary's office has undertaken and been
charged with the responsibility of the writing of insurance on Grand
!-edge properties, and in more recent years, compensation and liability
insurance as well as fidelity bonds for the constituent Lodges.
Br: reason of our continually expanding jurisdiction and the rapidly
changing and complex insurance contracts available, this task has asswned proportions which, in my opinion, require the advice and as-

sistance of men well versed in that field in order to assure Grand Lodge
that its insurance position is at all times adequate and proper.
The building of the California Masonic Memorial Temple also poses
many insurance problems concerning which the advice of experienced
men is essential to proper planning.
With the assistance of Deputy Grand Master, L. Harold Anderson,
who located the brethren for me here in the northern part of the state,
I have appointed an Insurance Committee of two qualified men, neither
of w:hom has any financial interest in the sale of insurance contracts, the
one, Brother T. James Carlile, Past Master of Oak Grove Lodge No.
215 of Alameda, who is a buyer of insurance and an assistant vicepresident of a bank, and the other, Brother Allerton B. Ebert, Past Master of East Bay Lodge No. 489, Berkeley, who is an insurance company
executive.
I trust that my successors in office may see flt to continue this committee, which is purely an advisory one, for assistance in solving the many
insurance questions which may arise from time to time in connection with
our valuable property holdings.

Music CoMMITTEE
A special Music Com•mittee was appointed this year consisting of
Harold Mueller, Grand Organist, Austin Mosher, Director of our Grand
Lodge Music and Arthur M. Warren, Past Grand Master.
The Memorial Temple Directors early in the year requested the appointment of such a committee to advise concerning the size and type of
organ and console and other musical needs to be installe~ in ?ur new
California Masonic Memorial Temple. Then too, the Cahforma Freemason in its Autumn issue of 1955 invited our musically inclined brethren to compose a Memorial Temple March such as was apparently done
when we first occupied the Temple at Post and Motgomery Streets in
San Francisco in 1863. In the past few months a number of compositions
·h ave been received by the California Freemason office, and I have asked
the Music Committee to obtain the assistance of music critics and to
consider making an award at the proper time to the composer of the most
fitting and acceptable march, commemorating our new Memorial Temple.

On Monday, May 7, 1956, I attended the Centennial of Clay Lodge
No. 101, in Dutch Flat. While there I learned that illness had prevented
the attendance that evening of a Past Grand Master who had always
been very close to Clay Lodge. On the day following, I routed myself
out of the mountains by way of Nevada City, the home of our Most
Worshipful George L. Jones, Grand Master in 1926-1927. Incidentally,
he was elected to the office of Grand Master on the occasion of my first
attendance at a Grand Communication. I made an unannounced call at
his home to pay him my respects. I found him fully dressed, including
collar, necktie and coat and sitting in the living room of his home taking
care of his personal accounts. Despite the fact that he was not at all up
to par, he had his radiant smile for me as he had for all, and seemed to
be highly elated to have the Grand Master visit. I shall always be grateful for this call because on June 22, 1956, our distinguished brother
passed on. Masonic services were conducted by Madison Lodge No. 23
in Grass Valley on June 26, 1956.
For Chairman of the Sojourners Committee, I had appointed a
brother for whom I had the highest fraternal esteem. Brother Harry P.
Ritchie was admired by m'any for his ability to get things done. Shortly
after his appointment however, he was stricken ill and was never able
to function in his official capacity, and on May 3, 1956, we permanently
lost his services.
Brother Leonard R. A villa of the Homes Endowment Board and
Brother Miles J. McClelland, Inspector in the Sacramento area, were
the other two members of the "family" who were unable to complete
the tasks assigned to them this year.
There was another passing this year which I feel I should mention.
While this brother was not serving in an official capacity at the time, he
had served this Grand Lodge both as an Inspector and as an appointed
Grand Lodge Officer. Brother Martin G. DeHaan had served at one
time as Inspector of my Lodge, prior to my own appointment, and in
fact, was present the night that I was raised to the sublime degree of
Master Mason.
Each of these esteemed brethren will be properly eulogized during
our Necrology Service on Wednesday morning.

NECROLOGY

Most of the brethren do not realize that one of the first tasks confronting a Grand Master-elect is the appointment of approximately four
hundred and fifty officers, committeemen, board members and inspectors.
With this large family of official workers in addition to twenty Past
Grand Masters, it seems to be necessary to report to you each year
through the Necrology Committee, the passing of a few of our most
faithful brethren. We are grateful indeed, that it is just a few, in fact
four in number who were currently serving Grand Lodge.

PERSONAL MENTION

You will remember that in 1953 there was created by action of this
Grand Lodge a Grand Lodge office to be known as Judge Advocate.
There was no appointment made to that office following the 1953 Session
nor was there any appointment made in 1954. It was therefore, my opportunity to appoint California's first Judge Advocate and to this office
I appointed a man who had been actually fulfilling the duties of such
office although holding a higher station in the Grand Lodge line. Our
Junior Past Grand Master, Henry C. Clausen, has been of inestimable

help ·to me in doing a tremendous amount of research work in connection
with the decisions rendered this year, and I owe him a debt of gratitude

In 1920, Grand Master Charles Albert Adams, issued the first Public
Schools Week Proclamation. Since that time, Public Schools Week has
grown into an important, statewide observance, not only among the
Masonic Lodges, but it is indeed, an integral part of the public school
program. No one can deny that the inauguration of this activity was
a step which has been of great benefit to our California school systems
as well as being something about which the Masons of California may
be justly proud.
The myriad of friends of our beloved Past Grand Master, Charles
Albert Adams, were overjoyed in learning very recently, that there is
a public school on the drawing boards to be erected in the near future
in Richmond. California, which is to be known as the Charles Albert
Adams School. Indeed, no one is more deserving of this signal honor and
we rejoice to see our distinguished brother so remembered. Recognizing
the fact that these things do not just happen, we also extend our thanks
to those unknown brethren who undoubtedly have been influential in
seeing that this recognition so long deserved has come to our brother,
and we hope that those same thoughtful and hardworking brethren will
see to it that the Grand Lodge of California is asked to lay the cornerstone of the school and to dedicate it, thus giving us additional opportunities to pay homage to this great Mason and citizen.
On August 8, 1956, I attended a meeting of Starr King Lodge
No. 344 in San Francisco on what they called "Wollenberg Night."
That evening I had the extreme pleasure of presenting to our beloved
Grand Master of 1929-1930, our traditional fifty-year emblem, the only
Past Grand Master to be so honored during the year and the sixth of
our living Past Grand Masters to be similarly invested.
Brother Wollenberg was also remembered that night by the Trustees
of the Masonic Homes with which he has been closely identified since
1917. Past Grand Master Charles Albert Adams, a veteran Trustee
himself. presented to Brother Wollenberg on behalf of all the Trustees
of the Masonic Homes, a magnificent scroll commemorating the occasion
and lauding him for his many decades of ardent and enthusiastic service.
No more gracious .presentation could have been made, and knowing. as
practically everyone present did, of the long standing friendship between
these "two Charlies" as they are affectionately called, this portion of
the evening was one not to be forgotten.

COMMERCIAL ISM

At our 1954 Annual Communication, the Grand Lodge Committee on
Publications, this year known as the Grand Lodge Committe.e on Commercialism, suggested a resolution wthich was adopted unammously by
Grand Lodge.
.. . .
.
That resolution authorized the Grand Master to institute action
in the courts of the State of California on behalf of the Grand Lodge
F. & A. M. of the State of California, to establish that its name and the
words, Mason, Free Mason, Free & Accepted Mason, Masonry and
Masonic and Masonic symbols and emblems shall not be used for fraudu..
lent purposes or for private gain or profl t • .•

112

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

At our 1955 Communication Grand Master Clausen reported that
he had filed four suits in the Superior Court of California for that
purpose.
Three suits are still .p ending. but on April 4, 1956, the San Francisco
Superior Court handed down a decision in our favor against the Masonic
World Publishing Company and its owner. the full text of which is
appended as Ex.hibit "I".
Summarizing. the court has very definitely established our right to
the names Mason and Masonic and the emblems and symbols, so that
they cannot be used for fraudulent putposes or for private .gain.
In addition to this, three new sections of the Corporation Code have
been adopted by the California legislature which permits the court to
enjoin the unauthorized use of the insignia and the name in commercial
ventures. etc .• so that today, as a result of long and arduous work on
the part of our Gmnd Lodge Committee on Commercialism and helpful
Masonic attorneys who were prominently involved, we have better legis#
lative and judicial tools at our disposal, to regulate the activity of those
few brethren who would use their Masonic affiliatioq for fraudulent
purposes and private gain, than ever before. Consequently, it is to be
expected that this evil whkh was so prevalent a few years ago may be
expected to diminish rapidly and eventually disappear. Our everlasting
thanks to our Judge Advocate, our Committee on Commercialism and
our many legal friends wfho worked with us to stamp out this blot on
the escutcheon of Free Masonry in California!
BUILDING AND LoAN INVESTMENTS

Immediately following our Communication of last year. I received
many inquiries as to the exact status of our regulations regarding Build~
ing and Loan Association investments. On November 15th, therefore.
I addressed the following letter to all of the Lodges:
"Grand Master Clausen, during ihis term. ruled that state and federal
building and loan associations are not proper investments for Masonic
Lodges, and Grand Lodge approved the decision.
"Resolutions which would have made such investments legal were
not adopted by Grand Lodge. as they failed to get the required five#
sixths majority vote. They did, however, receive a majority vote and
under Section 28 of our Constitution the proposition will lie over for
one year, being published with the Proceedings, and at the next sue#
ceeding Annual Communication be again broug:h t to vote, at which
time it may be passed by a two~thirds majority and henceforth become
a part of the Constitution.
"t therefore, direct that Grand Master Clausen's ruling be observed
in all future investments, but that such Lodges as now have investments
in building and loan associations need not necessarily dispose of them
until the decision of Grand Lodge is made final after carrying out the
procedure outlined in Section 28."

FLOOD RELIEF

Immediately following the disastrous floods in the northern part of
our state during Christmas week of 1955, I asked the Grand Secretary
to communicate with t:he Inspectors of the Lodges in the stricken areas.
assuring them that should it be necessary, Grand Lodge would lend
its aid and assistance to the Lodges wiho might be called upon to provide
food, clothing and shelter for stricken Masonic families, beyond their
ability to respond.
Great credit is due the Lodges in the area for almost without
exception, reports came back to us that, while many of the brethren and
their families were hard hit, the situation was well in hand and that
they were asking no ·help from Grand Lodge. This is not to say that
many of the brethren did not suffer greatly from the loss of their busi#
nesses, their homes, their possessions; but it is to say that their pride,
courage and ingenuity gave them the initiative indeed to Ii.ft themselves
up by their own bootstraps and to start to build anew. We, of course,
have ·heard many stories of generosity on beJhalf of our members
toward their stricken brethren-many tales of 'h eroism-but the most
thrilling of all concerns the spirit of those who suffered the greatest
losses. In true Masonic fashion, they proved themselves to be intrepid
builders and to them we doff our hats I
DEATH BENEFIT CLUBS

On December 30, 1955, I directed a letter to all Inspectors which
read as follows:
"Section No. 912 of Ross Digest which has been part of our law
since 1932 expressly forbids a Lodge from sponsoring Widows and
Orphans Funds. The first paragraph of Section 127 implements the
Decision of 1932.
"Decision No. 61 of Past Grand Master Clausen, concurred in by
Grand Lodge in October, 1955, states in part, 'Your attention is invited
to the provisions of Masonic Law prohibiting Lodges from engaging in
collateral financial undertakings, including sponsoring widows and
orphans funds . . (R.D.912).' 'A club, controlled or operated by or
throug·h a Lodge, in reality is the Lodge itself. Hence, what the Lodge
may not do directly, it may not do indirectly through a club.'
"In view of these two approved Decisions which are now our law,
I am obliged to declare tihat all Widows and Orphans Funds or Low
Twelve Clubs or benefit assessment organizations under any other name
are without the bounds of Masonic Law and must be discontinued
and dissolved.
"It has come to my attention that a number of Lodges have such
a club and sometimes a District, a group of Lodges or several Districts
are joined together in such a dub. This directive applies to all such
organi:retions existing for the purpose of providing payments to families
of deceased brethren by means of assessments on dub members.

"Where such organizations exist in your Districts, please see to it

been discontinued and describing the steps taken to dissolve the organization. The operation of such an organization beyond June 30, 1956,
will be deemed a Masonic offense."

As I expected there have been presented to Grand Lodge a number
of resolutions all pointing toward the legalizing of Death Benefit Clubs

still greater number have passed out of existence due to the unsound
basis upon which this type of assessment organization is usually founded.

DISPENSATIONS DENIED

A dispensation was requested from a Los Angeles County Lodge to
authorize them to hold their September Stated Meeting at the hour of
6:00 P. M. instead of 7:30 P. M. as required by the by-laws. The purpose of this request was "to permit the Committee of arrangements for
the Constitution Month program to better organize the event."
I advised that, in my opinion, the Grand Master did not have the
authority to issue such a dispensation. I further stated that "Dispensations may be granted for certain purposes only and these purposes are
set forth in our Constitution. The Grand Master may exercise his discretion in an emergency when there seems to be no other solution and
I believe Grand Lodge would back him to the limit under such circumstances. I see absolutely no reason however, why your Constitution
Month Observance has to be on the evening of your Stated Meeting.
A Stated Meeting of the Lodge is the Lodge's most important meeting
and should not be subordinated to any other meeting as important as
~s the Constitution Month Observance. There are other meeting nights
m the month when your Observance may be appropriately celebrated.
Your request for a dispensation therefore, must be denied."
A Los Angeles Lodge requested a dispensation to open Lodge in
another nearby Temple for the purpose of an open installation of officers.
. I declined to issue this dispensation as I do not feel that the provision
m our law empowering the Grand Master to issue such dispensations
contemplates their use in this type of case. To me, dispensations are
a means that the Grand Master has at his disposal to give much needed
relief in hardship cases and for emergency relief only.
Tihe sole excuse given in this request for a dispensation was the

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

117

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

inconvenience, including the parking problem, of moving from one hall
to another after opening Lodge in the regular hall which is the recommended way of accomplishing their purpose. I do not believe that this
is too much to ask the brethren to do once a year if they desire to have
a big public installation.
RECOMMENDATION

No. 1

During my thirty years as a member of Grand Lodge, I repeatedly have heard of the long hours spent by various committees during
our session preparing reports for Grand Lodge on the many pieces of
legislation brought before it each year. There is rarely a proposition
which escapes either the Jurisprudence Committee or fhe Policy and
General Purposes Committee. It is necessary therefore, for these two
committees to meet practically the entire Grand Lodge Week, not only
during the hours when you and I are enjoying the session but on many
occasions late into the night.
Because of the rush and the pressure under whifh these men are
obliged to work, it not infrequently happens that Grand Lodge adjourns
with some important piece of legislation still pending. Possibly we may
have approved the policy and have had no legislation enacted to implement it, as has happened several times recently. This creates unnecessary
confusion among the brethren, and, indeed, should not happen in such
a well regulated Grand body as ours.
It therefore, occurs to me and many others who have given the
matter serious thought, that a much more orderly process of initiating
legislation in our Grand Lodge would be to require that any proposition
to receive Grand Lodge action at an annual Communication must be
received in the Grand Secretary's office not later than ninety days prior
to the opening date of Grand Lodge. This would permit it to be sent
to the constituent Lodges within the sixty-day period now in vogue
and give the committees involved plenty o.f time to consider carefully
all of its ramifications. It would preclude any legislation being considered
that was received after that date, such proposition having to wait until
the next annual Communication of Grand Lodge.
As a safety measure, of course, such legislation should provide that
Grand Lodge could vote to consider any proposition on the vote of fivesixths of those present, regardless of when it was brought in. I have
given to the Jurisprudence Committee and the Policy and General Purposes Committee notice of t!his proposal with the hope that they will
be prepared to bring this proposition before you at this session that it
might be voted into our law to assure a smoother and more thorough
operation of our necessarily complex legislative procedure.
RECOMMENDATION No. 2
Section No. 53 of the Ordinances of Grand Lodge describes the
duties of an Inspector. T he last line of this Section r~adi? as follows:
0

"Each Lodge shall pay such necessary expenses of the Inspector as may
be incurred in the visitations herein required."
For some time this Section has been obsolete inasmuch as the Inspectors' expense accounts are paid by Grand Lodge after properly being
reviewed.
iln this far flung jurisdiction of ours, the Inspectors sometimes are
many miles from certain Lodges over which they have jurisdiction and
in such instances, it is most often true that those Lodges in the faraway
places can least afford to pay the Inspectors' expenses. Inasmuch as
these visitations mentioned are required by Grand Lodge, it seems only
proper that Grand Lodge pay them as it has been doing for many years
in the past. In order that there may be no confusion on this point as
has arisen from time to time, I would recommend the repeal of the last
line of Section No. 53 as above quoted. W1henever our law conflicts
with what has become accepted practice, I believe our law should be
changed to comply with t'he practice and that the law be declared
obsolete.
RECOMMENDATION No. 3
Having had firsthand experience this year with Masonic trials and
noting some of the results, I am convinced that at least some improvements could be made in our trial procedure and possibly, it might be
entirely revamped and simplified. For this purpose, I recommend that
the incoming Grand Master appoint a special committee of brethren
experienced in this field to report their findings and recommendations
to Grand Lodge next year.
DECISION No. 1
The question was asked whether a brother could reimburse a Lodge
for the cost of a trial without violating any Grand Lodge regulations.
I ruled that he could. Inasmuch as Section No. 313 of Ross Digest
provides that it is the obligation of the Lodge to shoulder the costs of
a trial, I suggested that the Lodge do so and then accept reimbursement
by t!he brother. Section No. 157 of Ross Digest provides that funds may
be used for any specified purpose when received by the Lodge in trust
for such purpose.
DECISION

No. 2

One of our Lodges makes it a :practice to send annually to its members a Roster naming the Lodge officers and the members of the Lodge.
It has included in the past a list of Entered Apprentices and Fellowcraft
Masons and tihe Inspector quite properly questioned so doing.
'I ruled that it is improper to list any but Master Masons. We have
a ruling against publishing the names of candidates for the degrees.
Some of our Lodges have very few degrees during the year, never more
than one Fellowcraft and one Entered Apprentice. Should we permit
the publication of a Roster including the names of the Fellowcraft and
Entered Apprentices, it would be tantamount to announcing the name

DEc1s10N

No. 7

I was asked by a District Inspector to rule on the following question:
"May the Master or Wardens, being present or absent, request a Warden. Past Master or other qualified brother to open and preside at a
Stated Meeting?"
In connection with this question, I also was asked to define the meaning of the word "presiding", as used in Section No. 772 of Ross Digest.
My answer was as follows:
fo order for a Lodge to open, it is necessary, of course. for the Master
or one of 1:!he Wardens to be present. He must also remain in the Lodgeroom during the time it is open. A Lodge must never be left without a
Master or Warden being present. This would imply that the ranking
officer is the officer in charge of the meeting whether or not he is seated
in the East and "presiding". Inasmuch as it is his prerogative to remove
tihe presiding officer, he is actually the one who is "presiding", or in other
words in charge. A·s long as a Master or Warden remains present. he
may invite any qualified brotlher to assume the Master's chair and confer
degrees or transact business. As respects a Stated Meeting for the transaction of business, it would be a most unusual case which would suggest
the propriety of such action.
In my opinion, the presiding officer is always the ranking Master or
Warden without whose presence the meeting could not be held, regardless of his position in the Lodgeroom.
DEc1s10N

No. 8

A question was posed regarding the propriety of a Masonic Lodge
participating in a parade, and also, the sponsoring of a Boat or vehicle
with Lodge funds.
I held that a Lodge cannot participate in a parade except with a
dispensation from the Grand Master, as Ross Digest, Section No. 124,
very clearly indicates. While this Section specifies parading in Masonic
clothing in its prohibition, the implication is surely there that it applies
to any Lodge of Masons, regardless of aprons.
I further 'held that the funds of a Lodge may not be expended for a
parade Boat, inasmuch as our laws specifically state the purposes for
whicli the funds may be used, and by no stretch of the imagination, can
the term "fraternal intercourse" be interpreted to allow expenditures of
money under this provision for suC'h purpose.

w

DEOSION No. 10
Shortly after the foregoing Decision was made, I received another
~~tter from _the MC}ster of the ~ame Lodge who put this question to me,
Is an applicant for the degrees elected if there being present at time of
balloting thirty-six members, but only twenty-nine voted as shown by
the count of balls, there being no cubes?"
My reply was as follows:
"T'he balloting for the_ degrees of Masonry is strictly a secret ballot,
not a. recorded ballot. Aside from the three officers whose duty it is to
examine the ballot box, no one is entitled to know the number of votes
cast for or against an a'Pplicant. No one therefore, has the right to count
the number of ballots and compare them to the number of members
present.
"It is the duty of a Master of a Lodge to see to it that his members
Vote. ~n the o~her hand, he cannot make sure that they do actually
depoS1t a ballot m the box. On some occasions when there is an unusually
large crowd present at a stated meeting, there may not be ballots
enough. for everyon~ present and many of the brethren may go through
~motions of ~alloti?g without a~tually ~epositing a ball or cube. While
not c~ndoning this method of voting , it sometimes becomes a matter
b!eexpediency, To my knowledge, the validity of such a ballot has never
n questioned, assuming of course, that there are the proper number

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

of cubes in the box as there should be in every properly prepared ballot
box. If no negative vote appears and the Master has seen to it that all of
his members have 'voted', it is quite proper to announce the 'unanimous'
election of the candidate.
"You have seen fit to refer to my Decision relative to the amendment
of the by-laws of your Lodge and imply that you are attempting to apply
the Decision to the balloting for new members.
"May I call your attention to the fact that there are two separate and
distinct methods of voting. That of balloting upon the applicants is
strictly a secret affair, while that ballot required for the changing of the
by-laws is •a recorded vote, the law on which was quoted you in my
Decision.
"The answer to your question is, yes, the candidate is elected and
in t'he same breath it seems proper to remind the Master that the ballot
is a secret one and is not subject to 'audit' other than as specifically provided for in our law."

122

CONDITION OP THE CRAFT

With the rapid growth of this golden state of ours, it is only natural
and proper to expect a comparable expansion of our fraternity within
our far flung jurisdiction. While it cannot be said that the growth of our
fraternity is keeping pace with our phenomenal rise in population, nevertheless it can be said, that both as to the number of Lodges and the
number of Masons, we are at an all time high and have shown a very
healthy and substantial increase during the past year. Numbers alone,
of course, do not build a fraternity, but the continual voluntary knocking
at our doors on the part of the uninitiated does indicate that those who
wear the square and compass are letting their light shine and are encouraging many by their lives and their actions to seek admission into
our ancient Order. The response of the brethren as shown by the many
Lodges on the Honor Roll for the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund,
and the Merit Roll for the California Masonic Memorial Temple, evidences a growing support of all Grand Lodge activities and is appreciated indeed by your Grand Lodge Officers.
This year has been a most productive one when, in retrospect, we
note that since our last Communication, in addition to the multiplicity
of our usual activities, we have actually started the building of the
California Masonic Memorial Temple, and, within this week, will lay
its cornerstone: we have inaugurated a Research Program and a Research Seminar which promises to eclipse all previous educational
efforts: we have practically ready for our printer our new California
Masonic Code Annotated which has long been a crying need: we have
awarded the first Masonic Scholarships and thus cemented more firmly
than ever our cordial relationship with our public schools: and we have
achieved through the due process of law, a method and means of dealing
with those who would commericalize our institution for their private

123

CONCLUSION

W, ere I to attempt properly to thank every Grand Lodge officer and
committeeman to whom I owe a debt of gratitude for making this year
what it has been, I indeed, would have to name them all. So that I do
not overlook any, I will mention none, but say, with the utmost sincerity,
to ~very member of m.y official "family", that I shall never forget the
assistance, the .court~s1es and the friendship extended to me by everyone of you durmg this, my most memorable Masonic year.
. To you ~ret~ren ~h~se suffrages have given me the unequaled privilege of servmg m this highest Masonic office, I express my unbounded
thanks for your confidence and for your support.
Brethren, the world has need of Masonry. It needs our organized
support of free public education. It needs our love for, and adherence to
the principles involved in the Constitution and the Bill of Rights. It need~
our steadfastness to the principle of the separation of church and state.
I~ needs our serious and solemn lessons of the brotherhood of all mankind and the fatherhood of God.
Yes, Masonry itself is a vital necessity for the preservation of our
American democratic way of life, and every brother who has put his
shoulder to the wheel of this great Craft of ours this year, may enjoy the
~nner satisfa~tion ~f knowing that he has helped to hold aloft the light
bf. Truth which will eventually permeate earth's darkest recesses and
~mg to us the ~eace we all seek. For the continued advancement of our
ti loved fraternity, let us ever remember and always heed that admonion from the Sermon on the Mount which seems to have been written
especially for us.
"Ye are the light of the world ... Let your light so shine
befo.re men that they may see your good works, and
glorify your Father which is in heaven."

Grand Master

EXHIBIT "H"

December 29, 1955
Mr. Walter C. Guy, Imperial Potentate
1000 Center Street
Little Rock, Arkansas
Illustrious Sir and Dear Brother Guy:
Reference is made to the Al Bahr Temple violation of Section No. 127
of Ross' Digest and our conference today.
It is my opinion that the violations of the laws which were intended
to correct various abuses in California were deliberate. This would seem
so especial1y in light of apologies tendered by members of the Al Bahr
Divan. I understand also, that you have requested the Potentate, Clarendon T. Smith, to resign and that he has refused.
It is my opinion that the activities of die Shrine or any organiration
that bases its membership on being Masons is under the jurisdiction of
the Grand Lodge on matters that relate to enforcement of Grand Lodge
laws or that affect public relations or public opinion. The primacy of the
Grand Lodge must be maintained.
T ,herefore, it is my order and edict that no Mason in California or
under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California hereafter shalJ
apply for membership in, join or affiliate with Al Bahr Temple, or solicit
or receive any application of any Mason desiring to join Al Bahr Temple,
or participate in confer.ring any work on anyone desiring to join Al Bahr
Temple, until the present elective Divan has been completely replaced.
This order and edict shall remain in ful1 force until it may be modified
by me or by the Grand Lodge of California.
Fraternally yours,
EDGAR V. STEWART, JR.

Grand Master

EXHIBIT "J"

PROCLAMATIO N OF THE GRAND MASTER
M. W. Edgar V. Stewart, Jr.
37th Annual Public Schools Week
April 23 to April 28, 1956, is designated as Public Schools Week and
will be the thirty-seventh annual observance of this important activity,
when we as Masons reaffirm our definite belief in and support of free
public education in our democracy.
This is the time we rededicate our energies to the extension of public
school teaching and public school facilities to the point where they meet
the needs of all who should be served by free public schools.
We pledge interest in, study of, and support for adequate, free
schools devoted to sound teaching, American ideals and high standards
of learning and entirely divorced from any political or religious domination. Public schools being the bulwark of the American way of life, and
Masonry in California having dedicated its operative activities for thirtysix years since 1919 to an annual period of well expressed leadership in
support of our public schools,
Now, therefore, I proclaim and direct:
That every Lodge in the Jurisdiction of California observe with
proper ceremony, functions or services, Public Schools Week, 1956,
during the week April 23 to April 28 inclusive.
That no Lodge meeting other than stated meetings be held during
that week so dedicated as Public Schools Week.
That the general suggestions presented by the Public Schools Committee be followed.
That a constant program of manifest interest, cooperation, study
and consideration be given to the issues, needs and problems of the public schools at all times, every week of the year.
That attention be directed during Public Schools Week to the importance of. and opportunities in, the profession of public school teaching as a life career.
That interest be stimulated through the Lodges in the two new Masonic Public School Scholarships of $1,000 each to be awarded for the
best thesis by graduate students working for doctorates in education,
on the subject of "The Origin, Development and Purpose of the American Public School System."
That this Proclamation be read in the Lodge at each stated meeting
prior to April 23, 1956.
EDGAR V. STEWART, JR.

Grand Master
Attest:
LLOYD E. WILSON

Grand Secretary
February 6, 1956

PROCLAMATION

PROCLAMATION

Masonic Homes Endowment Month

Constitution Month Observance
A great milestone in man's long march toward freedom was reached
in September, 169 years ago, when thirty-nine American patriots signed
the document which was to become the United States Constitution. Their
work has met the test of time and set an example for the world.
Through peace and war, through eras of pioneering, expansion, and
industrial growth, through years of prosperity and of panic, through
the long and varied course of events which has brought us to a foremost
place among nations, that great charter of free government has stood and
still stands solid, as a house built on a rock.
We as brethren of the Craft recognized an identity between the
principles embodies in the Constitution and those which underlie our
Fraternity. And as Masons were influential in drafting the Constitution
and in administering government under it during the intervening years,
so we are today in the front ranks of those who must shield it against
invasion from any quarter.
Not only should these things we stand for be made widely known, but
we should invite every good citizen to stand with us when, this year, we
once more commemorate the historic event of September 17, 1787.
I therefore proclaim the month of September, 1956, to be "Constitution Month," and direct that in observance thereof every Lodge of this
jurisdiction hold a special meeting open to the public at which a program
suitable to the occasion shall be given, and that every effort be made to
secure the atteiidance of the families, friends and neighbors of the brethren.
This proclamation shall be read at each stated meeting following its
reception and before the observance.

"And the greatest of these is Charity"
Henry Drummond in his classic, "The Greatest Thing in the World,"
makes it clear that the word charity to which we as Masons frequently
refer, is not to be confused with the odious word "alms," but in reality
can more properly be interpreted as love.
All of us throughout the Jurisdiction of California have the opportunity during the month of May to demonstrate our love for our less
fortunate brethren and their families by givins:i generously from our
abundance that they might have the normal comforts of life.
Our two Masonic Homes, for the oldsters and the youngsters, are
supported in part by a continually growing Endowment Fund which the
love of our brethren inspired many years as:ro. Traditionally in May, we
are given the opportunity to augment this Fund which will continue to
bless the needful beyond the lifetime of any of us. This is in reality an
opportunity to give in perpetuity.
In order that all the brethren may be made mindful of this privilege
and give vent to their generous impulses. I proclaim the month of May
to be Masonic Homes Endowment Fund Month, and direct that each
Lodge arrange appropriate publicity on this subject in at least one of
their May meetings and that a Masonic Homes Endowment Committee
be activiated in each Lodge for the purpose of giving each and every
member of the Lodge an opportunity to participate in this, our most
worth!)' undertaking.
This Proclamation is to be read at each Stated Meeting following its
receipt up to and including the month of May and at such other meetings
as the Master shall direct.
EDGAR

v. STEWART, JR.

Grand Master

EXHIBIT "M"

PROCLAMATION
Whereas, since 1947, the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of the State of California has been planning to purchase or
build a California Masonic Memorial Temple in the city of San Francisco and,
Whereas. one of the most beautiful sites in that city has been acquired by Grand Lodge for the purpose of building its own home, its
first after one hundred and six years of existence, and through the active

138

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

interest of thousands of our brethren throughout the jurisdiction, there
has been contributed to our building fund established for the purpose.
the sum of $11443,722.49, as of July 27. 1956, and
Whereas. since our groundbreaking day last October, a revival of
interest and enthusiasm has been engendered by the brethren throughout
our jurisdiction. and a contract entered into for the construction of our
Memorial Temple with the aim of having it completed for our Grand
Lodge Communication in 1957 and,
Whereas. the laying of the cornerstone of this magnificent Temple.
destined to be one of the most beautiful anywhere in the world. will be
an event of personal interest to thousands of Masons everywhere and
of historical interest to as many more,
I. therefore, proclaim Wednesday , September 19, 1956. to be Cornerstone Laying Day throughout our Jurisdiction.
·
Plans are under way to handle as expeditiously as possible the record
breaking crowd which we expect to attract to this public ceremony as
it is expected that every Mason who possibly can, will want to attend
in order to say, "I was there." Also our myriad of friends who appreciate
Masonry's stand on the fundamentals of our American democratic way
of life, will want to share the joy of the day with us.
The construction of our own new home will mark the beginning of a
new epoch in California Freemasonr y. We are each year making rapid
strides toward that position for which California Masonry must prepare,
that of its responsibility of leadership among the great Grand Jurisdictions of the world.
It is hoped that before Cornerstone Laying Day rolls around every
brother and sojourner in our jurisdiction will be able to say that he is
one of an army of builders of the Temple by reasons of having made a
voluntary contribution to this Masonic Memorial and that every Lodge
in our Jurisdiction will find its name in the tablet to be displayed in the
Temple indicating their earned place on the roll of merit Lodges.
Be with us when history is made on September 19. 1956!
Attest:

EDGAR V. STEWART, JR.

Grand Master

LLOYD E. WILSON

Grand Secretary

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF CONTRO L
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The annual report of the activities of the Board of Control should be
so worded as to impress Grand Lodge with the importance of the work
of our eighteen ( 18) Boards of Relief and our si~ ( 6). Em~loyment
Bureaus. The Board hopes that this may be accomplished in this report.
The Board of Control was organized by Grand Lodge to control
and supervise Boards of Relief and Employment Bu~eaus and. to see
that they conducted their offices efficiently and economically. I~ is ma~e
up of five members. each appointed for a 3 year term on a rotatmg basis.
It has been the practice of Grand Masters to select the membe~s geographically, so that each member might serve those Boards of Relief and
Employment Bureaus within their immediate area.
It was authorized by Grand Lodge in 1926 and its progress can be
easily divided into three phases.
During its early years its entire time was devoted to the study. of
case histories. wherein Boards of Relief or Lodges had requested reimbursement of funds advanced for relie'f. Then followed a period of adjustment wherein the Board cautiously commenced to exercise some of
the authority granted by the Ordinances .
The third phase shows the •assuming of the ·position intended by
Grand Lodge. During this period uniform comP.acts were accepted, .indi;,
vidual By-laws were discarded and a set of Rules and Regulations
were established and a uniform accounting system was set up so as to
make all of the reports comparable.
During these periods. several cases developed in which the Board
had to exercise its authority to correct misunderstandings. clashes in
personalities and other controversial circumstances. which might lh.ave
grown into serious Masonic problems.
In recent years there •h as developed a .full understandi ng between
the Board of Control and Boards of Relie:f. No longer is authority questioned, nor is it necessary. except in rare instances. to have to use the
authority granted by the Ordinances. Frank, open discussion of our
problems has resulted in lasting friendships.
We, of the Board, are indebted to those who have served the Craft
as representatives on our Boards of Relief. They have been generous

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

with their time, wise in their decisions, ·and keenly interested in the
problems of Masonic Relief. The Board of Control extends its sincere
thanks to them.
The Secretaries of Boards of Relief are all men of high Masonic
integrity. It has been a distinct pleasure for the Board of Control to
work with them.
Thousands upon thousands of our Brothers, their widows and orphans have called upon these men for aid and without exception they
·have received the kind care and understanding which you would expect
to be rendered to you, your son, your wife or your daughter.
It is not unusual to find our Secretaries using their own funds to relieve distress, even in cases which would easily qualify for Masonic
Relief. In many ways it is unfortunate that prudence does not permit a
review of individual cases, so that we might justly pay honor to these
men who have been so faithful to their duties. The monitary compensation which they receive in no way reflects their services to the Fraternity.
They serve on twenty-four {24) hour call-seven ( 7) days a week.
As Chairman of the Board of Control, I would like to take this opportunity to thank all of the Secretaries for their cooperation and friendship. Especially I would like to honor the three Senior Secretaries who
have served long and faithfully:
Andrew Burke, of the Board df Relief of San Francisco.
Walter F. Kress, of the Board of Relief of Pasadena.
William T. Corbusier, of the Board of Relief of Long Beach.
Also Samuel Worswick formerly with the Board of Relief of the
East Bay, now seriously sick at his home, and three others, now deceased, must also be mentioned:
Willard Tanzer of the Board of Relief of Fresno.
Earle Trimmer of the Board of Relief of Sacramento.
Earl Thaxter of the Board of Relief of Los Angeles.
Their work was a monument to California Masonry.
The Board of Control recommends our Secretaries to you, and suggest that you become better acquainted with them and their work.
The past Masonic year has been most interesting, yet it was beset
with unusual and critical problems. In each case however, the problem
•has been solved and the work of Relief and Employment continues to
progress in an orderly manner.
In this report we wish to emphasize-that in the entire history of our
Boards of Relief, we know of no Mason who has been buried in potters
field; that all requests for Masonic services have been granted. No
Mason in good standing, his widow or orphan has been permitted to
want nor to have their needs unfulfllled.
All of this without thought af reward or reimbursement.

REIMBURSEMENTS

The Board of Control has carefully reviewed t'he requests of the
Boards of Relief of San Francisco and Sacramento for reimbursements.
Each case has l?een judqed upon its own merits and we have recommended to the Finance Committee and we recommend to Grand Lodge
that the above Boards of Relief be made whole for the monies which
they have advanced for relief of our distressed brethren.
Each case is briefly outlined herewith :
Case 1. Involves a former member of Brady Lodge No. 628, Brady,
Texas. He presented a receipt 'Showing his dues paid to June, 1957.
Communication with his Lodge showed ·him to be suspended for nonpayment of dues. The receipt had been altered and had been used in
other jurisdictions.
The Board of Control prefers to have our Secretaries err on the
side of generosity. Board of Relief of Sacramento advanced twentyfive dollars ( $25.00).
Case 2. A member of Cammery Lodge No. H4, North Bridge,
New South Wales.
The Board of Relief of San Francisco advanced a total of ninety
dollars ( $90.00) to aid the brodier. Assistance has been given since
1950 most of which was repaid.
His Lodge has suspended him for non payment. Relief was extended
prior to the suspension.
Case 3. A member of Brady Lodge No. 628, Brady, Texas. The
Brother is now a patient at Agnews State Hospital. Twenty-five dollars ( $25.00) advanced by Board of Relief of San Francisco.
Case 4. Member of Coupar O'Fife Lodge No. 19, Coupar, Seo~
land.
Brother is in Oak Knoll Hospital with an incurable disease. The
Board of Relief of San Francisco is advancing twenty-five dollars
( $25.00) each month. The Grand Lodge of Scotland has contributed,

143

however there is still a two •h undred sixteen dollars and fifty-two cent
( $216.52 ) balance.
The Board of Control can report that every reasonable effort has
been made to secure payment of these accounts through customary
sources, without avail.
Our Boards of Relief have reported that they advanced $69,233.77
during the past year. The four uncollected cases total $356.52. We
think that the secretaries are to be commended upon their fine showing.
CONCLUSION

Employment Bureaus-The Board of Control is continuing its study
to determine the advantage and feasibility of maintaining such a service
from which relatively few receive benefit.
Surplus Funds within Boards of Relief.-Our Boards have developed surplus funds to prepare for emergencies. The Board of Control
has limited their amount to not exceed one year's operating cost. This
amount may still be too great. Further study ·should be given this
problem.
Masonic Board of Relief of Honolulu.-While vacationing in Hon<>lulu. I had the opportunity to meet with the Board of Relief. So much

1956 ESTABLISHED
The following general principles for guidance of the work of the
Committee were developed and advanced.
First: Constant vigilance in support of the ideas upon which public
education is founded and conducted in California is an obligation upon
the Masonic life expression of every Blue Lodge Mason in the province
of the Grand Lodge of this Jurisdiction.
Second: One week a year is not enough. Every week is Public
Schools Week in fhe thought, in the heart, as a responsibility for knowledge, study and understanding among Masons.
Third: Masons recognize that there are several great systems of
education-the Personal or Tutorial .plan, the system of Private Schools,
the Parochial Schools and the Public Schools or Public Education.
We seek not to evaluate nor to judge any schools: we determine only to
advocate, develop, maintain and support with all of our knowledge and
ability that great structure of Public Education, established by the
Constitution of our State, governed by the People, and financed and
administered in accord with legislation and standards most acceptable
and desirable.
Fourth: Our faith in Public Education as a fundamental essence
of a free society is basic as is our faith in God and our trust in our
Fraternity. Where there is the light of intelligence, the life of charity
and the structure of brotherhood all people will advance.
Fifth: We know that men are known by their works. Our ideals
we find in the teachings of our Fraternity, our deeds are actuated by
our love of Frat~rnity. No deeds of practical expression of our Fraternal teachings are greater than those deeds which bring about better
Public Schools.

REPORT PUBLIC SCHOOLS COMMITTEE
INTRODUCTORY

Thirty-six years of successive emphasis on the "Light of Fr~e­
masonry" as a foundation for serious concern for the support, perpetuity,
and strength of public education in California is the background for the
work of this Committee for this year.
A firm conviction that "operative Masonry" obligates us to advan~e
a vigorous frontier of knowledge of, interest in, 'and support for .public
education and public schools in our State is fundamental to our place
in American society.
The foundations for Democracy, the advancement of our ideals,
the protection of our very existence are based upon the co~tinuing
availability of adequate free public education for all who can improve
and advance therefrom.
A careful study revealed, some months ago, that our State and our
public schools were most depe~dent .upon active i~t~rest, loyal support,
and constant, penetrating consideration by good citizens. It was agreed
at once that Public Schools Committee activities for the thirty-seventh
year of the life of the Committee should be ;particularly and definitely
speci8ed.

GUIDING PRINCIPLES FOR

A WoRKING PROGRAM
As 'has been t:he case through the years, when the Public Schools
Week Pronouncement for 1956 was made, Lodges, members, committees, officers and associates went to work. It seems that this 1956 Week
and Public Schools effort was a time and an effort of extraordinary nature, of unusually fine participation, of outstanding accomplishments.
As we pause to express gratitude, compliment, appreciation and
thanks to the Grand Master, to officers of Grand Lodge, to Past Grand
Masters, to officers of the respective Lodges in our jurisdiction, we
especially commend the entire membership of the Fraternity for its
constructive and significant participation and contribution.
We thank, likewise, the related Masonic groups who demonstrated
interest and gave service this year. To the more than half a hundred
statewide groups, Civic, Community, Church, Service, Business, Commercial, Club, and Labor, we extend gratefulness for help, good spirit
and cooperation.

146

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Briefty, in fact, all too briefty, this is what has happened during ~e
Masonic year 1955-56 in the realm of the work of your Public
Schools Committee.
RESULTS

1. There are nearly 665 active Lodges in California. 621 of these
held special Public Schools Week meetings of distinction. These special
meetings were held in the Lodge, or in a School, and many were conducted in public places.
2. By careful and accurate estimate just about 1,100,000 people
were in attendance at some Public Schools Week meeting, event, or
activity, stimulated by Public Schools Week planning and direction in
which you were motivating leaders 1a nd of which The Grand Lodge
was the "Founding Father."
3. 525 of the more than 621 Lodges in the State w'ho had a particular
function for Public Schools Week this year made special report of
outstanding response to their efforts. These 525 Lodges did the following things, among many other things, of a speci.6c Lodge-School type
of contact.
(a) Provided honor awards for outstanding students w'ho presented
evidence of accomplishment of a significant type of Americanism, in
Sctholarship, in Leadership, in Service, in Citizenship or in Sports.
( b) These Lodges sponsored meetings, dinners, and pot-luck affairs
where large representative groups got together in a semi-social way to
meet one another, to meet school personnel and to meet students, to
become really friendly and acquainted with Public Schools and School
People.
( c) They sponsored "Youth Day" functions in the school community. Exhibits of school work placed prominently throughout the
community as well as in schools were extremely popular.
( d) There were awarded scholarships, certificates, and medals for
students at various levels, to encourage high standard study and learning and give Masonic recognition to pupils who were worthy.
( e) Many Lodges helped conduct Contests; in Essays, Oratorical
Presentations, Spelling "Bees" and Physical Fitness. Schools were
helped to prepare student speakers for service clubs, cliurches, Legion
and women's clubs as well as labor groups in order to bespeak the
History, Development and necessity for adequate Public Education in
our great American Democracy.
( f) There was conducted a program of "Be informed about our
public schools" effort through publicity, ·publications, student and home
relations, and through all public contact ·media-radio, TV, press, and
specially prepared brochures.

GRAND LoDGE SCHOLARSHIPS FOR GRADUATE STUDY

The 1956 activities of our Grand Lodge Public Schools Committee
are especially noteworthy because of the · flrst of the awards of the
Grand Lodge scholarships for graduate study in American Public
Education.
To establish this program, Grand Lodge through Grand Master
Stewart, following the initiation of the proposal of scholarships by
Grand Master Clausen in 1955, authorized the announcement of awards
of $1000. each for two such scholarships. One scholarship was to be
awarde~ m ~~rthern Ca~ifornia, one in Southern California. Six Colleges
and Universities, three m the North and three in the South indicated
interes~ in. thi~ si.gniflcant venture. Nominees were present~d by the
respective institutions, a contest was conducted, winners selected and
awards made. The signi.6cant aspect of this project is that it advances
the ~ursuit of 1?,t~~ledge. an.d writing in the fleld of "The Why of our
Public Schools, The S1gniflcance and Necessity of Public Education
in our Democracy," and the "Purpose of the American Public School
System."
The interest in and success of this effort warrants its continuance
and expansion.
CONCLUSION

The dynamics of this 1956 activity of Grand Lodge, conducted
through the Public Schools Committee reveals important conclusions:
Masonry needs the great opportunity afforded by Public Education
as a field for the manifestation of helpful interest, study, service and
support by Masons.
The public education program and our schools have and very rightly
should have, no keener expression of concern and cooperation among
citizens than that which Masons are pledged to offer.
Masons can ihelp make real the principle that "as go the Schools,
so goes the future of a Community, a Society, a Government."
As schools encounter needs and problems because of growth, shortages of .per~nnel and support, or lack of understanding; among the
flrst to mamfest concern, offer assistance, and be real 1helpers, must be
found the Masons of California.
We do not present the claim that our Public Schools are perfect.
None-the-less do we permit ourselves to ·h arp on what is wrong with
our schools: We are men of manifest Faith in Youth, our allegiance
to our Public Schools causes us to be ever anxious to give constructive
suggestions and vigorous loyalty to the making of our Public Schools
into the very best schools they can become.
In each Lodge an active Public Schools Committee should alert the
memb~ship h~ ~.eans of the Lodge publication, concerning the current
Frontiers, Activities and Accomplishments of the Public Schools of the
Lodge area.

The Committee tentatively awarded the steel contract to the low
bidder, Moore Dry Dock Company, subject to their ability to improve
the completion date, and they were so advised. After several meetings
with the architect, the general contractor and Moore Dry Dock Company. it was decided to award the contract to the next low bidder,
namely, Judson Pacific Murphy Co., to get a better completion date and
to avoid a 91 day delay on the part of MacDonald, Young & Nelson,
the General Contractor.
This decision was not an easy one, but after Moore Dry Dock
~ompany advised that they could not materially improve their completion date, and with the assurance of the General Contractor that, barring unforeseen delays, they would be ready for steel within 229 days
from the day they started work, it meant they couldn't finish the job in
500 calendar days if they were delayed as much as 91 days because of
steel delivery. Your Building Committee didn't want to see the job
closed down for 3 months for that would eliminate the 1957 Annual
Communication as the time for dedication. It would also result in loss
of revenue from the garage and from possible rentals for use of the
auditorium.
Before awarding the contract to the second low bidder for an additional net cost of $30,641, your Committee wanted assurance that the
shorter delivery date could be met. We were given that assurance based
on the fact that allocations for steel were made at the mill based on prior
~onsumption. This was confirmed by the other steel companies. Judson
Pacific-Murphy Co. then in the process of completing the new RichIDond-San Rafael Bridge (scheduled for opening Sept. 1, 1956). together with their participation in several other large projects, was high
on the list for allocation. In consideration for our having awarded
them the contract, provision was made in the contract that should they
fail to complete the work within the alloted time when the General Con-

TAKING Bms AND AWARDING CONSTRUCTION CONTRACTS
It will be recalled that at the last Annual Communication of this
Grand Lodge a resolution was adopted specifkally permitting the
Temple Committee, at its discretion, through the architect, "to negotiate
with one or more general contractors for a contract price based on a
fixed fee with a guaranteed maximum cost."
After serious consideration, it was decided that the best interests of
the Corporation and this Grand Lodge would be served by selecting not
less than three general contractors to bid on the General Contract. It
was also determined to take separate bids on the structural steel. Accordingly, the architect was instructed to submit plans and specifications
to the firms selected, fixing the time and place for opening bids as Tuesday, March 13, 1956, at 2:30 p.m., 25 Van Ness Avenue, San Francisco.
The Building Committee of the Temple Corporation, consisting of
Bro. L. Harold Anderson, Deputy Grand Master, Bro. Ira Coburn, Bro.
Paul A. Pfleuger, Bro. Arthur M. Warren and Bro. Edward H. Siems,
together with Bro. Edward J. Blickfeldt (who happened to be in San
Francisco on other business), Bro. Lloyd E. Wilson, Secretary of the
Corporation, and Bro. Albert F. Roller, Architect, met at 25 Van Ness
Avenue at 2:30 p.m. on March 13, 1956, for the purpose of publicly
opening bids on the General Contract and on the structural steel contract. Bro. Roller opened and read the bids:

Your Building Committee and architect have implicit confidence in
the ability of the contractors on the job. They are experienced construction 'People. There are conditions however that may cause delays beyond their control.
The unfortunate cave-in during the early part of construction and
the slide condition on the California Street _side of the property, are
conditions which have resulted in difficult engineering problems over and
above what were reasonably expected. They are not mentioned here to
make excuses, but to alert this Grand Lodge that there are serious
problems and there may be delays. We are confident however that the
technical know.-how of our contractors will hold them to a minimum. We
ha~e frequent meetings with the ·principals involved. They are keeping
us mformed to the best of their ability on their time schedule, and if there
are any serious delays we will so advise the lodges through the Templegram or throug·h the California Freemason, or both.

In the first category we can report that there have been but few violations of our law since the 1955 communication. In each instance we have

The only direct action taken during the year was that resulting from
