In the second category we should note the results of the legal actions
instituted by M. W. Henry C. Clausen, P.G.M. against certain publications purporting to be Masonic in name or character as authorized by
Grand Lodge.
At the time of the institution of such suits there were four such publications in existence. They were:
The Masonic Star and the Masonic Trestle Board, published by
Glenn and Gertrude Whitfield in San Francisco;
The Masonic World, published by Harry and James Adam in San
Francisco; 1a nd
The Masonic Independent Monthly, published by Robert Mero in
Huntington Park.
In the case of the Masonic Star and the Masonic Trestle Board, the
White6elds entered into an agreement to drop the word "Masonic" from
the title of their publication and to desist from doing anything to indicate, either orally or in writing, that the publications have any ·affiliation
with Masonry; and not to permit the appearance therein of the Masonic
emblem or any imitation or resemblance thereof. They also agreed to
eliminate the phrase "The Oldest Masonic Publication West of the
Mississippi" from all future issues of the "Trestle Board." This agreement, however, has not been completely complied with by the Whitftelds. Your committee, through investigation, has in its possession
evidence that these publications, and particularly "The Trestle Board,"
is continuing to use the same spurious billing methods: the same oral
'lbiarepresentations by telephone solicitors, although not with the same
success as heretofore. The result of this conduct prevented the dismissal
of the suit against the Whitfields, and it is still pending.
The suit against the "Masonic World" was prosecuted to completion

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Before making our report there are two acknowledgements which
should be made.
Written on an old brass square found in an ancient bridge near
Limerick and bearing date, the year 1517, these lines appear:
·
"Strive to live with love and care
Upon the level, by the Square."
These two lines typify to the members of this committee the philosophy, action and conduct of our Grand Master in his daily life and in his
Masonic life. Never have we been privileged to work with a man who
is more kindly and sympathetic or more understanding of. and courteous
to, others. He believes that the intent, motives and purposes of all men
are good, until they themselves prove otherwise; yet, when the chips are
down, h-e can and does smite the wrongdoer with a mailed fist in defense of those ideals and principles for which he and our Craft stand.
We acknowledge to M. W. Edgar V. Stewart, Jr., our Grand Master,
our appreciation for the privilege we have had in working with him in the
cause of Masonry. We here extend to him our deep fraternal affection
and regard.
To my colleagues on this Committee, and as its chairman, I acknowl~dge with sincere thanks their dedicated devotion to the principles and
ideals of Masonry and to the work of this committee; nor do I detract
one whit from any by singling out the one and only incomparable Worshipfu_l Brother Donald G. Campbell. He has served as Secretary of our
committee for three years. He has done more than his share of investigation work and written more than his share of reports. I am sure each
member joins with me in saying a special "Thank You" to Don.

Mark you well this last line above quoted as this report unfolds.
"All attempts to associate Freemasonry with or for business development are deeply deplored."
In the field of commercial exploitation of the good name of Masonry
by various means of promotion, other than advertising, we can report
that with one or two exceptions all is relatively quiet. There have been
isolated instances of the use of Masonry by individual members coupling
the square and compass to the opening of a jewelry store or displaying
it on business cards. These instances have been effectively handled by
the Inspector or the Master of the Lodge.
In this field an entirely new type of solicitation in the name of charity
was recently called to the attention of your committee. We have not
had sufficient time to make a thorough investigation, hence we are not
in a position to make a complete report either to the Grand Master or
to this Grand Lodge. Briefly, the facts available to us present the following picture:
In February, 1951, the Transportation Crippled Children's Club was
formed, by a group of employees of the Southern Pacific Railroad Co.,
in Los Angeles, as a non-profit charitable organization. Its membership is
limited to Masons who, we are informed, must be Shriners, their wives,
daughters, mothers and widows.
Its purpose is to raise money for the Shrine Hospitals.
Since its formation membership has spread to others outside of the
transportation field.
fo 1953 this club approached Associated in-group Donors, commonly known as A.l.D. and was approved as a recipient of A.l.D.
money. Originally donations came only from employees of the Southern
Pacific Railroad Co., but it now receives donations from the Telephone
Company and other outside organizations. The Club believes that the
administration of the A.l.D. program is headed by Catholics, so a percentage of the A.l.D. •money received by the Club is given to Catholic
Charities for appeasement.
While, as stated above, a complete investigation has not been made,
it appears that we have here the familiar pattern of a group of Masons
forming a separate pre-requisite organization, starting perhaps to solicit
from their own members only by ending with a general solicitation from
bot'h Masons and profane. Your committee is beginning to wonder
what will be thought up next.
A problem remaining to be resolved is the question of a cemetery,
Privately owned advertising itself as a Masonic .cemetery. Several instances of such use of our name and sy.mbols exist. Your committee
recommends that these cemeteries be investigated and if misrepresenta-

We •must, however, be ever vigilant. Masonry is easily sold because
the Craft is held in high esteem and affection by the public. We owe it
to them as well·as ourselves to see to it that this form of racketeering is
completely stopped for all time. We sincerely believe that the Craft
itself constitutes the greatest force to accomplish this much desired result. Your committee therefore respectfully requests the cooperation of
all Inspectors and Masters in calling to the attention of the membership
generally ,and to the heads of all so-called appendant bodies that there is
no Masonic publications other than our own California Freemason.

It reads as follows:
"The Board appeals to Brethren generally to take every means in

of the offenders and if they refuse to cease and desist that the Grand

The compelling problem still before us, however, is the use of the
good name of Masonry by many of the Shrine Temples in the promotion
of their annual circuses.
Last year we pointed out that in their contract with Pollack Bros .•
Shrine Temples granted the use of their good name to Pollack Bros. in
this promotion and agreed not to make any drive for public funds until
the last performanc e of the circus. Then the drums begin to beat for the
"underprivi leged" and "orphaned" child. Books of tickets are sent to
the membership. More books are sent to business firms and the public.
The inference given to the whole rpromotion by oral representati on, correspondence and statements accompanyi ng the tickets is that the ultimate
beneficiary is the "underprivi leged" and "orphaned" child. In truth and
in fact. the sole benefkiary of the profits received from the promotion of
such circuses are Pollack Bros., the promoter, and the Shrine Temples
who lend their names to such promotions.
Telephonic solicitation, which has heretofore been severely condemned by this Grand Lodge. is widely engaged in. The telephone
solicitors are usually employees of Pollack Bros. They use the name of
the Shrine Temple and Masonry to high pressure the sale of tickets.
Your committee received two complaints from the California Intelligence
Bureau, a business organization formed to protect its members from
rackets and high pressure salesmen seeking donations, complaining of
the manner in which their members were being solicited and the pressure exerted upon them.
ln one area complaint was made to the bunco squad of the local police department.
It is not necessary for us to tell you of the unfavorable impact that
is thus registered against the good name of Masonry.
Does not this method of operation by a pre-requisit e body of Masons
who encourage the public to believe that it is Masonically affiliated constitute an attempt to associate Freemasonr y with the development of a
business which was so deeply deplored by the Grand Lodge of England?
Is not Pollack Bros. receiving not only the use of the name and good-will
of such organization s, but the active assistance of Masons to further its
own business venture? Certainly no one could be so naive as to believe
that Pollack Bros. would seek to obtain the assistance of a Shrine
Temple if it could do the job alone.
Every fast promotional scheme reported last year had as its pattern

the Shrine Circus. Since then. other pre-requisit ie organizations, such
as the Sciots and the Grotto, have cleaned their houses, and they now
no longer conduct such ·promotions, and we point with pride to the fact
that not a single instance of this practice •has been reported during the
past year on the part of any other organization .
There is a ray of hope that the Shrine in California will likewise
clean its own house. We are informed that one Temple. which this year
did not use the "underprivi leged" and "orphaned" child as a means of
selling tickets, reports that the circus was anything but a success and
the profits derived therefrom much less than the year before. The Potentate of another Temple has stated that in his opinion the work involved in promoting a circus is not worth the profit received. He further
stated that in his opinion all such promotions should be stopped and the
dues of the membership raised to pr.ovide the money needed to carry on
the activities of the Temple. This last suggestion is, of course, the
proper one. W ·h en the ideals. principles, purposes and activities of any
fraternal organization are such that the membership thereof is not willing
to completely support it, thus necessitating an appeal to non-members
and the public generally for financial support. it ceases to be a true
fraternal organization . We do not believe that the principles and purposes of the Shrine are in that category. nor do we believe that its membership is so poor that it cannot afford to .p ay in dues an amount
sufficient for its complete operation.

of articles which appeared in the San Jose newspapers between dates of

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON LODGE FINANCING
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Lodge Financing takes pleasure in presenting its
report for the 1955-56 Masonic Year. Indeed. my brethren. this report
is a presentation of the evidence of what God is accomplishing through
His army of faithful California Masons, men who are dedicated to the
fundamental principles upon which our organization was founded, and
who daily practice those 'Precepts which have sustained it down through
the centuries.
These California Masons are continuing to build many new critically
needed temples with their own hands: they are strengthening their
Lodges and their fraternity by improving the business and financial
administration of temple properties; and they are making plans for
greater and more glorious Masonic endeavors to come.
While several new Masonic temples have been dedicated during the
past year. many others are in various stages of constl'1;1ction. Most of
the following will be ready for dedication in the immediate months
ahead:
Atwater Lodge No. 622, Los Angeles; Anchor Lodge No. 273,

Lodge No. 348, Damascus Lodge No. 648, Phoenix Lodge No. 178, San
Bernardino, and Rim of The World Lodge No. 711. Twin Peaks.
Your Committee on Lodge Financing takes justifiable pride in the
small part it has been called U'POn to 1play in the financing and building
of the temples listed above, and the scores of others which have .been
completed and paid for during the past several years. However'. the
real credit goes to the faithful few in every Lodge who have persisted
in overcoming every obstacle, every trial and tribulation, and it is they
who deserve the accolades of every one of us.
Your Committee on Lodge Financing wishes every Mason in this
great jurisdiction of ours could experience the thrill and inspiration that
come to its members while cooperating with the real working Masons of
California, following through with them in their respective temple building .programs. Usually the building program begins as an idea in the
minds of one or two progressive ·members of the Lodge. The idea then

becomes the dream of several. The dream takes shape in the form of
drawings and floor plans. There is then developed a program for raising
funds, because in ninety per cent of the cases no building funds are
available at the outset. Then an association is incorporated which provides a vehicle for raising funds which is not only consistent with civil
laws but Masonic laws as well. Financing committees are appointed and
door bells are rung. In time sufficient cash is on hand to acquire the
building site. Soon there is enough additional money raised to buy the
materials to enclose the building. A work organization is evolved. Then
comes the slow and painful. albeit great, rewarding task of raising the
building with volunteer labor donated by members of the craft which,
unfortunately, is s·h ared by only a small percentage of the ·membership.
Eventually. the temple is completed and dedicated, free and clear of
outside indebtedness. an everlasting credit to our beloved fraternity.
The foregoing recital points uip some of the obstacles which have to
be overcome in the building of a Masonic temple. They are formidable
enough. The obstacle most difficult to overcome, however, the one most
frustrating to rise above, is the opposition of a small, but very vocal
minority in the respective Lodges. No one doubts the sincerity of these
brethren. But their ·c ontention is powerful because of the responsibility
of those in authority to keep harmony in the Lodge. If there is one weakness in Masonry it is the determination to please all the members all of
the time. To do this would bring on the millenium which would be wonderful to behold but which has not yet appeared on the horizon of human
endeavor. In the meantime progress and democratic action require that
the majority must rule.
In California many more new temples might now be in existence for
the pleasure and benefit of the brethren and for the strength of Masonry
generally, if more thought and effort were applied to the finding of ways
and means for getting constructive things done, as opposed to ways and
means of defeating them.
Your Committee on Lodge Financing's activities continue to increase. More applications have come to the attention of the Committee
during the past ten months than in the .previous year, the busiest up until
that time.
It is a pleasure to report to the members of this Grand Lodge that
the Committee on Lodge Financing has during the past ten mont·hs consented to the construction of eight new Masonic temples, consented to
the acquisition of fifteen Masonic temple building sites, and approved
the incorporation of sixteen Masonic temple associations. Details of
these actions will be printed in the official proceedings of this Communication and your attention is respectfully commended to them.
The rapidly rising market price of land throughout the length and
breadth of California is posing a real problem to Lodges with .future

170

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

temple building programs. There is real danger of Lodges being priced
out o'f the market on adequate and desirable sites on whic'h to erect
Masonic temples. Therefore , it seems prudent for Lodges contem.plating
the building of new Lodge homes to give serious consideration now to
the seeking out and purchasing of suitable properties, before it is too late.
The problem confronting the more than one hundred Lodges in California that have constructe d new Masonic temples in '<:;:alifornia during
the past several years in meeting their quotas in the 8nancing of the new
Memorial temple in San Francisco, is also of deep concern to your Committee on Lodge Financing . While ·several of these Lodges ·have met
their responsibility in this respect, others are struggling valiantly to get
on the Merit Roll, lest reflection be cast on them. While there is no
doubt that these progressive Lodges will eventually meet their obligation
in the financing of the beautiful new Memorial temple, your Committee
on Lodge Financing believes that for .t he present they should be placed
in a special category, and that patience and understan ding be exercised
in their behalf.
The brethren of this Grand Lodge ,might be interes~d to know that
the 8nancing of the more than one hundred new Masonic temples in this
state represents a per capita investment of money, labor and materials ol
·more than three hundred dollars per member of the Lodges involved.
This has meant a real sacrifice to the membership, and makes every
effon to meet the Memorial Temple quota most difficult. It should be
pointed out, however, that these Lodges are making an outstandin g
contribution to the Memorial Temple building in ·per capita levies
through greatly increasing membership .peculiar to Lodges with new
temples.

These new Lodge homes will be two of the finest ever erected in California. The one in San Pedro will be situated on a large site with a commanding view above the shores of the blue Pacific, and the one in San
Bernardin o will cost nearly a half a million dollars when completed and
furnished. Both structures are soundly financed and will not involve any
outside collateral financing.
Other applications presented to your Committee at this meeting were
by rhe following: Coalinga Lodge No. 387, King David's Lodge No.
209. Phoenix Lodge No. 178, Guadalup e Lodge No. 237, Henry Clay
Lodge No. 95, West Gate Lodge No. 335; Buena Park Lodge No. 337,
Arlington Lodge No. 414, Clarence F. Smith Lodge No. 482, Alexande r
Graham Bell Lodge No. 595, Craftsmen Lodge No. 559, Moneta Lodge
No. 405, Manchest er Lodge No. 585 and Jordan Lodge No. 654.
Your Committee on Lodge Financing wishes to acknowledge with
profound appreciati on the use of the new facilities in Santa Maria, and
the gracious hospitality of the brethren of Hesperian Lodge, which contributed so much to the success of the meeting.
Masonry continues to prosper in California, but is still lagging behind the phenomenal growth in wealth and population of this great state.
There is need for five hundred additional new Lodges in this jurisdiction
at this very time. One of the important deterrents to the organizati on
of new Lodges is t'he lack of proper facilities in which Masonic Lodges
may meet. Therefore , your Committee on Lodge Financing will continue
to encourage the building of more ·and more new temples financed, of
course, on the sound principles and policies which have proved so ef·fective during the past several years. Your Committe e seeks the cooperation and assistance of each and every Mason in California in enabling
our beloved fraternity to reach its highest destiny.

SAN BERNARDINO MASONIC BUILDING Assoc1ATION - SAN BERNARDINO
On February 11, 1956, the above titled Masonic building association
made an application to the Committee on Lodge Financing requesting
consent to commence construction of a new Masonic temple in the City .
of San Bernardino. The proposed temple is a single purpose Masonic
Lodge building with multiple Lodge rooms, dining rooms, kitchens,
lounges, etc. Estimated cost of building and furnishings is approximately $450,000.00 and is to be financed through cash on hand in the
amount of $300,000.00 and the issuance of certificates in the amount of
$150,000.00, to be repaid out of income from properties owned by the
said building association. Having ascertained that the new temple building could be built, financed and maintained without placing a burden
upon the three Lodges involved, the Committee on Lodge Financing
granted consent to the construction of what promises to be the finest
Masonic temple of its type ever built in California. The brethren of
San Bernardino are to be commended .for their efforts to build a temple
worthy of Masonry's best traditions.

ALPHA MASONIC TEMPLE AssocIATION-Los ANGELES
After months of negotiation, Arlington Lodge No. 414. Clarence F.
Smith Lodge No. 482, and Alexander Graham Bell Lodge No. 595,
voted to join together and incorporate the Alpha Masonic Temple As.sociation under the non..-profit laws of the State of California. The purpose of the corporation was to provide a vehicle for raising funds for
acquiring and maintaining a Masonic temple for the use and benefit of
the three Lodges. Based on the information furnished, the Committee
not only granted consent to the incorporation of the said temple association. but also granted consent to each Lodge to invest from their general
funds $100.00 in a Regular Membership of the association to provide
preliminary costs of filing the proper papers. Much credit is due to the
brethren of the three Lodges for their successful efforts in this forwardlooking Masonic endeavor, emulating once again those who best can
work and best agree.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
OLD MASONIC HALL AT LOS ANGELES

months the actual restoration work should begin. The State Legislature
passed, ·a nd the Governor approved, an appropriation bill providing
funds for expenditure on the project in this fiscal year of 1956-57, as
follows:
( 1 ) For acquisition of additional real property within the approved
ultimate boundaries of the Pueblo de Los Angeles State Historical Monument-$900,000.
( 2) For development work within the Monument-$250,000.
It is proposed that the development work will be concentrated at
this time in the area of the monument designated as the Pico-Garnier
block. This includes the Pico House. Merced Theater. Los Angeles Fire
House, Garnier Building, and the Masonic Hall. Arrangements have
been made for a structural analysis of these 'buildings, including the
preparation of measured drawings. This will be done under the management of the Department of Recreation and Parks of the City of Los
Angeles, which has been designated as the "Operator" of the Monument for the three governments involved. Funds are available for the
preparation of these drawings, including the Masonic Hall.
Property acquisition and planning work has been progressing for
some three years on this Pueblo Monument. Restoration work is now
about to begin and it is hoped that this will soon include the Masonic
Hall, one of the oldest brick buildings in Los Angeles, and one which
represents an important •part of the history of the city.
Since writing the above summary. Mr. Price has verbally informed
the Committee that the authorities of the City of Los Angeles have
taken the necessary action to deed the property to the Monument and
the papers are being prepared for the proper signatures. This was the
last major hurdle that had to be taken before we could know that the
building would be preserved.
We can now look forward to its complete restoration. When that
is accomplished, we will be expected to furnish the second floor as a
replica of the old Lodge.
No expense has been incurred by the Committee and we do not
anticipate any for the immediate future. We recommend the continuation of a Special Committee and the authority, previously granted, for
the Grand Master to make nominal expenditures, if necessary.
Respectfully submitted,

To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
In order that this report not be prolonged, we refer you to the report
of this Special Committee made at the last Communication in which we
reviewed the background of and circumstances surrounding this first
Masonic Hall in Los Angeles.
Mr. Glenn Price, Curator, State Division of Beaches and Parks, and
the State official in Los Angeles working directly on the Pueblo de Los
Angeles State Historical Monument, has summarized the current situation relating to the Old Masonic Hall, as follows:
Plans are going forward for the restoration of the Lodge building as
part of the "living monument" to the life and history of Los Angeles.
Plans are not 'Complete at the present time but current thinking is that
the second floor will be refurnished and equipped as it was in the early
American period of Los Angeles when it was used as t'he meeting place
of the Lodge. The ground floor will be a store, as it was historically,
perhaps handling antique furniture (or replica antique), and gift items
with emphasis upon household furnishings.
A matter of urgency in connection with the Masonic Hall is the
acquuisition of title to the property by the State of California, thus
enabling the State to expend funds for the rehabilitation and restoration of the building. At the present time, title rests with the City of
Los Angeles. The Pueblo de Los Angeles State Historical Monument
project is a cooperative effort of the State and the City and the County
of Los Angeles, and it might be feasible for a lease arrangement to be
concluded which would make it possible for the State to expend funds
on the building.
Whether by a lease arrangement, or by acquisition of title by the
State, it is important that action be taken on this matter as soon as possible. The building is unstable and unsafe and has been condemned as unfit
for occupancy by the City of Los Angeles Bureau of Building and
Safety. Another complicating factor is that the Masonic building has
a party wall with the Merced Theater, which is also unstable and shoring work needs to be done immediately to prevent partial collapse of one
or both buildings. All parties concerned with the development of the
Pueblo Monument agree that the Masonic Hall is, and must be, an
integral and valuable portion of the historical monument and it is hoped
~t this complication will be resolved very shortly.
The value, interest, and usefulness of any one of the historic buildings in the Monument area will be enhanced by the restoration and
presentation of all the others. At the present time, work is progressing
on 't he :preparation O'f the Master Plan of Development and before many

COMPREHENSIVE PUBLIC LIABILITY-BLANKET COVERAGE
GRAND LoDGE AND ALL CONSTITUENT LoDGES

According to information available to us, we understand that 559
lodges have voluntarily asked to be included under this blanket policy
and that there remain only l 04 lodges who have their protection under
individual policies.
Because of the complexity of the exposure inherent in the operations
of a Masonic Lodge and its affiliated bodies, and because of the necessity
of writing a specially tailored policy-not only to cover the known hazards, but most important, to pick up the unknown exposures, we highly
recommend a program similar to that of the Workmen's Compensation.
(i.e., that coverage under a blanket form negotiated by Grand Lodge be
mandatory and~for simplicity of operation and also an additional saving in premium-the premium be advanced by Grand Lodge who, in turn,
will recover from the constituent lodges on a rper capita basis.)

194

PROCEEDINGS OP THE
MEDICAL PAYMENTS COVERAGE

Because of the fact that volunteer labor is excluded from the Workmen's Compensation :policies, we strongly recommend that Medical
Payments coverage, in the amount of $1,000, be considered by each
lodge-to take care of the lodge member who might be injured while
voluntarily performing a service for his lodge. The cost of this coverage
is reasonable and fulfills the lodge's moral obligation to the member.
TRAVEL ACCIDENT INSURANCE

We recommend that serious consideration be given to the purchase
of Travel Accident Insurance to cover those officers, including inspectors,
while traveling and while sojourning on ·Grand Lodge business.
INSURANCE MASONIC CLUB HOUSES

We recommend that the entire insurance program on the Club
Houses in Berkeley and University of California, Los Angeles, be integrated with that of Grand Lodge, and that coverage thereon be included under the Grand Lodge blankets wherever possible.
GENERAL COMMENTS

Our recommendations above are strictly from the standpoint of protection to Grand Lodge and its constituent lodges and are without consideration to the designation of agents or brokers. We feel that it is not
the prerogative of our Committee to enter this phase of the program.
Generally ·speaking, we have found that the insurance program presently in effect covers any foreseeable loss that might occur. However,
the efforts made to broaden the .protection, as well as obtain lower costs,
are commendable and should be pursued further. We recommend specifically tailored blanket coverage wherever possible.
Since the liability to which Grand Lodge and its affiliated bodies are
exposed is highly complicated and very great, in the absence of an insurance manager to keep constant watch over the program, we recommend, if it is feasible, that all insurance of Grand Lodge be placed
through one agent or broker. T 'he office selected should have sufficient
manpower to engineer the risks properly, and be agreeable to allocating
ipart of its commission to other agents or brokers as designated by Grand
Lodge.
In closing this report, we would be remiss if we did not mention the
very fine cooperation of the Secretary's Office of the Grand Lodge and
also of the agents or brokers with whom we consulted.
Respectfully submitted,

T. JAMES CARLILE
ALLERTON B. EBERT

FRANKLIN'S UFE, A LESSON TO MASONS
WAKEFIELD TAYLOR, Grand Orator
Brethren:
As your Grand Orator, during the past year it has been my privilege
to give short addresses at the constitution of new lodges and the laying
of cornerstones and dedications of lodge temples and public schools
throughout the state. I have also attended and enjoyed many receptions
given for our Grand Master.
These experiences have been a true inspiration to me. The constitution of more new lodges this year than in any year since 1923 is evidence of the growth and renewed enthusiasm of Masonry in California.
The construction of so many beautiful Masonic temples indicates a love
for the fraternity and a rededication to the ideals of Masonry. In some
instances these temples have resulted in large part from the unselfish
practice of operative masonry by the brethren themselves. The surprisingly numerous school cornerstones and dedication ceremonies show
good public relations and that the people generally are now aware of
the tremendous support our free public school system is receiving from
the Lodge. Not least among the pleasures of this year has been the
privilege of witnessing the magnificent work .performed by the Grand
Master, and his warm and affectionate reception by the brethren throughout the state. Blessed with the ability to impart in a direct and meaningful way his qualities of spiritual faith and gentility, he has made
a profound and lasting contribution to Masonry in California. It has
been a great honor to serve with him.
The purpose of a grand oration is to impart a message of value to
the brethren. This I prefer to attempt by the accepted Masonic method
of precept and example. This year, the entire world is making note of
the 250th birthday of Brother Benjamin Franklin, Grand Master of
Masons of Pennsylvania, great Mason and true American. This, together with the fact that we are meeting in Constitution month, makes
it particularly appropriate to point up some characteristics of this great
man which might be guideposts to our own lives in Masonry.
There are many who will strongly contend that between the time of
Leonardo Da Vinci and the present day. there has never lived a genius
of such diversity of interest and accomplishment as Benjamin Franklin.
A summary of the cold record will disclose that he was born in Boston
in 1706, the son of a poor candle maker: that he was the 15th child of
a family of 17: that he left home at the age of 17, and arrived in Philadelphia with three pennies in his pocket: that due to inherent wisdom
and hard work he became a successful publisher, and had amassed a
considerable fortune at the age of 44: that the remainder of his life
(over 40 years) was devoted exclusively to the services of his fellowmen.

196

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Franklin's gifts to his community and to the nation were so great
in number and variety, it is impossible to list t'hem all. He gave us the
wise and practical philosophy of Poor Richard's Almanac, and our first
circulating library. His scientific experiments, particular ly in the field
of electricity, were hailed the world over. He founded the first American
fire insurance company, reformed the police and fire departmen ts of
Philaddph ia, and organized the first Amerioan hospital. He planned and
helped establish the University of Pennsylva nia, and instituted the
American Philosophical Society. He formed the first society in Amerioa
for die abolition of slavery. He reorganize d the postal system. Outstanding though these accomplishments may seem, his greatest contributions,
as we all know. were in the field of diplomacy and statesmanship. He
was the only man who signed all four important documents, The Declaration of Independence, The Treaty of Alliance With France, The
Treaty of Peace, and the Constituti on of the United States.
Franklin's Masonic career was no less impressive. In 1731 he became
a member of St. John's Lodge in Philadelphia, in 173Z he drafted a set
of by-laws for his Lodge, in 1732 he was elected Junior Grand Warden,
and in 1734, at the age of 28, Gl.'land Master of Pennsylva nia. In August
of 1734 he published the first Masonic book printed in America. There
is good reason to believe that as Grand Master, he laid the cornerstone
of Independe nce Hall. In 1776 he affiliated with Masonic Lodges in
France. He assisted at the initiation of Voltaire, and officiated at his
Masonic funeral services. Over a period of 60 years he held numerous
high Masonic offices and led an extremely active Masonic life upon
w1hich I have barely touched.
It is not my purpose today to attempt a biography of this manysided man. I am merely citing him as a great man, whose Hfe stands as
a practical application of so many Masonic principles. The course he
charted in his day for meeting important issues we still must face, can
be a forceful and effective example today.
In Franklin's day, the education of the people was a real problem,
as it is today. Franklin, in all his wisdom. realized that government by
the people could not endure or be a blessing unless the people were
sufficiently enlightened to shoulder the responsibility. In a letter to Samuel Johnson written August 23, 1750, Franklin said, "Nothing is of more
itniportance for the public weal than to form and train up youth in wisdom
and in virtue. Wise and good men are, in my opinion, the strength of a
state: far more so than riches or arms, which under the management of
ignorance and wickedness, often draw on destructio n instead of providing for the safety of the people."
Nor did Franklin limit his action to words alone. As I stated, he
planned and helped to establish two great institutions of higher learning,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNI A

197

and led the clharitable movement sponsored by freemasons to establish
free schools throughou t the province of Pennsylva nia.
The problem of free public education is, of course, still with us today,
and has become an increasingly important part of our Masonic program.
In the public schools, we Masons envisage the great training ground of
our democracy. Here students from homes representing all races, religions, political beliefs, and economic levels rub shoulders and learn
to live with one another in harmony, as we must in our adult life. Here
they learn to be tolerant of die other fellow's convictions, and to be
understan ding and sympathetic toward his problems. Here children
study the basic freedoms guarantee d by the Constituti on. They learn
tihe true meaning of Democrac y and how to make its processes function.
Here youngster s are inspired to patriotism by an appreciation of the
founding fatihers and the great American heritage.
Yes, we want our public schools to be places where inquiry and
exploratio n are encouraged: where teachers are not inhibited by ancient
tradition or by present fancy, but are academically free to test new ideas
and to open up t!he unbounde d vistas of the future: where students are
free to ask of t!he propositions expounded, "Are these rliings true, and,
if so. what is their significance in the general pattern of life?" The purpose of free education should be to stimulate an insatiable hunger for
knowledge and a lifelong dedication to the pursuit of truth.
We Masons recognize, 'as Franklin did in his day, that tlhis type of
eduoation is an absolute requirement, if our free form of government is
to continue and flourish. Human progress occurs only in an atmospher e
of liberty of mind and conscience: stagnation is the handmaiden o'f
superstition and controlled thought.
Yet, with all of tlhese basic trut!hs before us, are we, as Masons and
Americans, doing our part to foster our free public schools? When some
immediate issue is called to our attention, we defend our schools from
unwarran ted criticism, or express ourselves on legislation. This is good
and is to be encouraged. But are we also following Franklin's example,
and doing something by way of a constructive contribution? Free institutions are under constant surveillance by those opposed to them. A
weakness in the ·s ystem is an invitation to attack. The real question is
"W1hat are we doing to continuou sly strengtihen and improve our schools,
to raise them above petty criticis·m, thus to stand respected by the community and desfred by all parents?"
We oannot honestly deny that our public school system today has
many marked deficiencies. For years in densely populated sections of
tlie country we have had seriously inadequat e school housing. In many
places in California students are victims of double or treble sessions. Of
even greater concern is the shortage of good teachers. This is due primarily to insufficient salaries and to a failure to acoord to this. the mother

198

199

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of all professions, the public standing and dignity it so richly deserves.
As President Eisenhower recently said, "Good teachers do not just
happen. They are the product of the highest personal motivation." But
the enterprising young man of today is naturally concerned with his
ability to give to his family the basic material comforts and the advantages of higher learning. He thus becomes reluctant to enter the field of
education. Yet in no other field is it so important to have people of unquestioned ability, and intellectual and moral integrity. for here we are
dealing with all our hopes for the future of this great nation.

from autocracy, swept by a relatively small group of violent men, into
a ruthless, inhumane and soulless dictatorship.

Yes, if the incomparable Franklin were alive today he might ask
these questions: Are we in the front lines on much needed school bond
issues and tax rate elections, not as mere voters but as sponsors? Are
we willing to assume our share of the financial obligation which adequate
teachers' salaries and school facilities require? Are we giving of our time
as school trustees, or on the numerous committees appointed in each
community to solve school problems? Are we as parents and good
citizens giving every encouragement to those upon whose shoulders fall
the sacred task of educating our youngsters, and thus of perpetuating
our beloved country?
Benjamin Franklin's life warns us against hasty and thoughtless
action, but, at the same time, exemplifies firmness and unflinching courage
in the face of tyranny and the threatened extinction of the light of freedom. This wise and thoughtful man practiced, in the most trying of
circumstances, the conservatism which Masonry has always recognized
as a virtue. Thus when the colonies became increasingly restive toward
Great Britain, Franklin was sent to England, and remained there over a
period of almost 18 years in an attempt to work out a modus vivendi. He
was successful in having the Stamp Act repealed, though he could not
avert war. However, once the die was cast, there was never any question
where he stood.
Herein lies a lesson to us all. We as Masons should not be conservative in the sense of being lulled into a belief that we have reached
the millenium in human progress. Such an attitude presages regression.
The mind of Franklin was ever open to suggestion, and constantly
sought new avenues of progress, both in science and in the field of human
relations. Yet Franklin had a wholesome respect for the lessons and
contributions of the past and the advantages of the present. Before
recommending any future radical action he encouraged the exploration
of every peaceful and conservative approach to the burning issues of
the day. He cautioned for patience and thoughtful action. He was fully
aware of the great harm to humanity that can come from the unseasonable and unreasonable conduct of men.
The validity of Franklin's policy in this respect has been forcefully
illustrated within our own century. We have seen Russia in its transition

In this fast moving era, we are constantly confronted with important
issues, both in our personal lives, and as a nation. For example, today
we are witnessing a crisis in the political, social and economic life of the
Southern states. The issue cuts deep and feelings run strong. in this
great segment of our country. We should all pray that restraint and
reason will rule the day, and that the necessary transition in the lives
of the people will take place without giving way to racial hatred, bigotry,
emotionalism, and violence. May the conservatism and patience o'f Benjamin Franklin be practiced by those upon whose shoulders fall the
solution of this modern national problem.
In our own individual actions toward our fellowmen, we also should
practice those great Masonic virtues of patience and temperance. We
should make a real effort to reason out our differences and arrive at a
common ground of agreement. But, like Franklin, we must recognize
that where the sacred guarantees of human liberties are endangered,
there can be no compromise, but only determined and courageous opposition.
Franklin's religious convictions have been a matter of historical
argument. There is no doubt that he had a firm belief in a benign. God.
His active life in Masonry and his many written references bear witness
to this fact. Being a thinker and a scientist with a realization of the
magnitude of the universe and the orderliness of its oper~tion, he co~ld
not conclude otherwise. As he grew older, he was at least impressed with
the goodness of true Christians and the virtues of the Christian faith.
The great contribution he made to the religion of this country was
his insistence, with other great Masons of his day. that freedom of
religion be guaranteed in the constitution to all people. His magnanimous
mind despised religious bigotry, fear and superstition wherever he found
it. As a youth in Boston, he, with his brother, attacked fervently an~ effectively the witch burning tactics of Cotton Mather. As an aged diplomat in France, he gave comfort and encouragement to the great Voltaire
in his exposition of ecclesiastical abuses.
Franklin's insistence on prayer at the Constitutional Convention is
evidence of his humility and his belief that religious and moral values
are indispens,a ble to our national life. He realized that regardless of how
technically perfect any governmental machinery may be, it cannot bring
peace and happiness to the people unless it stands on a foundation of
religious worship and conformity to high moral standards. This is true
of the Constitution of the United States. and it is likewise true of the
Constitution of the United Nations. No set of man-made laws, regardless
of how thoughtfully conceived, can obviate the long and arduous task of
inculcating in the individual a devotion to Almighty God, together with

200

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

201

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

a power and willingness to distinguish between right and wrong in dealing with his fellowmen.
As Roscoe Pound, Dean Emeritus of the Harvard Law School has
said, and I quote, "World wide, respecting every honest creed, but requiring obedience to none-Masonry finds its sphere in helping to main·
tain and develop the moral order. While it reminds us of our natural
duties to ourselves, and the duties we owe our country as the embodiment
of the social order, it insists above and beyond all these, upon our duties
to our neighbors and to God through which alone the perfection of the
moral order may be attained."
With the example of Franklin in mind, we must ever remember that
a firm faith in God is the foundation of our fraternity and our nation. Let
us also be grateful that Masonry does not impose die requirement of any
particular creed or religious sect upon its members; that we encompass
good men of all faiths; that we, as citizens and as Masons, will defend
the ristht of all men to worship as they desire; that we decry expressions
of bigotry and intolerance wherever found or heard; that '}Ne discourage
vigorously any attempted imposition of religious doctrine upon our
public schools or other free institutions.
One of the most remarkable aspects of Franklin's life was the rare
combination of extensive scientific discovery, particularly in the field of
electricity, and an unexcelled achievemen.t in the field of human relations, that is, philosophy, morality, diplomacy and statesmanship. There
is reason to believe that Franklin's flrst love was in things mechanical and
scientific. He described himself in his will by the simple term "Printer".
His scientific experiments were pursued with obvious enjoyment and
zeal. There is also reason to believe that he considered the first obligation
of his matchless resources, to be in the field of human relations. While
we Americans marvel at Franklin's scientific accomplishments, we revere
him primarily for his homespun advice and philosophy, and his contributions to the establishment of this great free nation. In surveying his entire
life, there can be little doubt that he considered the matter of individual
freedom, and harmonious and righteous human relationships, of far
greater importance to mankind than the pursuit and development of material values.
The correctness of this line of reasoning h:as become more apparent
with the passage of the years. Since Franklin's day, scientific and industrial expansion has completely changed our mode of living. In this great
country we have all but banished poverty, and even those with meager
incomes enjoy modern luxuries and conveniences. We travel between
distant parts of the world in a matter of hours. Medical achievements
have rolled back the destructive forces of disease and lengthened the
span of human life. Yet, while enjoying the fruits of these great scientific gains, we live in a veritable state of constant anxiety and fear of
total extermination. There can be little argument with the proposition

that in the field of human relationships between men and between
nations, we have railed miserably to keep pace with our material development.
I recently heard a great atomic scientist explaining the unlimited
power potential latent within the bowels of the earth and the rays of the
sun. He stated that even now, were the nations of the world able to
resolve their differences, and thus convert the production of destructive
weapons into peacetime atomic development, it would be a relatively
short time before all peoples, including the starving and impoverished
masses of Asia, could be enjoying a standard of living equal to our own.
Yes, the most pressing problem of the day is that science continues
to outstrip and outdistance the humanities. T •here can be little doubt,
either, that the achievement of ·harmonious !human relationships is more
difficult. While the scientist deals with the constant and unchanging laws
of nature, the philosopher, statesman, or moral and religious leader
grapples with the emotionalism and uncertainty of the human mind.
It is becoming increasingly evident that unless the world achieves a
better balance between science and morality, dire trouble lies ahead for
us all.
The emphasis on Masonry in Franklin's life is added evidence of his
realization of the necessity for men to learn and practice its great moral
and social virtues. His gifts to humanity and to his country clearly illustrate that to him Masonry had a practical aspect. It was not sufficient to
learn and absorb the fine moral and religious lessons inherent in our
ritual and Masonic teachings. The real test of a man's Masonry was
whether he made useful application of those teachings outside the Lodge
room, and in his every day dealings, not alone with Masons, but with
all men.
Obviously it Is given to few men to possess the faculties of a Benjamin Franklin or be capable of such tremendous contributions. Therein
lies no excuse for any of us. The question is: Are we as Masons, within
our own limitations, performing our obligations to our respective communities and to our country? Are we performing the regular duties of
good citizenship within a democracy? Are we doing our part to sponsor
the numerous youth organizations which are attempting to develop
charaicter in the future citizenry? Are we taking the time to give adequate
parental guidance to our own cliildren in this fast moving age? Are we
lending our presence and support to our religious institutions? Are we
giving succor to the crippled, the sick, and the poor, by supporting our
great volunteer charitable and welfare agencies? As I have asked before,
I will ask again, are we givinst real support to our own local public
sohools? Are we strictly honest and fair in our business dealings? And
last, are we cultivating and practicing tolerance and understanding
toward all men 1

202

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

These are practical. not theoretical. questions. These are questions
whicli all good Masons should constantly ask of themselves. The answers
to these questions should tell us whether we are doing our individual part
as Masons to effectuate a better world, a world based on morality and
reason. Masonry, because of its universality, and the broad base of its
membership, can become an instrument of tremendous and world wide
influence in bringing righteousness into the relationships between men
and between nations: in dispelling the nightmare of gloom and despair
which now threatens all mankind.
As Albert Pike said, "Masonry should not be a mere watch-tower.
built upon mystery, from which to gaze at ease upon the world, with no
other result than to be a convenience for the curious"-"It is the duty
of Masonry to assist in elevating the moral and intellectual level of
society;"-"to harmonize conscience and science". "To this duty and
work the Initiate is apprenticed. He must not imagine that he can effect
nothing. and, therefore, despairing, become inert. Many great deeds are
done in the small struggles of life. There is, we are told, a determined
though unseen bravery, which defends itself, foot to foot; in the darkness,
against the fatal invasion of necessity and baseness. There are noble and
mysterious triumphs, which no eye sees, which no renown rewards,
Wlhich no flourish of trumpets salutes. Life, misfortune, isolation, abandonment, poverty, are battle-fields, which have their heroes,-heroes
obscure but sometimes greater than those who become illustrious."
In conclusion on this 250th year of the birth of Benjamin Franklin,
great man and great Mason, we should reconsider the less~n of. his life
and rededicate our own lives to a furtherance of the American ideal he
helped to establish.
.
If Franklin were to return to life today. as he often expressed a desire
to do, his eyes would behold a strange new material world. a world of
magic and scientific wonders. Yet, with all this progress. he would recognize the same basic social issues that perplexed man in the 18th Century,
magnified and still unsolved. He most certainly would now. as he did
di.en, throw his tremendous capabilities into the struggle.
Today then, let us take this occasion to reaffirm our unshakable belief in a wise and all-powerful God. Let us rededicate ourselves to the
education and enlightenment of our youth, to the interests of our great
Democratic way of life. Let us be temperate, and understanding. in our
approach to all problems involving our fellowmen. Let us, like Franklin,
stand unflinching in the face of any assault, be it direct or subtle, upon our
sacred heritage of freedom of thought, expression and religion. Yes, let
us have the satisfaction of knowing that we are bearing that share of the
public responsibility which good citizenship and good Masonry imposes.
The oration was received with a standing ovation.
On motion of Past Grand Master Leon 0. Whitsell, the Grand
Secretary was authorized to have the oration printed and distributed to
the Lodges.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California:
Your Committee on Charters reports as follows:
Three Lodges were continued under dispensations at the last Communication of Grand Lodge. During the year, 11 new Lodges were instituted. Of the 14 Lodges U. D., 11 have applied for charters.
We have examined the work and proceedings of the 11 Lodges
seeking charters and have conferred with their delegates. We found
the work and proceedings of these Lodges to be satisfactory, and that
they were clear of all indebtedness. In some cases there were errors or
omissions in keeping records and presenting same to the Committee.
Those of major consequence were promptly rectified.
We, therefore, recommend that Charters be granted to: Channel

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
CONSTITUTIO N MONTH OBSERVANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
This is a report somewhat in anticipation, for it deals as much with
events to be as with those which are already past. This is so because
the Annual Communication, being early this year-opening in fact on the
birthday of the Constitution-man y of the planned observances have not
yet been held.
"A free people," said Elbridge Gerry. delegate from Massachusetts,
near the close of the Constitutional Convention, "are the proper guardians of their rights and liberties," and Edmund Randolph of Virginia just
before the document was signed observed that "a constitution ought to
have the hearts of the people on its side."
These two declarations have deep meaning for us today, and lie behind the thought which prompted the Most Worshipful to proclaim for
1956 a public observance by the constituent lodges of this historic anniversary. For the voices of these patriots, echoing across the 169 intervening years, admonish us that the preservation of free government
depends as much upon the way we, its beneficiaries, feel about it and
how hard we try to keep it, as upon the charter itself.
The system devised by our Constitution is, in a sense, a loom upon
which, if they would realize and perpetuate "the blessings of liberty,"
the generations of Americans must weave the fabric of freedom. The
founding fathers gave us a sturdy and durable instrument, but the
weavers determine the quality of the cloth.
The great principles set forth in the Constitution we may think of as
the "working tools" of .freedom, in the use of which it is essential that
eac:h one of us be proficient. This proficiency it is not enough that Ma-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

207

sons alone possess. To the extent that any part of the people do not
know, do not try, or do not care, the edifice of American democracy,
super-structure and foundation alike, is weakened.
Every American in whose heart burns the love of freedom must be
enlisted as a "guardian of our rights and liberties," and wherever the
flame is feeble or has died out. it must again be kindled. In such a mission it is most fitting that Masons, always the disciples of freedom,
should assume the role of leadership.
One of the ways to exercise that leadership is to make our Constitution Month Observance a public event to which our friends, our neighbors and the whole community are invited-a patriotic festival from
which all may derive new inspiration, new faith, and a surer sense of
direction.
Constitution Month thus also may take its place as an effective counterpan and aid to Public Schools Week, for the sustained support of
our public schools which we know to be so vital requires full understanding and appreciation of constitutional principles by awakened and discerning citizens.
Such is the theme and such are the purposes which mark the twentieth observance of Constitution Month by Freemasonry in California.
In order to assemble data for the Committee's annual report, it was
necessary to try a device other than the after-it-has-happen ed .form
customarily used to record the history of a thing accomplished. Accordingly, the worshipful masters of the several lodges were asked to inform the Committee by letter of their plans. The Committee is pleased
to report that t~e response has been splendid. The many letters received
from lodges large and small and widely dispersed are convincing evidence that Masons the length and breadth of our State have answered
with enthusiasm and energy the Grand Master's call for special meetings
open to the public.
The Committee did not attempt to establish a set pattern for lodge
programs. In a letter to the masters, it expressed the confidence that
within each lodge would be found "the genius and the will to prepare a
suitable observance." The plans reported fully justified that confidence.
They indicate that much thought and effort !have gone into the planning
and speak well for the quality of leadership in our lodges.
The suggestion that several lodges join forces in sponsoring a program was carried out in many cases. Joint meetings of two or more
lodges appeared to be about equal in number to observances by single
lodges.
That interest in studying the Constitution, its history, meaning and
application, is widely shared is evidenced by the varied walks of life
from which speakers were drawn. And it is encouraging, also, to note
that many lodges found among their own membership qualified speakers
for the occasion.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The two Research Lodges likewise gave assistance, providing 'Speakers for a number of programs. In addition, several lodges made use of
published materials which have been prepared by the Research Lodges.
Boys from DeMolay were featured extensively in flag ceremonies,
while Jobs Daughters and Rainbow G~rls ·contributed their musical
talents and helped with serving refreshments.

"The Constitution of the United States should be the basis of a
Freemason's •Catechism, taught in every public school in the land. Upon
the bedrock of fundamental principles laid down in the Declaration of
Independence, they built the foundation of a nation: and they built it
square, and they built it level, and they built it plumb, that the temple to
be erected thereon might endure forever. You will search the Constitution in vain for a ruling class, for a state religion, or for a special privilege. But you will find a nation amply guarded, in which all have an equal
. ,,
v01ce.
All in all, we may 1feel assured that the Grand Master's call for a
public observance has met with outstanding success. The credit is mainly
due, brethren, to you and your lodges, whose willing response, resourcefulness and effort have made the work of the Committee light. To you
and all the brethren who ihave given their help, we express our sincere
gratitude.
And as we look toward the future, we share the hope set forth by the
master of American Lodge No. 475 in his letter to the Committee that
"each year will bring forth 1a spontaneous response to a Constitution
Month Observance program."
We conclude this report with the farther hope that the idea of a
public observance may be promoted and expanded until it becomes, like
Public Schools Week, one more community project in which Masons
have led the way.
To enable next year's committee to carry on its important work, we
recommend an appropriation equal to that for the year just ending.

·In some instances, youth also participated as speakers. One example
may be cited. At the joint observance of which Point Loma Lodge No.
620 in San Diego was host, a series of three-minute talks was given by
selected members of DeMolay, Jobs Daughters and Rainbow Girls on
"W•hat the Constitution Means to Me."
Not satisfied with confining their observance to one meeting, a few
lodges planned something extra. By way of illustration, Truth Lodge
No. 628 in Los Angeles, in addition to its regular program already held,
will follow its degree work later in the month with a round table discussion on salient features of the Bill of Rights.
"We have found this year," the master stated in his letter, "that
round table discussion, if the subject matter is prepared in advance, is
well received and yields good returns."
To add to the spirit of the occasion, San Clemente Lodge No. 671
plans to give each person in attendance a small American flag, to be
held high during the singing of the national anthem.
Extensive publicity was reported from many areas. The means used
ranged from special bulletins, drculars and newspaper stories to radio
and television.
Guadalupe Lodge No. 237 and Hesperian Lodge No. 264, at Santa
Maria, obtained announcements of their joint observance for ten days
in advance by two radio stations, and a television interview with their
observance committee chairman. Personal letters of invitation were
sent to 100 leading citizens.
The lodges of District 364 arranged for special announcements in
public schools •and churches of the peninsula communities regarding
their joint public meeting to be held Thursday evening of this week.
One of the most attractive printed programs coming to the Committee's attention was that given out by Downey Lodge No. 220 and Tyre
Lodge No. 741 in connection with their joint meeting at Downey.
Inspiring messages by masters ·featured many of the monthly bulletins and trestle boards received by the Committee. All would merit
quoting here. However, we select as representative and particularly
appropriate an excerpt from ~he master's message of Peninsula Lodge
No. 745 at San Mateo. We quote:

To the Most Worshipf ul Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on By-Laws have had under consideration 107
amendments and resolutions affecting By-Laws and meeting places of
Lodges.
Fifteen lodges increased their fees and only one lodge decreased its
fees. One lodge increased its annual dues to $24.00: eight lodges increased their dues to $18.00; six lodges increased their dues to $16.00:
and twenty-on e lodges increased their dues to $15.00. Twenty-s ix lodges
adopted amendments changing date, time or meeting place of stated
meetings. Sixteen amendments provided for time of meeting when the
stated meeting falls on a legal holiday. Twelve lodges adopted the Uniform Code of By-Laws.
It has come to our attention that during the past year a number of
proposed amendments to by-laws had to be returned to the lodge because
they were not adopted at the next stated meeting after their introduction
as required by Sections 133 and 134 of Grand Lodge Ordinance s. We
desire to emphasize the necessity of conforming strictly to this requirement and that if for any reason an amendmen t is not adopted at the next
stated meeting, new written notice should be given.

by the Grand Secretary and the Grand Master as to form and Masonic
Law requirements. Our Committee has carefully examined and approved
them and recommend their approval by Grand Lodge:

James E. Hogin, District Superintenden t of the McCloud School
District and Doctoral Degree candidate at the College of the Paci8c
was winner of the $1000 Scholarship award presented by the Grand
Lodge of California for a year of Graduate study in Public Education.
Hogin was the winner in a competition open to quali8ed graduate
students of the University of California and Stanford. Candidates for
the award were required to submit essays on the Origin, Development
and Purpose of Public Schools. Hogin's paper traced Public Education
since the emergence from the European tradition through its early
American development to the present day program. Hogin earned his
Master of Arts degree at the College of the Pacific in 1934 after
graduating from the University of California in 1926 and teaching
music for several years in the Modesto Elementary and High Schools.
In 1939 he became Band, Orchestra and Music Theory teacher for
McClatchey High School in Sacramento. After four years of Military
Service with the Coast Artillery from 1942 to 1946, Hogin returned
to McClatchey School as head of the Music Department continuing
advance study at the College of the Paci8c where he was awarded
a Sehool Administration Credential in 1948. In 1950 he was named to
his present supervisory post. The Masonic Scholarship award will make
it possible for ffogin to complete his residence requirement for a Doctor
of Education degree at Pacific.
A similar scholarship of $1000 was awarded to A. Lee Wintz, Jr.,
a student at the University of Southern California, who resides in
Artesia, California.
These two sc'holarships were granted by the Grand Lodge of Cali~
fornia during the Grand Mastership of Henry C. Clausen.
During the past year this Grand Lodge has suffered the loss of that
universally beloved Past Grand Master, George L. Jones. It has been
the custom of the Committee to record the last resting places of Past
Grand Masters. Past Grand Master Jones was interred in the Jones
Family Plot, Row 13, Lot 36 in the old Masonic Cemetery, Grass Valley,
California.
Respectfully submitted,
LEON 0. WHITSELL
0. J. WOHLGEMUTH

of the numerous Loeddgtes m their own originality and initiative in planhave been encourag
o use

ning an educational 1program for their respective Lodges and it is a
tribute to the caliber of men in the ranks of Masonry, as well as the
wisdom of the Masters who selected the committees, that there has been
an unprecedented stir among the Lodges in the direction of research.
While methods and results have varied from Lodge to Lodge. the net
effect has been to make the Fraternity aware of the need for Masonic
education and to move us appreciably closer to the goal of full understanding by each individual Mason.
These two 'Principal anchors of the research program this year, the
district meetings and the Lodge Research Committees, probably would
not ·have been effective except for the beneficient influence of the two
Research Lodges of Northern and Southern California. These bodies,
containing so many devoted and capable Masons, all plural members,
have now been active for many years, their effons have been fruitful
and beneficial and they have been used generously in 'Promoting this
year's accomplishments. They have been especially helpful in providing
the programs for district meetings where outside assistance was requested. In behalf of the committee, I acknowledge our everlasting debt
of gratitude to the officers and brethren of both Research Lodges for
their effective work, the many miles traveled and the time and effort
expended, all without reimbursement except the gratitude and appreciation of their bretheren. Northern California Research Lodge has reported some 85 separate appearances, Southern California 70. The total
mileage traveled by participating brethren was 8300 and the total estimated audience which heard this segment of the research program was
14,500.
The Grand Secretary has compiled and now has on file, the names
of all Research Committee Chairmen in the constituent Lodges. It is felt
that this mailing list may prove of considerable value in the future because it represents brethren selected for their interest and ability. The
mailing list has been used to good advantage during the past year for a
series of releases from this Committee in the months of February, March,
June and August. Copies are attached to this report as exhibits and will
be filed with the Grand Secretary.
A questionnaire circulated during August disclosed that practically
every chairman replying believed that his Lodge ·had benefited by research efforts this year and that Grand Lodge should continue with a
research program. A tabulation of the questionnaire also discloses that
an average of six meetings were held in each Lodge, devoted in whole or
in part to research purposes. This means approximately 4,000 meetings
for the Jurisdiction and a total audience of 200,000. Many of those attending were repeaters, that is, they attended more than one meeting but
it seems safe to say that every active Mason in the Jurisdiction has been
exposed to at least one research meeting.

·

contents of the four information booklets published by Grand Lodge
and given to the candidate as ·he receives his degrees. From there you
can branch out into "One Hundred Years of Freemasonry in California,"
the current or back numbers of "California Freemason" also published
by Grand Lodge, a good Masonic encyclopedia or text book.
Don't try to discuss all of Masonry at one time. Select a single subject such as one of the degrees, history, symbolism, charities, the Constitition. If a question is too difficult you can def er the answer to a later
meeting. And avoid abstract or advanced discussion. Simple, elementary facts on common subjects will please your audience most.
OUTSIDE SPEAKERS

If you do not want to be the speaker yourself, your Master will
doubtless authorize you to invite some other brother in your Lodge or
community, or you may wish to avail yourself of one of the Research
Lodges located at San Francisco or Los Angeles and described in the
enclosed brochure. If you want a Research Lodge speaker or panel for
an entire evening's program, or in connection with a stated meeting, contact the Research Lodge Secretary nearest you. Plan two months ahead
if possible. No expense is involved except for outlying Lodges which
usually provide overnight lodging and possibly help on transportation.
It is always a courtesy to offer dinner to an outside speaker.
GENERAL SUGGESTIONS

Make it clear that every Mason has a right to his own interpretation
of the ritual, except where Grand Lodge has spoken. The purpose of the
program is to encourage each brother to think for himself, not to impose
an opinion upon him. Secret work, obviously must not be discussed in
an open meeting. It is always safer to have discussions in a tiled meeting.
The Grand Lodge Committee on Research hopes that the foregoing
may assist you in formulating a successful plan of Masonic education in
your Lodge, however this Committee will welcome ideas and suggestions
and you need not change any plans you have already made simply because of this letter.
Before the next Annual Communication a questionnaire will be sent
out to ascertain what has been accomplished. Please have your program
organized so that a report can be made by August 1st, 1956. We want
to be able to inform the Grand Master that your Lodge has complied
with ·his expressed wish for incerased emphasis on Masonic education.
Sincerely and fraternally yours,
Committee on Research

other coi:n~ittees of the Lodge. In this spirit, we caII your attention to

May-Masonic Homes Endowment Month
Special committees may be appointed in your Lodge .for each of these
events. You,_ of course, are not to interfere with their plans but if you
can be of assistance to them it will be timely and a proper field for educational efforts.
Pr~nted material is available for your assistance in such a project,
Some is enclosed herewith and other items may be obtained by mail.

for 1956. This has been prepared by the Grand Lodge Committee on
Public Schools.

SELECTED EXAMPLES OF SUCCESSFUL
RESEARCH PROGRAMS
EXAMPLE I
THE PANEL WITHIN A DISTRICT IDEA

In one, the chairmen from the Lodges in the district organized themselves into a panel with one man to act as moderator and each of the
others researching and being prepared to answer questions such as
these: How old is Freemasonry? What does Freemasonry stand for?
What are the meanings of common Masonic symbols? Is the work the
same in all jurisdictions? etc.
Thus prepared, the panel plans to appear at the stated meetings for
June in each Lodge. Interested brethren in the audience propound the
questions and the members of the panel answer them.
Another has followed substantially the same idea except that the
panel appears before the District Officers Association.
Another does likewise and uses its Inspector as moderator.
EXAMPLE II
SINGLE LoDGE DINNER

One Lodge is a pioneer in the .6.eld with its Round-table on the third
Thursday of each month. Meetings are in the banquet room and start
with a dinner followed by a speaker or open discussion.
EXAMPLE III
DISTRICT BREAKFAST

For seven y.ears, one District has had a Sunday morning breakfast
club, meeting once a month at 9 a.m. to disseminate Masonic information
and carry on an educational program.
EXAMPLE IV
STATED MEETING PLAN

Several Lodges have had a research program at each stated meeting,
usually a speaker who appears either at dinner preceding the stated meeting or in the Lodge room if the subject is not .proper for open discussion.
EXAMPLE

v

CANDIDATES' PROGRESSIVE CLASSES

Another Lodge calls a •meeting of candidates and their coaches to
answer candidates' questions and discuss history and symbolism. A
separate meeting is held for the candidates of each degree after they pass
the proficiency lecture and before advancing further. T 1his does not interfere with or delay the conferring of the degrees.
EXAMPLE VI
HISTORY IN REVERSE

Another Lodge reports that a great deal of interest was generated in

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

222

a series of discussions at stated meetings, spaced three or four months
apart, and working from contemporary to ancient history. Subjects were
"History of Our Lodge"; "Masonry in California": "Colonial Masonry", etc.
EXAMPLE VII
STUDY CLUBS
One Lodge believes that a sufficient number of members can be interested and instructed in a study club to meet at times which do not
conflict with Lodge meetings. Masonry is divided for study under five
subjects: Ceremonial, Symbolical. Philosophical, Legislative and Historical. If the study club plan is adopted, care should be taken to see
that information developed in the Club reaches the Lodge membership
generally.

August 1, 1956
To: Chairman of Research Committee
From: Grand Master
Dear Brother:
Please consider this a personal letter of thanks for the assistance you
·h ave rendered this year. I will express myself more fully in my Annual
Message and I hope you can be present to hear it but, if not, I want you
to know that the progress made in research this year has been most
gratifying. Few, if any, jurisdictions are more active than ours in making Masonry more meaningful to the individual brother.
You will take special interest. I am sure, in the Seminar arranged by
the Committee on Research. It is to be held on Tuesday, September
18th, from 7 to 10 p.m. at 25 Van Ness Avenue, San Francisco. Those
attending Grand Lodge will have an opportunity to sign up at the registration desk in Polk Hall for a wide variety of classes. I wish it were
possible for every Research Chairman to attend the Seminar but, since
it is not, you may want to mention it to those who will represent your
Lodge.
My final request is that you promptly fill out and return the enclosed
questionnaire so that we may know what has been accomplished in our
jurisdiction and may have the benefit of your suggestions for the future.
