To The Most Worshipful Grand Ledge of California:
In his message to the Grand Lodge at its 1955 Communication.
Grand Master Henry C. Clausen recommended the appointment of a
special committee to study the present admission policy to the Masonic
Home at Decato under which applicants not P'hysically eligible for admission are cared for under a program of Outside Relief. He expressed
the belief that indigent and handicapped brethren should be cared for at
Decato instead of in private nursing homes.
The Special Committee has made a thorough study of this problem,
examining the present admission policy as it affects the physically handicapped, interviewing those now cared for by Outside Relief, and surveying the possibility of expanded facilities and staff at Decato to care
for such applicants.
The hospital at Decoto consistently cares for an average of 80 pa·tients which represents the maximum capacity for which it is licensed.
An average of 65 patients are permanent: while an average of 15 are
temporary.
In addition to those receiving hospital care, there are approximately
60 men and women being provided with special quarters and special
treatment, feeding ,and care. Out of a total population then of 340 on
August 15, 1956, 140 were in the hospital or special care section of the
home ... over 40% of the total guests.
It becomes immediately apparent that if the Masonic Home at Decoto
is to accept applicants who are physically handicapped and will require
special care, additional facilities and staff will be required.
As of August 15, 1956, there were 21 recipients of Outside Relief as
fornished by the Masonic Homes. A careful study of each recipient
showed that only seven were not physically eligible for the Home. The
balance of 14 are living with sons and daughters or other relatives, are
capable to administering to their own needs, and need only supplemental
income currently being furnished either by the Masonic Homes or by a
combination of aid from both the Masonic Homes and the Lodge. The
total amount of Outside Relief assistance contributed by the Masonic
Homes in the 1954-55 fiscal year was $17,223, or an average of $820
annually per recipient.
Contact was made to determine the present status of each recipient
of Outside Relief who was physically ineligible for admission to Decato.
In each instance it was the opinion of the Committee that such recipients
would require full hospitalization if admitted to Decoto and were not to
be classified as "nursing home" or "rest home" patients, although they
might ,have been so classified when application was first made.

228

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The Committee feels that the Masonic Home could, through improvisation, care for the additional seven patients who are now in nursing and rest homes, even though the present facilities would be sorely
taxed.
The Committee feels, however, that these seven patients do not represent the total problem. If they did and their admission would satisfy
all concerned, the Committee believes the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes would find ways and means of meeting their hospitalization
requirements.
The major 'Problem is represented in the great influx of applications
which must be anticipated if the Masonic Homes were to admit those
physically ·handicapped ineligibles. It is conceivable that there are many
members of Lodges and their wives who are now being cared for by
their families both at home and in private rest homes who have not made
application because of the present rules of admission. Many of these
members in the older ages receive state old age assistance which would
cease upon admission to the Masonic Homes. The present policy of
granting Outside Relief as a supplement to family and lodge contributions does not preclude their receiving State aid.
The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes is currently faced
with the problem of expanding its hospital and special care facilities to
provide for those guests who were admitted in average good health but
become incapacitated after admission. Even the present admission policy
requiring average good health for age is no guarantee that the guests will
not require special nursing service soon after admission.
If a more liberal policy on admission is adopted, then the expansion
of facilities and staff would be an immediate and expensive problem.
It is not within the province of this Committee to recommend such
policy to Grand Lodge. This Grand Lodge may, if it wishes, move to
expand its fraternal benefits beyond the present scope of the Masonic
Homes by providing funds for the building and staffing of additional
hospital and nursing home facilities.
The Committee does wish to point out that such a project is one of
major proportion and expense. Suc:h facilities must be of first-class construction, they must anticipate long term needs, and the staff must be
highly qualified. The Department of Public Health of the State of California has advised the Committee that nursing home units require approximately 30 square feet per bed. Thus a unit capable of serving 100
patients (and we believe that a smaller unit would not be realistic considering the growth of the Fraternity in a growing state) would require
a mimimum of 30,000 square feet. Because of the specialized nature of
the building it must be estimated that the cost would be between $800,000 and $900,000. The cost of staffing and maintaining such a unit for
100 patients is estimated at $20,000 a month or $240,000 per year.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

229

While this estimate may appear exaggerated the Committee feels
that facilities for 100 additional guests would not be excessive if long
term planning and anticipated growth are considered.
On the other hand, the Committee believes that the present program
renders satisfactory service within its realm and obligation. The recipients of Outside Relief not eligible for admission are being fully and
adequately provided for at a minimum cost to the Lodges of this jurisdiction. Lodges and families seem satisfied with the present approach
to a difficult problem.
In summary, the Committee concludes rliat the present system renders a satisfactory service within its intended limits. It recognizes the
existing problem of rendering increasing hospital and nursing home care
to those ·already admitted to the Home. It admires the charitable and
warm-hearted nature of the recommendation of Past Grand Master
Clausen.
Until Grand Lodge decides how far it shall go in its benefits to its
members, the Committee recommends that the present policy of admissions be maintained and that Outside Relief as a means of alleviating
want and distress among the physically handicapped be continued to its
fullest capacity.
Respectfully submitted,

J. LEO HALLEY
IRVING MAGNES
RALPH H. HEAD

Adopted . •

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON DeMOLAY
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
This past Masonic year has been a busy and most gratifying one for
your Committee on DeMolay. We would like to take this opportunity
to thank our Grand Master for the privilege of serving Masonry as part
of his official family.
The members of your committee have given unstintingly of their
time and energies in carrying out the charges placed upon them by the
96th Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge and in upholding the
precedents established by the committees who ihave worked so diligently
during the ten intervening years.
All requests to appear before groups of Masons to discuss the Order
of DeMolay were gratefully accepted. It has been our pleasure to appear
individually before Masonic Boards of Relief, Officers' Associations,
Lodges and Regional DeMolay Advisors' Associations. Each meeting
has served to further the understanding that we desire to have exist
between the Order of DeMolay and the body of Masonry.

230

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

The relative merits of the Order of DeMolay and their value in promoting a way of life among young men that is truly Masonic in character have been extolled in every annual report of this committee since its
·
inception and this committee concurs in their findings.
We understand that Masonic recognition of the Order of DeMolay
has taken rapid strides during the past few years. At the present time
ove~ 30 Grand Lodges fully endorse the Order. During the Grand Mas~;rs Conference held in Washington, D. C., last February. the subject
Is DeMolay a proper activity for Grand Lodges and the Subordinate
Lodges?" was debated. At the conclusion of the debate a straw ballot
was taken and the result was two to one for the affirmative.
At the last communication of this Grand Lodge a resolution presented by Brother Carl 0. Olsen, Past Master of Fremont Lodge No.
497, was referred to this committee for study and report on the recommendation of the committee on Policy and General Purposes.
The resolution read as follows: "Resolved, That The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge refer to a committee this resolution with the suggestion that investigation be made regarding the possibility of improving
the present status of DeMolay sponsorship within the State of California and under the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge."
The resulting studies made by this committee have provided certain
facts that should be cause for our concern.
First, though 14% of all the present members of the Order of DeMolay throughout the world reside in the State of California, this enviable position has resulted because of the dedicated service of a relatively
few Master Masons and cannot be considered as a credit to the activity
of California Masonry in general. W ·hen we consider the reports of law
enforcement officers and civic leaders which laud the effect of DeMolay
Chapters in the various communities, our imaginations are staggered by
the tremendous effect for good that could be had if the principles of the
Order of DeMolay were to be brought within the reach of all of the
eligible young men in our state.
Second, we found that the success or failure of an individual DeMolay chapter is entirely contingent on the quality of the adult leadership available to it. In some areas, where there are sound organizations
made up exclusively of Master Masons which can sponsor chapters, we
usually find a healthy situation. In many areas of this state, where the
only Masonic organization is a Lodge of Master Masons, which is presently precluded from sponsoring a chapter, we find that chapters exist
only where clubs comprised of Master Masons have been formed to
sponsor them.
. These clubs basically lack the necessary reserve of manpower and,
smce the local Masonic Lodges are prohibited from having anything to

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

231

do with them, do not have the sense of responsibility to Masonic principles which is very important to the continued successful operation of a
DeMolay chapter. This results in a gradual deterioration in the quality
of the adult leadership and consequently in the effectiveness of the chapter itself.
In many areas young men are deprived of the benefits offered by the
Order of DeMolay, because the present policy of this Grand Lodge
which prohibits Lodge sponsorship has made individual Masons reluctant to assume the responsibility for .forming a club of Master Masons for
the purpose of sponsoring a chapter.
Third, the Order of DeMolay by its constitution and ritual is emphatic in its statement that it is not a junior Masonic organization and
does not assure its members of future membership in Masonic bodies.
However, its principles, teachings and objectives are Masonic in nature
and definitely promote among young men the desire to live and act according to precepts which any Master Mason could be proud of.
Every year since the Order of DeMolay was founded in 1919, the
relationship between the Order and Masonry in general has been increasingly accepted by the public at lar~e to the extent that today the
success and reputation of the DeMolay Chapter in any given community
has become a direct reflection on the Masonic institutions in that community. Conversely, an unsuccessful DeMolay Chapter furnishes subject matter for unfavorable comment towards the whole Masonic .family.
In view of the foregoing. your committee recommends that the following steps be taken with the 6.rm conviction that the best interests of
Masonry will b~ thus served.
One. That the Committee on DeMolay be authorized to publish an
informational brochure in sufficient quantity so that an adequate supply
can be sent to each constituent lodge with the request that it be mailed
to each member thereof in conjunction with one of its regular mailings.
Adequate funds should be budgeted for this purpose.
This brochure should be of such size that it will be convenient for
either open or envelope mailing, with the back outside page left blank
for address purposes, if necessary. for the present established mailing
practices of some Lodges. An eight page, three fold size of approximately three and one half by six inches would be the most convenient.
The front page should be "eye catching" and inst~ll a strong desire in
the recipient to open and read it. The brochure should be prefaced with
a statement of the related policies of this Grand Lodge. The middle
portion of the text should contain a summary of the origin of DeMolay,
its purposes and requisites. In closing, the brochure should relate the position that California holds statistically in the international movement
and inspire a strong desire among its readers to maintain and improve
this position. The names and addresses of the members of the Commit-

232

PROCEEDINGS OP THE
GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

tee on DeMolay should be given with the invitation to make use of .their
services. The brochure thus described would cost about $1500 to publish in the quantities needed.
Two. That the committee be continued and that the sum of $1000
be appropria ted to cover its necessary expenses in the expanded program
contemplated.
Three. That this Grand Lodge recognize the inherent advantage s of
a clearly defined policy of assistance consistent with our ancient landmarks and charges. That the teachings of the Order of DeMolay. which
include the championship of the public schools and the inculcation of the
precepts of Filial Love, a belief in God, Courtesy, Comradeship, Fidelity,
Cleanness and Patriotism, are deserving of the unfettered attention of
Masonry.
To make this last recommendation effective, we submit the following
resolution and move for its adoption:
"Resolved. That every Chartered Lodge shall have the power to
sponsor Chapters of the Order of DeMolay, such sponsorsh ip to entail
the providing of competent adult leadership and the promotion of interest
in the purposes of the Order.
No Lodge shall be permitted to use Lodge funds in connection with
the sponsorship of a Chapter of the Order of DeMolay ."
Respectfully submitted,

Second: Demands have been made on one or more Lodges, and
upon the Grand Secretary that a transcript of the trial proceedings and
testimony taken at a masonic trial be furnished to the accuser and his
attorney. or to the accused and his attorney, it being urged that such a
transcript was necessary for a proper presentation of the appeal taken
by one or the other of the parties. In response to such demands we have
advised that such demand be refused. To furnish such a copy of the
proceedings would, be believe, be to violate the secrecy which should
su.rround the archives of the Lodge and those of Grand Lodge. and
might result in making public the record of the trial. We have. therefore,
advised that while it is entirely proper for the accuser and his masonic
counsel. or the accused and his masonic counsel to be allowed to examine
and study such trial record in the presence of the Master or the Secretary of the Lodge, neither the record, nor a copy thereof should be delivered to anyone, other than an authorized officer of the Lodge or of
Grand Lodge. This conclusion is in accordance with the spirit of Section
325 of our Ordinances as well as of Decision No. 731, made by Grand
Master Bledsoe, approved by Grand Lodge in 1915.

incarceration for some sex offenders in specialized institutions rather

R. G. R., a member of William D. Stephens Lodge No. 698, was

been found not guilty each time. Because of the seriousness of the

Counsel for the accused, at the trial made an attack by demurrer

While ·a demurrer, as such, is not provided for by our ]aw, we 8nd that
we must agree with the contention of the accused. A Mason charged
with unMasonic conduct must be confronted with allegations sufficiently
clear and definite to enable him to meet them. This specification was
a mere statement of conclusions with no particulars as to time, place nor
acts, and we believe that we should recommend to Grand Lodge that
the 8nding of guilt upon that specification be disapproved, To permit

it to remain in effect would establish a .precedent which we believe

A detailed study of the evidence leads us to the belief that the following facts were established by substantial evidence. As to Speci8cation 1

action was filed by the Catholic Bishop in the Superior Court of the

advertisers to believe that The Catholic News was an authorized Catholic Publication: that through his attorney the accused stipulated that
a final judgment might be entered against him enjoining him from such

against him. The accused presented his explanation of these facts to the

As to Speci8cation 2, the evidence contained in the record establishes

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1472
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of the State of California:
Your committee, to whi~h was referred trial record No. 1472, reports
as follows:
The accused, F. M. W., as Master of his Lodge, was charged with
un-Masonic conduct based upon specifications in substance as follows:
( 1 ) That accused violated sections 295 and 960 of Ross Digest. by
wilfully failing to call a special meeting to elect trial commissioners after
~harges of un-Masonic conduct against a brother was presented to him:
that said charges were not frivolous and charged Masonic offenses:
( 2) That accused held said charges five days and then returned
them to the accuser and refused to accept them or act on them and refused to can a special meeting to elect trial commissioners:
( 3) Same as specifications 1 ·a nd 2 but alleging in addition that accused failed and refused to have a copy of said charges forwarded to the
Grand Secretary:
( i) That accused violated the by-laws of a Temple Association
which was a subsidiary of the Lodge in that he refused to have the minutes of said Temple Association read at a Lodge meeting.
Accused was found not guilty on each specification and not guilty of
un-Masonic conduct.
An appeal has been taken.
It is true that the charges referred to in the specifications were subsequently forwarded to the Grand Master by the accusing brother and the
Grand Master held such charges to be sufficient and ordered the matter
to proceed to bial.
It is likewise true that our law contemplates that whenever charges
are presented to the Master of a Lodge he must give them consideration
and if he finds them sufficient he must call a special meeting for the election of trial commissioners.
The .fonowing sections of our Ordinances are pertinent:
Section 292. The charge itself shall be a general one of un-Masonic
conduct, defined in a specification or specifications to follow, setting
forth, with clearness and precision, the offense or offenses complained of.
and giving time, place, and all necessary particulars relating thereto, as
distinctly as possible, so that the accused may have full knowledge of an
that he may be called upon to explain, disprove, or justify.
Section 293. Such charges shall be presented to the Master of the
Lodge having jurisdiction thereof. and a copy shall forthwith be forwarded by the Secretary to the Grand Secretary.
Section 295. Upon the presentation of such charges, the Master
shall carefully examine the charge and specification, and, if they are
evidently frivolous, or if the act or acts with which the accused is
charged, is or are clearly such as do not constitute a Masonic offense, he

248

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

may refuse to entertain them. But, should it appear otherwise, and it is
known to him that the accuser is a Master Mason in good standing, he
shall call a special meeting of his Lodge, as soon as practicable.
Grand Lodge has held that the Master alone can pass upon the su·f ficiency of the charges in form and substance. (See Section 959, Ross
Digest).
The evidence discloses that the accused, when presented with the
charges against the brother, as referred to in the specifications, consulted
with P. G. M. Arthur Paulson and Judge Joe Shell, the Chairman of this
Committee, both of whom informed him that the charges were too loosely
drawn, contained much evidentiary matter and were replete with conclusions. They suggested to •him that he return the charges and suggest
to the accusing brother that they be redrawn and put in proper form.
This the brother apparently refused to do.
We are of the opinion that where, as here, a Master exercises his
discretion in good faith and acts upon competent advice, he is not guilty
of un-Masonic conduct even though the Grand Master might hold a
different opinion concerning the same Charges.
There is likewise no merit in the fourth specification that the accused
refused to read the minutes of the Temple Association.
The record shows that the accused, ·a t a meeting of his Lodge, announced that if there was no objection the reading of said minutes would
not be ordered as the hour was late. The accuser was present and offered no objection nor did he request that t'he minutes be read.
Judge Joe Shell deems himself disqualified and therefore did not participate in this decision.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
That the findings of the trial commission in Trial Record No. 14 72 be
ratified, affirmed and approved.
Adopted.

4. That during the course of a jury trial the accused withdrew his

plea of not guilty to two counts of the indictment, and entered a plea of
nolo contendere to said two counts:
5. That on or about February 21, 1955, the Federal Court in Los
Angeles imposed a fine upon the accused of $10,000.00 upon each of the
said two counts.
At the Masonic trial the accused appeared, admitted t'h e plea of nolo
contendere to each of the two counts of the indictment, and the imposition of the fine of $20,000.00, but urged upon the trial commissioners his
contention that fraud on his part was not involved in the making of the
false returns, and that •h e entered his plea of nolo contendere upon the

States Court.
The Masonic trial commissioners found adversely to these conten•
tions of the accused, voted unanimously to find him guilty of each speci·
fication, and voted unanimously for expulsion.
The ·accused has appealed to Grand Lodge from the findings and
verdict of the trial commission. Were it not for the appeal your Committee on Grievances would have reported this trial record for affirmation
in our omnibus report, but the filing of an appeal by the accused makes
this separate opinion necessary.
In •his appeal brief the accused attacks the sufficiency of specifications
3, 4 and 5 of the charge herein. Your Committee finds itself in agreement
with him. It Is not a Masonic offense to be indicted by a Grand Jury:
neither is it a Masonic offense to enter a plea of nolo ·contendere, nor is
it a Masonic offense to be fined $20,000.00. Therefore, the conviction
of the accused by the Masonic trial commissioners upon specifications 3,
4 and 5, would not justify 'his expulsion.
But there is no question as to the sufficiency of specifications 1 and 2,
charging the accused with filing false income tax returns for the calendar
years 1946 and 1947. Neither is there any question as to the sufficiency
of the evidence to justify the trial commissioners in finding the accused
guilty of each of those specifications. The penalty of expulsion imposed
by the trial commission is in complete accord with many prior decisions
of this Grand Lodge.
·
The accused contends fa his brief on appeal that the notice of expulsion sent to him by his Lodge is erroneous and incomplete. We have
examined the notice and find it to be in complete conformity with the
requirements of our ordinances. He also contends that, and I quote from
his brief:
" ... it should be noted that throughout the United States there have
been many Brothers of the Lodge who have found themselves involved
in tax situations, which have resulted in the same conclusion as that of
Brother A.C.A.'s matter. Yet, no disciplinary measures or proceedings
were taken against such Brothers."

251

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

Of course the foregoing statement can have little weight. As hereinbefore stated, the policy of this Grand Lodge, w.hen a brother has been
convicted of income tax evasion by a Masonic trial commission, has been
.
.
to expel the brother. .
We see no reason for adopting any other course m the instant matter,
and withholding approval of the conviction of the accused of specifications 3, 4 and 5, we offer the following resolution, and move its adoption:

privileges of Masonry, be and the same is hereby ratified, confirmed and
approved."
Adopted.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1485*
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1485, reports as follows:
Accused C. T. S. of Normal Heights Lodge No. 632 was charged
with un-Masonic conduct in five specifications.
The Trial Commission found him guilty of the first and fifth specifications and not guilty of the second, third and fourth specifications.
They also found Accused guilty of un-Masonic conduct and fixed the
penalty at suspension.
The first specification charged that on or about the 15th day of October, 1955, Accused then and there being Potentate of Al Bahr Temple
Ancient Arabic Order Nobles of the Mystic Shrine, and as such Potentate responsible for the activities and business of said Temple. did
sponsor advertising in a publication published by and on behalf of said
Temple and purporting to be Masonic in name or character, to wit:
"Al Bahr 18th Annual Shrine Charity Game and Pageantry" football
program: that said Temple is an organization requiring Masonic affiliation as a condition of membership.
The second, third and fourth specifications charged Accused with
inserting, placing advertising and printing advertising, respectively, in
the publication referred to in the first specification.
The fifth specification charged that Accused on or about April. 1955,
attended a meeting called by the Most Worshipful Henry C. Clausen,
Grand Master of Masons of the State of California, and that he was
then informed by said Grand Master that the sponsoring, inserting,
placing and printing of advertising in a publication published by or on
behalf of said Temple and purporting to be Masonic in name or character constituted a violation of Section 127 of the Ordinances of Grand
Lodge.
That, thereafter, about the month of May, 1955, Accused attended
a meeting of Shrine Potentates at which were present two members of
the Committee on Publications of the Grand Lodge of the State of California; that said Accused and the other Potentates there present were

informed by the members of the publications committee .that the sp.onsoring, inserting, placing or printing of advenisements m the pubhc~­
tions above referred to was a violation of Masonic law as set forth in

said personal knowledge by Accused, he did, as Po~ent~te of. Al Bahr

The flnding of guilty of specifications 1 and 5 are amply supported
by the evidence and your committee concurs in these flndings.
The evidence showed an attempt to evade the requirements of Section 127 of the Ordinances by having the program published by San
Diego State College, the college to pay all costs of publicati.on and the

as a subterfuge.

accordance with this established policy. the penalty m this case should
be raised .from suspension to expulsion.

was charged with un-Masonic conduct by several specifications alleging
that as a Director of the John L. Spreckels Masonic Temple Assn., he
failed to keep records of funds raised; no accounting rendered to the
association; attempting to .falsify records of said association, making a
profit on land bought for association; received a real estate commission
for the purchase of land .for association; .failed to make an annual report
to shareholders of the association.
Trial was held in Point Loma Lodge No. 620 at which time the accused was found guilty of the specification charging the accused with
receiving a commission for the purchase of property by the association of
which he was a Director, and not guilty of all other specifications and
not guilty of un-Masonic conduct.
This whole controver·s y centers around the John D. Spreckels Masonic Temple Assn. The accuser, a Past Master of John D. Spreckels
Lodge became disappointed because the association would not support
him in certain plans he proposed for the new temple, and in general
would not cooperate with him during the year he was Master of John
D. Spreckels Lodge. After the accuser retired ·a s Master he filed
charges against the accused, one of the Directors of the ·association.
The charges w~re lengthy and contained evidentiary matter as well
as conclusions of law. The Master of John D. Spreckels Lodge rejected
the charges as not being in proper form. The accuser thereupon forwarded the charges to the Grand Master who ordered the accused tried
on the charges.
A fair and impartial ·t rial was held in Point Loma Lodge No. 620
located in the same city as John D. Spreckels Lodge No. 657.
After examining the trial record, your committee is of the opinion
that there is sufficient evidence to support the verdict of not guilty on all
specifications except No. 3.
As to Speciflcation No. 3 the accused, while a Director of John D.
Spreckels Masonic Temple Ass'n., is charged with allowing a commission to be charged on a real estate transaction in which he was the real
estate salesman. This transaction involved the purchase of a Masonic
Temple site by the John D. Spreckels Masonic Temple Ass'n. A full
disclosure of t~ese facts was made to the lodge at their stated meeting
and also the Directors of the Masonic Temple Ass'n. Under these circumstances your committee fails to find any violations of civil or Masonic law.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1496*
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1496, reports as follows:
The Accused, J.M. N., a member of San Diego Lodge No. 35, was,
by order of the Grand Master, charged with un-Masonic conduct and
tried in S .. W. Hackett Lodge No. 574. The specifications were to the
following effect:
First: That on or about October 15, 1955, Accused did print advertising in a publication purporting to be Masonic in name and character,
to wit: "Al Bahr Eighteenth Annual Shrine Charity Game and Pagean-

255

Ordinances of Grand Lodge.
Second: That on or about October 15, 1955, Accused did insert advertising in the publication named in the first specification in violation of
said Section 127.
Third: That Accused did the acts set forth in Specifications First
and Second in violation of his Masonic obligation in that he failed and
refused to comply with the laws, rules and regulations of the Grand
Lodge of California, under which his Lodge is holden.
Accused was present at the trial and represented by counsel. He
plead guilty to the first and second specification and not guilty to the
third specification.
The Football Program referred to in the specifications was introduced in evidence. It obviously purported to be Masonic in name and
character. Accused testified that he was connected with a printing
company which had previously printed several similar football programs
for Al Bahr Temple of fhe Shrine; that originally Al Bahr Temple
planned to have the program printed; that prior to the publication of the
program Accused was informed that it was illegal to publish the program
for Al Bahr Temple but that it would not be illegal if it were published
for San Diego State College. Accordingly, San Diego State College
contracted for the publication o'f the program; that he placed an advertisement in the :program at the solicitation of a member of the Shrine;
that if he had known that publication of the program for San Diego
State College was in violation of the Ordinances of Grand Lodge he
would not have published it; that his company printed a publication
called Al Barometer for Al Bahr Temple; that he knew of Ordinance 127
and that because of it he knew that advertising could not be placed in
Al Barometer.
Accused having plead guilty to specifications 1 and 2, no vote was
taken on them. The Commissioners found Accused guilty of specification 3 and of un-Masonic conduct and fixed the penalty at suspension.
The evidence amply supports the findings of the Commissioners and
these findings should be affirmed. However, the penalty of suspension
is not in accord with the established policy of this Grand Lodge concerning such violations of Section 127 of its Ordinances. It is the policy of
this Grand Lodge that for such violations Grand Lodge should be vested
with the right to pass upon the future applications, if any, of the Accused
for restoration. When the penalty is expulsion, Grand Lodge retains
that right, whereas, w'hen the penalty is suspension, Grand Lodge does
not have that right.
Resolved that the action of the Trial Commissioners in Trial Record
No. 1496 finding J.M. N. guilty of un-Masonic conduct is ratified, con-

by Al Bahr Temple and containing the individual photographs of the
Pageant Committee members wearing the Fez of the Temple, together
with a full list of all members of the assisting committee could have been
prepared without 'his knowledge.
The evidence at the trial, while conflicting on the issue of "knowledge," was sufficient to sustain the findings of the Trial Commissioners
that the accused did have knowledge that the program was Masonic in
character and was guilty of Specifications 1 and 3 and said findings are
affirmed.

Commissioners that the alleged conduct of which they had found the
accused guilty did not constitute un-Masonic conduct. In this we cannot
concur.
In numerous decisions involving this same Section 127 of the Ordinances, this Grand Lodge has, without exception, held that violations of
the nature of those of which this accused was found guilty do constitute
un-Masonic conduct.

reversed and that by action of this Grand Lodge that said accused be

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1501
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee to which was referred Trial Record No. 1501, reports as follows:
The accused E. A. H .. a member of Normal Heights Lodge No. 632,
was charged with un-Masonic conduct in two specifications:
1. That on January 1, 1956, accused did convert to his own use certain narcotics, the same being legally in his care by vinue of his .profession as a doctor.
2. That accused fraudulently wrote 'Prescriptions in the names of one
or more persons to implement Specification 1.
At the trial. there was introduced certified copy of court records
showing that the accused pleaded guilty to a charge of failure to keep
proper records of the narcotics in his profession. The accused testified
in his behalf that he suffered substantial pain when working under pressure and that he used for himself part of the demerol (a narcotic) which
he prescribed for patients. Further, that he stopped doing this before the
narcotic agents made an examination.
The trial commissioners found the accused guilty of Specification 1,
not guilty of Specification 2, and not guilty of un-Masonic conduct.
The finding of not guilty of un-Masonic conduct is entirely inconsistent with the finding of guilty on Specification 1. Having found the
accused guilty of converting to his own use narcotics which he obtained
for his patients. such conduct certainly constitutes a Masonic offense.
Your Committee feels that the penalty in cases involving narcotics
should be expulsion and therefore offers the following resolution:
Resolved: That the Trial Commissioner's finding in Trial Record No.
1501, that E. A. H. is guilty of Specification 1 be approved and affirmed;
that the finding that he is not guilty of un-Masonic conduct be disapproved and a finding of guilty be supplied: and that the penalty be and
it is hereby fixed at expulsion.
Adopted.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1507
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
C. E. J., a member of Oxnard Lodge No. 341, was charged with being part owner of a cafe dispensing liquor, and being a bartender
thereof. He was tried, found guilty and expelled.
However the summons was served on the accused by registered mail

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

259

six days prior to the trial. He r~sided in Camarillo. Our ordinances
plainly provide that if the accused is within the jurisdiction of the lodge
he must be served personally or by leaving the summons at his home or
place of business at least ten days before the trial. If he resides elsewhere in the state he may be served by mail at last thirty days before
the trial.
The accused herein did not appear at the trial or file any answer.
He ·did not submit himself to the jurisdiction of the trial commission.
The service by mail only six days before the trial was fatally defective
and the commission had no authority to try the accused on the date set.
We must remand the case for proper proceedings. We note also there
was not a separate vote on the specification and on un-Masonic conduct.
We therefore offer the .following resolution:
Resolved, That the expulsion of C. E. J. by Oxnard Lodge No. 341
be reversed and the matter remanded to that Lodge for retrial.
Adopted.

BOARD MEMBERSHIP

with one of the children. In addition to the dinner there are games, gifts
and group singing. It is not the mere dinner but the personal fellowship
and companionship which makes this a memorable event for the children
and a real thrill to all who participate in it.
Summer activities increased this year. Forty members paid nominal
dues during the six weeks summer session and not only used the Club
facilities but carried on a summer social program.
The members of our "Honorary" organization ·have ceased to rest on
their laurels and have become active in promoting regular Club activities. This brings back to the campus a number of students who have
graduated and whose experience is most helpful.
Another group which is becoming more active and more important
consists of the married students. They have formed an informal group
within the Club and are operating not as a special clique but to further
the social functions of the whole group. As the University develops its
graduate schools, we will have an increased number of married students
and it is important that this group be integrated into the Club program.

The Grand Master nominated and your Board elected three new
members to the Board to flll existing vacancies, bringing us up to our
fu~l membership of flfteen. The terms are for three years, flve members
being elected or re-elected in May of each year. We shall indicate at
the end of this report the year in which the term of each member terminates.
The three new members are Brothers Frank Jenkins (Lodge No.
528 >: ~eorge Kussman ( 506). and Dr. Tyler Parker ( 599). Brother
Jenkins daughter attended U.C.L.A. and was an active member of the
C~ub .. He has attended many of the Club functions and is quite familiar
with i~s problems. Dr. Parker, a former Inspector, brings many years of
experience to our Board. Brother Kussman also has been very active in
Masonry fo_r many years and is most interested in this new assignment.
Our Board is deeply appreciative of the Grand Master's nominations.
We regret to announce the retirement from active membership on
the Board of Past Grand Master Ellsworth Meyer. He had served the
Board for twenty years and probably no one man has done more than
he _to shape the policies of the Club. We appreciate however that his
retirement from the Board was not to relieve him from Masonic work
but to enable him to devote more time to his other varied and important
Masonic activities.
STUDENT AcTIVITIEs

The students carry on their activities through their own Club organiz~tio~, their own officers and Student Council, operating under a
Constitution approved by the Board. The Board provides the facilities
direction and supervision, but the students through their own dues and
charges carry on the social activities. These are many and varied. Last
year as part of our report we furnished Grand Lodge with a complete
digest of the year's program. Mrs. Sheldon, our very capable Director
has furnished us again this year with a complete report. It describe~
fo~~-.four special events, in addition, of course, to the daily use of the
facilities of the Club for study, informal social gatherings reading
games, television, snack bar, etc. We note that the attendande at thes~
special functions varied from approximately 50 to 230.
The latter number represents the attendance at the Grand Master's
Reception, which is always the biggest social event of the year. It is put
on .by the s~u~ents at their own expense and is their way of showing
their appreciation to the Masons of California as represented by their
Grand Master. The address of Grand Master Edgar V. Stewart, Jr.,
was much appreciated by the students.
. Anot?er annual event Which is always a success is the Thanksgiving

di~ner giv~n to unde11privileged children from All Nations Foundation.
It is held in the Club House. Each student buys a ticket for and sits

PUBLICITY

We have repeatedly reported that the one major problem is to increase membership. From the student's standpoint this will result in
more dues and increased activities and benefits. From the Board's standpoint this will result in the Masonic program being just that much more
effective and at no f\Ubstantial increase in overhead cost and hence at a
lower cost per student member.
There are. two basically different approaches to the problem. First,
in working from the total student membership at the University and
seeking out those with Masonic affiliations. Second, in working through
the Masons of California who in turn cause the students to seek us out.
It is essential of course that we pursue both approaches.
The flrst is done best through the student organization and they are
doing their part through orientation programs, open house, floats and
other participation in University programs, the school paper, etc. In
addition attractive brochures are sent to all new students each year
with an invitation to avail themselves, if qualifled, of the Club facilities.
The second must be accomplished through the Masons themselves.
Publicity through Grand Lodge, such as Proclamations read in Lodges,
have been helpful but have not resulted in any substantial increases in
membership. We have considered for some time the desirability of a
motion picture such as the one used to publicize the endowment program
of the Masonic Homes. The members of the Board sitting with the
. Student Council have encouraged the latter group in their efforts to develop their own colored fllm of Club activities. While several such projects have been started, none has been completed.
Recently the idea has been given momentum through discussion

266

PROCEEDINGS OP THE
GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

of the problem with Brother Julian Harmon who wrote the script for the
Masonic Homes motion picture. While that picture was produced at a
greatly reduced cost through the actors donating their services, etc., the
cost of even that type of film would be prohibitive for us. Our approach
would have to be on a do-it-yourself basis but under expert supervision
so as to assure ·professional quality both in story and mechanical reproduction. We are advised that the basic cost of film and processing including sound would be about $1000 for a twenty minute film, and that
if the students did all the work a professional quality picture could be
produced for twice that figure. This is less than one-tenth the cost of the
Masonic Homes film, which in turn was produced at only a fraction of
normal cost. Brother Harmon has volunteered to supervise such a project.
At the time of writing this report the project has not been sufficiently
ex,plored to enable us to decide whether it is completely feasible or
whether the estimated cost is realistic. It should not be done at all, of
course, unless it is done right. The idea however has great possibilities
and we expect to explore it .further.
Respectfully submitted,

INVOCATION

0 God, before whom our little span of years is like the brief shining
of a can~le, whe~ the flame of this mortal life flickers and one day must
go out, give us faith that beyond the shadows is Thy eternal light. Create within us a deeper seriousness that yet needs not be sad. As we come
nearer to the day when earthly possessions and pride must pass away,
help us to seek more faithfully those inner riches of the soul which nothing can destroy. Increase our longing for life in God, and of Thy mercy
lead us on toward the beginning of its fulfillment here and now. Let us
come unafraid toward the gate of death, with trust in the wonder that
waits on the other side. Amen.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON NECROLOGY
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The inexorable passage of time again brings us to the hour when we
pause in our deliberations to exipress our love, respect and admiration,
for those of our brethren who since the last communication of the Grand
Lodge have answered the call of the Supreme Grand Master.
Our Fraternity does not solicit members, nor in its ritual. nor in its
activities does it compel any man to labor in its interest. The time and
effort given in its behalf by its members is voluntary, given for the love
of the organization, and without hope or expectation of material reward.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

269

It is a labor of unselfish devotion, given by thousands of good men, and
in all the acts of life none are freer of selfish motives.
With a full realization of the debt we owe to all those who have
preceded us, and especially to those of our brethren who have in the last
year gone on to the great beyond, we give our thoughts and our thanks,
for there are duties which we owe to our dead that are equally sacred
with those due to the living. Thanks to the healing influence of time
the trials and tribulations of everyday life are wiped from the memory,
but the death of those near and dear to us is a sorrow we never fully
relinquish. Washington Irving, the great American author, beautifully
expressed the thought when he said "sorrow for the dead is the only
sorrow from which we refuse to be divorced. Every other wound we
seek to heal--every other affliction to forget; but this wound we consider
it a duty to keep open-this affiiction we cherish and brood over in
solitude."
Since the last communication death has taken 326 members of the
Grand Lodge. One Past Grand Master, George L. Jones of Nevada
City; two Committeemen, Leonard R. A villa of Palo Alto, and Harry
P. Ritchie of Los Angeles; one former Committeeman, Warren E. Libby
of Los Angeles: one Inspector, Miles J. McClelland of Sacramento; two
former Inspectors, Martin G. DeHaan of Los Angeles, and Horace E.
Vedder of South Pasadena.
In the passing of the Masters and Past Masters the heaviest losses
were suffered by Petaluma Lodge No. 180 and Los Banos No. 312, each
losing five Th9se losing four each were Emmanuel No. 318, and Garden
Grove No. 586. Eleven lodges lost 3 each; 56 lodges lost 2 each, and
163 lodges lost 1 each.
The limitation of time prevents our giving in detail the accomplishments of each of our 326 deceased members although they have earned
and merited our approbation. Our thoughts go to several who are
sorely missed and whose contributions have covered long periods of
time, and have contributed greatly to our success and to the success of
the communities in which they lived. James Herbert Kew. Organizer
and first Master of Inglewood Lodge No. 421: Fred Charles Granholt,
Past Master of Sequoia Lodge No. 349: Herbert Ivar Thomas, Pentalpha Lodge No. 202: William Chaney, Past Master, San Benito Lodge
No. 211: James Reade Watson. Past Master Mount Jackson Lodge No.
295: and Elbert Neil Clintsman, Past Master, Apollo Lodge No. 396.
LEONARD R. AVILLA
Death, as it must to all men, came to Judge Leonard R. Avilla Saturday night, February 25th, 1956, at his home at 1717 Middlefield Road,

270

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Palo Alto. Watching television with his 'family he was stricken with a
heart attack and died a few minutes later.
A native son, born in Oakland December 5, 1902, he was raised on
a dairy ranch at Hughson, near Modesto.
He took his A.B. degree at Stanford University in 1925. and engaged in business until 1929, when he entered Stanford Law School. In
1931 he was admitted to practice Jaw before federal and state courts.
In 1940 Judge AvilJa became Assistant District Attorney of Santa
Clara County, and was named District Attorney by the board of supervisors in March, 1945, to replace John P. Fitzgerald, who died in office.
Leonard Avilla was the highest type of public official. discharging
his duties without fear or favor. After months of investigation and with
the aid of special groups of police organized by him he obtained enough
evidence to bring an indictment, trial and conviction of those operators
of vice, gambling and slot machines in Santa Clara County. Governor
Earl Warren appointed him Judge of the Superior Court in September,
1947.
Brother Avilla entered Masonry in 1940. Initiated March 12, passed
March 30 and raised May 28, in Palo Alto Lodge No. 346. He was
Master of the Lodge in 1947. His keen interest and enthusiasm for the
Fraternity soon Jed him into other branches and he became a member
of the Roya] Arch, Knights Templar and the Order of the Eastern Star
of Palo Alto and of the Scottish Rite Bodies of San Jose. Our present
Grand Master recognizing his ability and wiJJingness to further the interests of the Fraternity appointed him a member of the Homes Endowment Board.
Brother Avi11a's other affi.Jiations were the Elks Lodge and Lions
Club of Palo Alto. He was also a past president of the Palo Alto Parlor,
Native Sons of the Golden West, and he was a state official of that
organization.
The Judge is survived by his widow, the former LiJJian Lanthier of
Palo Alto, whom he married in 1934, and a teenage daughter Lynne
EUen; also a brother, Roy H. AviUa of Los Gatos, and a sister, Mrs.
Ray D. Leavitt.
We lament the passing of this distinguished brother and pray that
the Great Architect of the Universe wi]] grant him the peace and comfort he so richly deserves.
WARREN EDGAR LIBBY

It saddens the heart to have to record the passing of a brother who
has worked so Jong and so hard.
On December 22, 1955, Warren E. Libby died at the age of 67 at
the Broadview Nursing Home in Los Angeles.

271

Born April 8, 1888 in Lisbon, Maine. He obtained his common
school education in the public schools of Lisbon and Auburn in the state
of his birth. In 1909 he received the Bachelor of Arts degree at Bates
Co11ege, Lewiston, Maine. In 1909 and 1910 he taught and coached
athletics at Goddard Seminary in Perre, Vermont. He later graduated
from George Washington Law Schoo], Washington, D. C.
He began the practice of his profession in San Diego, California in
1912, transferring his activities to Los Angeles in 1923. In 1928 the firm
of Libby and Sherwin was founded.
His interest and enthusiasm for his high caUing caused him to devote
much of his time to the service of the legal •profession. He was a member of the State Bar of California, Los Angeles Bar Association, American Bar Association. and the American Law Institute.
Warren served as a member of the State Bar Committee to Revise
Corporation Laws, State Bar Legislative Committee, Chairman of the
Conference of State Bar Delegates, Chairman of the County Courts of
State Committee, member of the State Bar Board of Governors. He was
chief counsel of Pickwick Stage System until it merged with the Pacific
Greyhound Lines in 1932.
His Masonic career was as active and outstanding as his professional
career. August 4, 1909, he was elected to receive the degrees in Raboni
Lodge No. 150 in Lewiston, Maine. He received the Master Degree
on August 24, 1909. completing the entire course in a period of three
weeks. He demitted from his mother lodge in 1913 to become a charter
member of Blackmer Lodge No. 442 of San Diego. and he retained his
membership in that lodge until his death. He served the lodge as Master
in 1919.
Warren Libby's activities in the Grand Lodge were many and varied.
He was appointed Senior Grand Steward in 1919 and again in the years
1931 to 1933 fiUed the office of Senior Grand Deacon. A member of the
Grievance Committee 1921-22; the foUowing year Chairman Committee on Charters; 1924 member Committee on pay of members: 1924 to
1931 a member of the Credentials Committee: 1933 to 1935 member
Committee on By-Laws, and he; was for several years Chairman, Committee on Clandestine Masonry.
His Masonic activities extended beyond those of the Blue Lodge.
He was a member of Melrose Chapter No. 140 Royal Arch Masons
joining in 1932, the same year he took the degrees in Southern California Council No. 35 Roya] and Select Masters; and in 1934 became a
member of Golden West Commandery No. 43.

272

273

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

He received the highest ·honors from the Scottish Rite Bodies. Graduating with the spring class of 1930 he received the rank and decoration
of Knight Commander of the Court of Honor in 1939, and in October,
1947, h~ was elected by the Supreme Council to the 33rd degree. His
coronation as a 33rd degree gave great happiness to his many friends in
those bodies.
In civic affairs Warren was ever willing to give of his time and
experience. In World War I he was chairman of the Minutemen of
San Diego County, and in World War II was a member of a local draft
board. He served as president of the Men's Club of Beverly Hills, and
devoted much time to his church, The First Church of Christ Scientist of
Beverly Hills.
He is survived by his widow, Mrs. Elsie Pomeroy Libby, whom he
married in San Diego in 1913.
Warren Libby was the Lord's true and faithful soldier: a great
Mason: a flne citizen, a kind and loving husband. We leave him in
God's hands. thankful that he was our friend and brother.

Harry is survived by his wife Mary, a daughter Harriet, and a
brother, Mart.
His life was an embodiment of all the strong virtues, an example to
his brethren and an inspiration to all who knew him.

HARRY p. RITCHIE

The Grand Lodge suffered a grievous loss on May 3, 1956, when
death claimed the Chairman of the Sojourner's Committee Harry P
Ritchie of Los Angeles.
'
·
Harry was raised in Menorah Lodge No. 623 in 1945. His earnestness. zeal, industry and ability on various committees and in the appointive offices soon earned him the honor of the Master's chair. One of
the proudest moments of his life was his installation as Master in 1954
by Edgar V. Stewart, Jr., now Grand Master.
'
In addition to his work in Menorah Lodge ·he was active in the Scottish Rite Bodies of Los Angeles and also in Al Malaika Temple of the
Shrine.
Harry Ritchie was an excellent speaker and used his talents on many
occasions to further the flnancial interests of the new Grand Lodge
Temple in San Francisco. He was eminently successful in obtaining
many donations to that worthy cause.
Harry was born December 23, 1904, in the City of Fullerton, California, received his early schooling in that city, and after graduation
from t~e P~<::iflc Military Aca~emy .entered the School of Pharmacy at
the University of Southern California. After graduating as a pharmacist
he owned and operated a number of drug stores. He conceived the idea
of packing nuts in small sanitary containers and selling them in drug
stores. Later he extended this business to theatres and became the
largest retail distributor of nuts in the United States. His product had
large sales in Canada, Cuba, Mexico, Alaska and the Hawaiian Islands.

MARTIN GREENWALD DEHAAN

It is with a heavy heart that we report the passing of an untiring
community, civic, religious and Masonic leader.
Martin G. DeHaan died suddenly Tuesday, November 8, 1955, at
his home, 911 Oxford Way, Beverly Hills. He was age 56.
Born November 19, 1899. in Memphis, Tennessee, •he was brought
to Los Angeles by his parents when 12 years of age. He obtained his
education on the public schools of that city. His business life was spent
in mercantile lines. For many years he held one of the highest positions
in Bullock's Department Store. and at the time of his death was a manufacturer's agent covering the Paciflc Coast area.
Martin's Masonic career began November 24, 1919, when he petitioned West Gate Lodge No. 335. He was initiated January 8, 1920,
passed February 2, 1920, and raised to the sublime degree March 8, the
same year. Passing through the chairs he occupied the East in 1927.
In 1944 Claude H. Morrison, Grand Master, appointed him Inspector of District No. 76 and ·he filled that office with distinction for 6
years, resigning in 1950. In 1954 Grand Master Harwell appointed him
Grand Sword Bearer, and at the One Hundred Fifth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge he filled that office with distinction and honor.
He was a 32nd degree Mason of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite
Bodies of Los Angeles.
Martin DeHaan was an ardent follower of his religion and for 20
years was head usher at the Wilshire Boulevard Temple, and for the
last flve years of his life was a member of the board of trustees. Masonic
funeral services were held in that beautiful temple under the able direction of Brother Abe Blumenthal. Past Master of West Gate Lodge.
The eulogy was delivered by Rabbi, Brother Edgar F. Magnin.
He is survived by his widow Ruth, a brother, Saul, and a stepson.
Martin DeHaan enjoyed the confldence and esteem of his brethren
and discharged his duties with good judgment and with devotion °to the
ideals of the Fraternity. He will be sorely missed.
HORACE EGLESTON VEDDER

Being in ill health for several years Horace Vedder closed his
earthly existence March 19, 1956, at Wadsworth Hospital, Sawtelle,
California.
Son of Albert G. Vedder. a lumber dealer, and his wife Anna Neu-

274

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

bauer Vedder, Horace was born in Schenectady, New York, August
17, 1887.
Horace attended Schenectady High School. graduating in 1906:
Union College, graduating in 1910, and Albany Law School. graduating
in 1912. His fraternities were Union College, Ohi Psi and Albany Law,
Phi Delta Phi.
Immediately after graduation from law school he came to Los Angeles. He opened offices in the Van Nuys Building. specializing in
probate and real estate law. In 1925 he was admitted to practice before
the United States Supreme Court.
He was ever mindful of 'his civic and patriotic responsibilities and
served as councilman for the City of South Pasadena .from 1924 to 1927.
Appointed city attorney in 1927, he served through 1941. In World
War I he was first lieutenant. aviation division of the Signal Corps, and
at his death was Captain of Reserves. He was president of the Valley
Hunt Club, Pasadena 1941 -42.
Horace Vedder was a member of South Pasadena Lodge No. 367
having been initiated June 13, 1922, passed October 10, and raised
November 28 the same year. His outstanding record as Master of South
Pasadena Lodge claimed the attention of the Grand Master and John
Stewart Ross appointed :him Inspector of the 91st District in 1931, and
he filled that office with great credit to himself and to the fraternity for
the 16 succeeding years. He was a member of the Royal Arch of Los
Angeles and a 32nd degree Mason of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of that city.
He was married to Ruth Ahlsmede of Pasadena, June 7, 1916. He
is survived by his widow, a daughter Mrs. Frank A. Thomas, and two
grand-daughters. Ann Maria and Joan Louise. He was buried with full
military honors at Veterans Administration Cemetery, West Los Angeles.
Horace Vedder had many claims to greatness, but only his closest
friends were aware of them. for the chief mark of his greatness was his
humility, and the deepest of his virtues was his sincerity.
"Faith shines in the eyes of M~sons, inspired neither by fear nor
rote, their faith rests in the conviction that God is a friend, understanding and kind. and a source of light when the world is dark."
We say to our departed brethren that it is our deepest wish that those
who come after us will benefit as much from our labors as we have benefited from theirs. Until God grants us meeting-farewell.

GEORGE Louis JoNES

By Leslie E. Wood, P.G.M.
On Friday. the twenty-second of June, nineteen hundred and flftysix, one month and eleven days after his eighty-third birthday, this
mortal life ended for our sixtieth Grand Master, George Louis Jones and
a long and distinguished career came to an end.
Brother Jones was born in Truckee, California on May 11, 1873. A
year and a half later ·he moved with his parents to Grass Valley and
resided in that city until his marriage in 1905 to Miss Helen Crocker
Mott, when the young couple took up residence in Nevada City, where
he spent the remainder of his life.
He was a graduate of the Grass Vally High School with the class of
1889. He was graduated from the University of California at Berkeley
in 1895 and Hastings Law College in 1897. He returned to Grass Valley to practice and in 1900 became associated in a partnership with the
late Lloyd P. Larue. This partnership continued during the time he
served as city attorney of Grass Valley and later as district attorney of
Nevada County.
He became judge of the Superior Court in 1908 and served in that
capacity until 1925 when he resigned to become president of the Nevada
County Bank. When this institution merged with the Bank of America,
he was named the first president in Nevada City. But this calling apparently was not to his liking because •h e soon returned to the practice of
law and formed a partnership with Frank G. Finnegan. In 1938 he returned to the Nevada County bench where he served as Superior Court
Judge until his retirement in 1947. He operated the Jones Memorial
Hospital in Grass Valley after the death of his brother, Dr. Carl Power
Jones in 1944.
He was a fifty year member of Madison Lodge No. 23, F. & A. M.
and was Grand Master of this Grand Lodge in 1926-27. His zeal for
the fraternity kept him active in the fields of Masonry until his recent
illness. He was a fifty year member of Grass Valley Lodge No. 12,
Independent Order of Odd Fellows, where he served as Master of that
lodge and later as Grand Master of the state. He held a fifty year membership in Quartz Parlor No. 58, Native Sons of the Golden West and
served as President and Trustee of that parlor. His fourth flfty year
recognition was as a member of the University of California Alumni
Association. He was a member of Grass Valley Chapter, Royal Arch
Masons, Nevada Commandery No. 6, Knights Templar and the Nevada
County Historical Society.
On May 5, 1952, the Nevada County Historical Society, joined by
church, fraternal and civic organizations of western Nevada County,

276

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

held a dinner in his honor where he was named the "Citizen of the
Year."
In addition to his fraternal and legal accomplishments Judge Jones
was active in civic work. He was instrumental in founding the Nevada
County Chapter of the Red Cross, The Nevada County Tuberculosis
and Health Association, county chairman for civil defense during World
War 1, thirty-three years a scouter with the Tahoe Area Council of the
Boy Scouts of America and was a former council officer. He was chairman of the Salvation Army Advisory Board and chairman for many
Salvation Army committees. He was interested in 4-H and other youth
organizations and many other less known but time consuming programs
and endeavors.
Truly George L. Jones lived a full and useful life-dedicated to the
service of his fellow creatures. He was kindly and sympathetic by nature and possessed of that rare quality which enables one to understand
the problems of others and to overlook human frailties in his fellow
men, yet so strong was his belief in justice and right that he never
compromised with wrong.
In paying this last tribute to him we express our appreciation for the
magnificent contributions he made to this Grand Lodge and Masonry
throughout the jurisdiction. The record of his accomplishments as a
committeeman, an officer and finally as Grand Master testify to his zeal.
his ability and deep affection for the fraternity.
No greater tribute can be paid to any man than to say that he was
faithful to his creator, a loving and kind husband and father, a Ane citizen and an ardent and true Mason.
May God in His infinite wisdom, grant that this beloved friend and
brother may find peace in his Father's house.
AGAINST ANXIETY

We conclude this service of memory, 0 God, realizing that in thee
is our peace for today and our reliance for tomorrow. Lift us above our
little fears to a steadier faith in thy goodness which does not fail: so
that we may walk the same changing roads as our brothers who have
gone on before us, knowing that thou wilt be with us all the way. even
unto the end. Amen.

ADDRESS OP THE GRAND MASTER

Brother Grand Lodge Officers, Most Worshipful Past Grand Masters,
Distinguished Guests, Mg Brethren and Friends:

PRESENTATION OP THE GRAND MASTER

Ladies and gentlemen---our guests here today-and mg Brethren:
I am L. Harold Anderson, Deputy Grand Master of the Grand Lodge
of Masons in California and chairman of the cornerstone ceremony
committee.
Before introducing our Grand Master, I should like, on behalf of the
committee, to express our thanks to many individuals-within and outside of the lodge-who have cooperated to make this event possible.
We have had fine assistance in making our arrangements from the
Honorable Board of Supervisors of the City and County of San Francisco, Mayor George Christopher, Chief Administrative Officer Thomas
A. Brooks, Police Chief Frank Ahern, the Public Utilities Commission
of San Francisco and its manager, James H. Turner, and the city's Art
Commission through whose cooperation we are able to present the
Municipal Band directed by John Afendras. We thank all of these representatives of the City for their excellent help.
As committee chairman, I want to express my personal thanks to all
those who have contributed in the planning and organization of this
cornerstone ceremony. I hesitate to take the time to read all their names,
but I can assure you that these unsung men-as usual-are the ones who
really make such presentations as this possible.
And now, it is my privilege and pleasure to introduce the man who
will preside over this program, the Most Worshipful Edgar V. Stewart,
Junior, Grand Master of Masons in California. Brother Stewart.

It is indeed a pleasure to greet you on this, one of the most historic
days in the annals of California Masonry. That you realize the importance of this occasion is proved by the fact that so many of you have
come to share the joy of the day with us. We welcome you all and
we rejoice in your friendship and your loyalty.
Before proceeding further, I must pay tribute to the individual who,
more than any other, is responsible for the myriad arrangements made
for our comfort and convenience. The responsibility of this entire program has been in his hands, from the arranging for the music to the
blocking of this thoroughfare. It takes a big man for such responsibility
and in our Deputy Grand Master, from whom you have just heard, we
have such a brother, literally and figuratively. I assure you, Right Worshipful L. Harold Anderson, that your services on this occasion will
never be forgotten.
.
In the one hundred and six years of our existence as the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of California, we
have never owned our own home. We have always been tenants. You
may imagine, therefore, the thrill that is ours in the anticipation of building on this site a Temple worthy of our institution, and of performing
for ourselves the cornerstone ceremony that we have done so often for
others. And on.this dedicated ground, Masons of California and of Hawaii are erecting more than just a Masonic Temple. It is also, and more
important, a memorial to their brothers who, as members of the Armed
Forces, have given their lives in defense of our country, a memorial to
the services and sacrifices of those free men of every age who have promoted and defended the great basic freedoms which we as citizens of
these United States enjoy as our birthright. Yes, from the earliest times,
Masonry has sought to advance the freedom of not only its own members but of all mankind.
It is a happy coincidence that we are laying this cornerstone in the
same September week when one hundred and seventy-nine years ago
was laid that great cornerstone of freedom, the American Constitution.
It is no coincidence however, that the majority of those who labored to
complete and who signed that Constitution and presented it to the
several states, were members of our beloved Craft.
The preservation of that Constitution with its wise provision for
freedom of speech and of assembly, of complete separation of church
and state, is a matter to which Masons give their constant and vigilant
attention. Upon it depends the proper education of the youth of today.

290

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

By proper education, we mean free education in schools owned and
operated by the fathers and mothers of the children who attend those '
schools, schools that are open to all and free from every semblance of
political or sectarian influence.
We do not hesitate to say, but are proud of the fact, that the beliefs
and convictions of the founding fathers of this country are the real
foundation stones upon which the fraternity of Freemasonry is erected.
A proper understanding of the necessity for our freedoms will make our
nation stronger and hasten the day when man will recognize the parenthood of God and the brotherhood of all mankind made in His image and
likeness.
To Masons, our new Temple, atop this beauti'ful and world renowned
hill, will be sanctified by the great principles of freedom, faith and truth
and as an enduring reminder to all that as long as right, justice and liberty shall exist, there always will be Masons ready to defend them. As
the great cathedral across the street stands as an emblem of the grace of
God, so may this Temple stand beside her as a symbol of the dignity
and sovereignty of man.
It is fitting that as we are assembled for the purpose of formally
commencing the erection of what will be a magnificent ornament on the
top of San Francisco's proudest hill, that we should have as our guest.
one who properly can speak for the populace of this city on this important occasion. I have the great pleasure and honor of presenting to you
the Mayor of the City and County of San Francisco, the Honorable
George Christopher.

Grand Master, the cornerstone of our national Capitol was laid with
essentially this identical ceremony.
We should like to remind you too, that this ceremony is symbolic.
To those unmindful of its symbolism, it will be but a form, meaningless,
but in truth and in fact, it is fraught with significance. You will find
reference made in the ceremony to corn. wine and oil. May I call to your
attention that these commodities are mentioned, in the same grouping.
many times in the books of the Old Testament. They long have been
indicative of the wealth of the people, their most cherished possessions,
which in olden days were sacrificed on important occasions such as this.
Our use of them is ex.plained in the ceremony itself.
You will note also, that various Grand Lodge Officers will be asked
to try the stone by the traditional working tools of Masonry. the square,
the level and the plumb. Freemasonry as a fraternity has long since lost
its skill in the operative building crafts. It is obvious therefore, that this
act too, has an esoteric significance. We are concerned today with the
building of human character and surely these same implements may be
applied as a test for "that house not made with hands, eternal in the
heavens."
With these brief hints of what may be discerned by the alert in this
age old ceremony, the officers of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of
Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California will proceed in
accordance with ancient custom to lay the cornerstone of the California
Masonic Memorial Temple.
The Grand Master then laid the cornerstone in due and ancient form.

Grand Master-Thank you Mr. Christopher. We indeed appreciate
your kind remarks and we are grateful that you could be with us again
to represent the citizens of San Francisco on this eventful morning when
Masonic history is being made.
Before we commence the ritualistic portion of the ceremony. a few
words concerning it may enable you to appreciate and enjoy it more fully.
Be assured first of all that this ceremony is by no means an innovation
of the Grand Lodge of California. It is as old as Masonry itself, whose
beginnings are lost in the pages of antiquity. With this same ceremony
the foundation stones of many public buildings, schools, churches and
Masonic Temples have been laid, not only throughout our state, but indeed, throughout the nation and the world, over a period of hundreds of
years.
The cornerstone of this state's Capitol building in Sacramento was
laid with Masonic rites. So too, were the foundation stones of many of
the important government buildings in Washington, D. C., including
the White House, and with our brother, George Washington, acting as
