ADDRESS OP THE GRAND ORATOR

with our American way of life. Americans smart under unnecessary restrictions or regulations of any kind. The appeal to the free will of the
individual to do that which is right and proper toward his fellow men
and his institutions commends itself to freedom-loving peoples. This is
the principle upon which all of our great charitable institutions have been
founded. It is indeed heartening to know that the willing response from
thousands of Masons throughout the State has made this tremendous undertaking possible. This joint effort will most certainly result in strengthening our fraternal ties, enhancing our cooperative spirit and giving us a
universal pride of accomplishment. It will have a most beneficial effect
on the entire craft.

We are gathered here today to lay the cornerstone of a beautiful and
significant edifice. This much-hoped-for ·home for Maso~ry in Ca.lifornia has been on our minds for many years. It naturally gives us satisfaction to witness the preliminary steps toward its construction. It is a
good time to recognize and to thank the leaders who have been responsible for this realization of our dreams. Theirs was the monumental task
of persuading the Lodge that the temple should be built, determining its
location, studying and approving its plans, undertaking the fund raising,
and dealing with the hundred and one details that all these duties involve.
Speaking for all of us, I extend our heartfelt gratitude to Past Grand
Master Siems, and his tireless committee, to the temple committees in the
constituent lodges, and to all others who helped in this fine undertaking.
A word concerning the location of the temple seems appropriate. San
Francisco combines the vigor and enthusiasm of youth with the maturity
and wisdom of the ages. Born in the ·hectic Gold Rush days, it was a
full-grown city almost from its beginnings. This community, in its hundred-odd years of existence, has withstood the whimsical conduct of
early day speculators and gamblers. It has survived the onslaught of
mass migrations from all parts of the world, and the lawless and violent
days which always accompany a town built on gold. It has experienced
ordeal by fire, and rebuilt itself into one of the beauty spots of America.
A cosmopolitan city, where all of the races of the world live harmoniously
side by side, it epitomizes the great American ideal that people of all
races and religions may here find opportunity and contentment. It stands
like a glistening jewel on the crossroads of the world's sea lanes, where
all mankind may view it, and be impressed by its message of tolerance
and true democracy. And of all of the city's beautiful locations, none
exceeds Nob Hill. The early gold and railroad tycoons, Stanford, Huntington, Crocker, Hopkins, Flood and Fair selected this spot for their
mansions. Today, with its towering cathedral and fine hotels, Nob Hill
lends a superior location to the spiritual and material needs of the
populace.
And where could one find a more suitable home for Masonry in California? Masonry, like this city, combines the vigor of youth with the
wisdom of ages. Masonry, too, has experienced its darker moments and
yet has survived ordeal by fire to give its lesson to all the world. Masonry, too, embraces the concept of true universality. and invites good
men of all races and beliefs. Yes, like this city, Masonry stands out as a
symbol of tolerance and charity, holding high the torch of freedom, and
encouraging harmony and understanding among all mankind.
We Masons should take great pride in the manner in which this
temple is being financed and built. Voluntary subscription is in keeping

A word also should be said, on such an occasion, concerning those
brave men in whose memory this magnificent temple is being erected. We
like to think that from its very birth, this great nation has conducted its
affairs upon high principle, rather than base expediency. Unlike the
•people who have fomented some of our great world revolutions, the
founders of this nation, many of whom were Masons, were for the most
part men of high education, real substance and material wealth. They
were willing to sacrifice vast property holdings and personal comfort for
the principle of freedom from foreign domination. The prized liberty
which they won for us has always been and should ever be our most
coveted heritage. Throughout our entire national history, the threat to
our sacred freedoms has presented itself time and time again in many
forms from sources both domestic and foreign. Our young men have
never been found wanting. They have met the challenge: they have kept
the faith. If the»e is one resounding lesson which the recurrence of world
conflict in 1941 emphasized to all freedom-loving peoples, it is the fact
that liberty is not something that can be won and firmly established for
all time to come. Rather, the threat and therefore the conflict is a continuous one. The admonition of John Curran, that "Eternal vigilance is
the price of liberty," is as true today as it was a hundred and seventy
years ago. How fitting it is, then, that this great, beautiful and enduring
Masonic monument should be dedicated to our war dead, to serve as a
constant reminder of the great debt owed to them by this nation, and
thus to keep us ever alert and zealous in the continuing struggle against
the forces of tyranny and oppression.
Let us consider the symbolism of this ancient rite. History informs us
that the laying of cornerstones in public buildings was a common practice among the Romans. It was a time of celebration and solemn dedication. The passage of the centuries has extended and enriched the
meaning of the word "cornerstone." Today it is frequently used in referring to the foundations of our individual lives and our national existence. We speak of the home, the church, and the school as cornerstones
upon which a full and worthy life can be predicated. We speak of the

295

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

United States Constitution as the cornerstone of the government and
our democratic way of life. To us, the term denotes an object of strength
and stability upon which we can plan and build. Thus it becomes a matter of concern that this stone should be true and trusty and well suited
for its intended use. As a Masonic symbol it reminds us to base our lives
on a solid and trustworthy foundation, to develop properly our Godgiven talents, and to be just and honest in our thoughts and action. The
stone is laid in the northeast ·corner of the building. Two of its sides are
thus exposed to the world. The north is the side of darkness, and reminds us to turn our backs upon the forces of ignorance and falsehood.
The east side faces the source of all light and directs us to acquire wisdom and pursue the truth.

design, nor precious building material gives to a structure that last significant characteristic so necessary to its real beauty. The temple, standing alone, is a mere shell provided for man's use.

294

There is a tendency in this material age to value things entirely from
the utilitarian point of view. I would like to comment on the significance
of this great edifice as a monument. When in the service of World War
II, I made my initial visit to Washington, D. C. I remember, as though
yesterday, viewing for the first time the George Washington Masonic
Memorial from across the Potomac. There, visible for many miles, and
towering toward the skies, was an enduring reminder to all men that
George Washington was a Mason. It was with great pride that I informed my companion that our first president was Master of his Lodge,
and had laid the cornerstone of the National Capitol while acting as
Grand Master of Virginia. This monument to the Father of our Country
signified in a singular way, to Masons and non-Masons alike, that Masonry could be a great ·motivating force in the lives of men. It reminded
us that Franklin, Jefferson, Madison, John Marshall, Paul Revere and
many of the other great men surrounding Washington were Master
Masons. It reminded us that Masonry had a very substantial place in
the creation of this great free nation.
Now there is to be a Masonic monument on the West Coast. It will
serve a purpose comparable to that of the Washington Memorial on the
East Coast. To Masons, to the thousands of citizens who will travel
this thoroughfare or view the temple from the streets below, it will represent a force for good in this community. It will call the attention of the
world to the contributions of Masonry to our national life. It will represent a citadel of freedom and a beacon of hope. It will remind men of the
duties they owe to God, to their fellow men, and to the nation. Yes, as
a monument, as a symbol of enlightenment, and wholly apart from its
us~fu!ness as a building, this temple will serve to inspire men to lofty
thinking and wholesome action.
In the final analysis, whether this great temple will achieve the supreme in grace and in appearance depends upon how some 500,000
Masons (including sojourners) residing in this State conduct themselves
as citizens and as men. History well records that neither location, nor

Some of the most beautifully designed buildings ever erected will
always be ugly, grotesque, and reprehensible in the minds of right-thinking men. Adolph Hitler's summer retreat at Berchtesgaden in the
Bavarian Alps with its inspiring view met all the requirements of location
and modern architecture. Yet because of the brutal and selfish conduct
of its occupant, and the destruction he visited upon the world, it is loathsome to behold. Stalin's summer home on the Black Sea records itself
in the camera's eye as a costly and beautifully designed structure, but in
the minds of decent men and women throughout the whole world it signifies ruthlessness and an utter disregard for human rights. On the other
hand, an event in Bethlehem almost two thousand years ago so elevated
mankind that it beautified a common stable .for all time to come. There is
a plain and crude log cabin memorialized on the Lincoln farm in Kentucky which in the minds of Americans symbolizes honesty, courage and
self-sacrifice. Because of the life of the man who was born there, it has
become an object pleasant to the sight of all Americans.
Yes, we Masons will put the finishing touch on this building. If we
will live by the tenets of Freemasonry, it will assume a luster and a
beauty in the minds of men and in the eyes of God which will surpass
our fondest hopes.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee ·h as completed the third year of the publication of
the California Freemason. This year, quarterly issues of 52 pages were
distributed to approximately 30,000 subscribers.
Our experience to this time indicates;
1. A quarterly magazine of this character is preferable to one issued
at shorter intervals. It reaches our members often enough to obtain their
interest without boring them with too much Masonic reading.
2. For maximum reader interest, the publication must be attractively
printed with a goodly number of illustrations. Pages of printed type
repel many readers but a few illustrations attract attention and lead the
peruser into the printed content.
3. Grand Lodge affairs must be reported and explained .for the prime
purpose is to keep Masons in contact with their Grand Lodge.
4. In line with this policy, the line officers of Grand Lodge must be
thoroughly and constantly introduced to the readers because in the past

5. Readable articles showing the Masonic point of view should be
presented. In each issue, various tyipes of material should be used. The
quarterly is one of the important arms of Masonic education and may
reach many who are out of touch with other methods.

6. Some space should be used to present matters of particular interest to the active officers and workers in the lodges.
7. The original !function of the Correspondence Committee is fulfilled by presenting reviews of the proceedings of other grand jurisdictions. These are made more succinct than formerly and endeavor to
present actions particularly interesting to Californians.
8. Our subscription list will not consist of more than 10% to 15%
of our membership, while voluntary subscriptions are required. We know
this because of the experience of other jurisdictions. This was the approximate ratio of subscribers to the New York magazine after 20 years
and until the New York Grand Lodge started sending it to every member
at a cost of about $.60 a subscription. Even in Iowa these percentages
are not exceeded although there is no charge for the subscription-all
that is required is a request in writing from the member at least once a
year.

9. As soon as practical, the California Freemason should be sent to
every member. It may be argued that if the .member doesn't subscribe he
isn't very interested. This is not entirely true. The inertia in connection
with sending in a subscription is great. The members think enough of
the Craft to pay their dues and would not discard the official Grand
Lodge publication without looking at some of it. The loss might be considerable but the leverage resulting from the contacting of 228,000
Masons will be tremendous. As the number of copies printed increases,
the unit cost 1per copy decreases rapidly. The present publication could
be distributed to our full membership at a cost of from $.50 to $.60 each.

year ending July 31, 1956, is as follows:

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Whereas, the preservation of American principles of freedom and
the welfare and purpose of public schools, cornerstone of American
democracy, long has been a special concern of American Masons; and
Whereas, there are grave dangers and threats .facing our freedoms
and public schools today, which have alerted four justices of the United
States Supreme Court to observe in the Everson case:
"Two great drives are constantly in motion to abridge, in the name
of education, the complete division of religion and civil authority which
our forefathers made. One is to introduce religious education and observances into the public schools. The other, to obtain public fonds for
the aid and support of v·arious private religious schools;" and
Whereas, the recent split decision of a court has opened the door in
California to forced public tax support by tax exemption of non-public
schools that compete with the rpublic schools but are private in purpose;
and
Whereas, said non-public ·schools comprise mainly sectarian sc'hools
that teach 1and instruct on sectarian doctrine forbidden in the public
schools, including those of one particular sect that teach obeisance to an
alien power, hostility toward American principles of separation of
church and state, the public schools, and any religion than its own, and
would receive about 90% of the tax exemption benefit; and
Whereas, there is therefore a crucial need that the people of California be informed and given the right to pass protective laws to prevent
such forced public tax support of non-public schools as would cripple our
public school system, divide our children along sectarian lines, and
destroy our American freedoms,
Now, Therefore, Be It Resolved: This Grand Lodge declares that
an amendment which has been proposed to the Constitution of California, in form substantially as follows, is a matter of statewide public
school welfare and purpose within the meaning of Section 126, Ross
Digest:
No Forced Public Tax Support by Grant, Tax Exemption or Otherwise for Non-Public Undercollegiate Schools, Including Those That
Teach or Instruct on Sectarian Doctrine Forbidden in the Public
Schools, and Excluding Those for Crippled Children.
The state, any political subdivision thereof, legislature, county, city,
city and county, town, school district, or other public district, body or
corporation shall not subsidize, aid, support or maintain, directly or
indirectly, in whole or in part, any non-public school of less than collegiate grade, including among others those that teach or instruct in any
form or amount on sectarian or denominational doctrine forbidden in the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

free, open-to-all. tax-supported ipublic schools, and those not under the
exclusive control of the officers of the ipublic or common school system
referred to in Article IX hereof. nor any property of or used in whole or
in part for any said undercollegiate non-public schools, nor any owner,
operator or pupil thereof. by appropriation, transfer, loan, use or payment of money, ipublic tax funds, transportation, building, construction,
property, tuition, scholarships, salaries, bonuses, gratuities, books ~r
materials or in any other manner, shape or form. Property of or used m
whole or in .part for any said undercollegiate non-public schools shall
not be tax exempt nor deemed to be within the exemption provided for
in Section 1c of Article XIII of the Constitution of the State of California. The provisions of this section shall not apply to property of nonsectarian and non-denominationa l schools of less than collegiate grade,
which property is used and sehools are operated exclusively for children
who are crippled, mentally afflicted or physically handicapped, and are
or shall be exempt from taxation under the Constitution and laws of the
State of California. 1£ any part, sentence, clause or phrase of this section
is for any reason held to be invalid, it is intended that all the remaining
provisions thereof shall continue to be fully effective.
The resolution deals with fundamental law as written into the Constitution of the United States, as it relates to separation of church and
state, :and is in keeping with the stand which the Grand Lodge has
historically taken regarding our public school system. To introduce religion into our public schools would be only the first step to abridge the
laws which have been handed down to us and which have stood the test
of time.
No one would deny the right of private schools to exist, providing
that those who beneflt from them are willing to pay the cost, but it is
repugnant to this committee, and we believe to Grand Lodge that there
should be forced public tax support of these institutions.
We feel that the resolution, as presented, is in perfect keeping with
Masonic principle and in full accord with Section 126 of Ross Digest
which reads in part as follows:
"Statewide public schools welfare is a •proper subject for discussion
in Lodges."
We, therefore, recommend the adoption of the resolution.

HAWAIIAN REPRESENTAT IVE OF GRAND MASTER
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had referred
to it the resolutions from several Past Masters of Lodges in the Hawaiian Islands proposing that the present Inspectoral districts be abolished and that an Assistant Grand Lecturer be appointed with supervision over all of the eight Lodges in the Islands.
The resolution further proposes that the office of District Deputy
Grand Master be created for these Lodges as the personal representative
of the Grand Master, with such authority as may be delegated by the
Grand Master.
While your Committee was considering the resolution, there appeared before us the duly accredited representatives of these eight
Lodges. They stated that the Lodges were not in favor of the resolution-that they are satisfled with conditions as they now exist and asked
that the resolution be not adopted.
Your Committee carefully considers every resolution that comes
before it and has done so in this case, but we feel that the statements of
the representatives is the expressed wish of the Lodges affected and we,
therefore, recommend that the resolution be not adopted.
A motion to adopt the original resolution was defeated.

EXPENSES OF CORRESPONDE NCE COMMITTEE
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has carefully considered the resolution to amend Section 68 of the Ordinances to provide
that the Correspondence Committee be entitled to transportation allowance for attendance at the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge.
This Committee is performing an important function in Grand Lodge
through the compilation and publication of the California Freemason
for the dissemination of Masonic news ·a nd information to the craft, and
your Committee feels that their presence at Grand Lodge is not only desirable, but necessary for the proper performance of their duties.
We, therefore, recommend the adoption of the resolution.
The Committees on Jurisprudence and on Finance reported their
concurrence.
Adopted.

METHOD OF LODGE VOTING
Brothers Williams, Owen, Collins and Campbell, all Past Masters,
have presented a resolution upon the subject of balloting the substance
of which is to prescribe the method of voting and to perm.it three or more
brethren of the Lodge to demand a secret ballot on slips of paper except
where our law provides that the vote shall be taken otherwise, such as
a vote by balls and cubes.
The right to a secret ballot, when so requested, is generally accepted
as a proper method of determining the wishes of the qualified voters.
It is provided for in the regulations governing such matters in this
Grand Lodge. We see no objection to extending this principal to proceedings in Constituent Lodges as a part of our laws.
We therefore recommend the adoption of the policy and the enactment of the amendment to our ordinances in the form recommended and
approved by the Committee on Jurisprudence.
Committee on Jurisprudence reported their concurrence.
Adopted.
See report of Committee on Jurisprudence for legislation.

BOARD OF CONTROL RECOMMENDA TION
A recommendation of the Board of Control that the chairman of that
committee be sent to Honolulu by Grand Lodge, at least every other
year, has been referred to the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes.
We appreciate the advantages of close contact between the Board
of Control and the Boards of Relief in the Islands and fully realize the
benefits which ·accrued to those island Boards when the Chairman of
the Board of Control met with them to discuss their problems while he
was vacationing recently in Honolulu.
We do not feel that the visit should be made mandatory by action
of Grand Lodge, but should be left to the discretion of the Grand
Master, who under present ordinances may authorize suc.h visitation
if to him it seems necessary or desirable.
We, therefore, do not approve this recommendation of the Board
of Control.
The report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes
was adopted.

MUTUAL BENEFIT ASSOCIATIONS
A number of resolutions have been presented seeking changes of
our law to permit the operation of Widows and Orphans Funds or

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

303

funds of similar character under several different names. For all practical purposes, the fonds operate in the same manner.
From time immemorial, Masonry has been and now is an association
of friends and brothers bounded together in love and affection to disse.minate knowledge. promote the welfare and happiness of one another
and to aid a distressed worthy brother, his widow and oriphans. It is
a charitable ·association in its broadest meaning but it is not now, never
has been, nor should it ever become, an insurance fraternity. It, therefore, should not sponsor, encourage or permit insurance organizations
or associations to operate in its name, use its name, or form insurance
groups composed solely of its Masonic members.
To relieve the distressed widow and or¢>.ans of a deceased brother
is incumbent upon all Masons as well as upon the Lodge of which the
deceased had been a member. That duty and the performance of it
is simply a part of the broader Masonic charitable work.
The essence of these widows and orphan fund groups is that they
are in reality insurance associations made up exclusively of Masons.
Fund members make contributions to a purse which is to be presented to
the widow or orphans of a deceased Mason, who, during his lifetime, had
been a member of that group making similar contributions. At the demise
of each, if ·he had continued to be a contributing member of the growp,
a similar purse is delivered to his dependents, frequently, and quite
generally, whether or not they were in distress.
Stripped of all its kindly and fraternal language, the contribution
so made is simply the paying of a premium upon a policy of insurance,
the .principal of which, on his death, is to go to his dependents. That is
insurance, not•charity.
The group of resolutions on the subject of widow and orphans funds
proposed to legalize that which would constitute the first step in making
Masonry an insurance fraternity instead of a charitable association
of friends and brothers practicing true charity in all its senses.
While the foregoing appears to be self-evident truths, your Committee understands that many of these "fund Groups" have been in
operation over a long period of time and that the methods of operating
are almost as varied as the number of the associations. Further, if dis.solution were to be ordered forthwith, the allocation of assets on hand
and the methods of termination of operation are not going to be simple
matters.
We feel that all the aspects of both the operations and the terminations, if required, deserve the most careful study to evaluate the consequences of a proposed solution of the problem.
We therefore recommend that the Incoming Grand Master appoint
a Special Committee to investigate, evaluate and make recommendations to the next Annual Communications of this Grand Lodge on all
phases of these matters and all other things that to the Committee appear

304

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

related thereto, to the end that a full understanding may be had before
final action is taken.

CORNERSTONE PROGRAM
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

MEMORIZING CHARGES

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes have reviewed the
resolution introduced by Ralph W. Collins, Keith W. Schlaegel, and
Edward J. Blickfeldt.
We are heartily in accord with the purpose of the resolution. We
believe that each part of the impressive ceremony was fully appropriate
to the significance of the occasion. The distribution of ·Copies and the
permanent record of the ceremony in the proceedings will increase the
number who will be inspired by reviewing the remarks of the several
participants.
We recommend that the following resolution be adopted. The Committee on Finance reported their concurrence.
Be It Resolved that a resume of the program of the laying of the
Cornerstone of the California Masonic Memorial Temple together with
the complete address of the Most Worshipful Edgar V. Stewart, Jr.,
Grand Master, and the Cornerstone Oration as given by the Grand
Orator Wakefield Taylor be made a part of the Proceedings of this
Annual Communication, and
Be It Further Resolved that the above be printed in pamphlet form
for distribution to the Lodges by the California Masonic Memorial
Temple Committee.

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes to which was
referred the resolution from Normal Heights Lodge No. 632 requiring
each candidate to commit to memory the charge of the degree in which
he is being examined in pursuance with the requirement of Section 241
of the ordinances, reports as follows:
The memorizing of those charges would serve no useful purpose.
The candidate's lectures, which are a part of our esoteric work, were
designed for the very purpose declared in this resolution. The third
degree candidate's lecture has been in use for nearly fifty years and
those of the other two degrees for a much longer period.
We believe the requirement of the above resolution would not only
cause an additional burden on the candidate, but would discourage
many from becoming proficient in the third degree candidate's lecture
which is not a mandatory requirement.
The Committee on Ritual concurs with your Policy Committee that
the resolution be not adopted.
I, therefore, move the resolution and recommend a no vote.
A motion to adopt the original resolution was defeated.

The Committee on Finance reported their concurrence.

Your Committee on Policy has had referred to it a resolution from
Naval Lodge No. 87 and a resolution of similar nature from Paul Revere
Lodge No. 462, resolving that the Grand Lodge formally sponsor a program of scholarships enabling the education in the universities of
selected students that they shall be properly equipped to follow their
careers as enlightened leaders of the !future.
Your committee is wholeheartedly in accord with the aim of the
resolutions as to the great good that can be accomplished in the field
of education.
However, it has ever been a fundamental principle of our fraternity
that we as individuals working with the proper agencies accept our
responsibilities in these worthwhile endeavQrs.

307

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

Our Masonic teachings may well lay the ground work for citizen
leadership in this field.
Free Masons have long progressed on the premise that while we
well may receive our incentive to shoulder responsibility through our
Masonic teachings, we as individuals should accept the challenge and
lead the way.
It is the opinion of your committee that on this basis we ,can better
serve mankind.
The committee therefore recommends that the resolution be not
adopted.
A motion to adopt the original resolutions was defeated.

Further, we have been taught in Masonry -that men should not be set
apart by groups or classes and that all Masons meet upon the square·
without regard for class, religion or race. Masonry is a great melting
pot, joining together men of good will and purpose in a common bond
of brotherhood.
The most successful Lodges in our Jurisdiction are those that set up
no barriers either on the basis of religion, race or other lines of demarcation.
Our doors are open to all who meet our test. Brethren who come
here from other lands are free to join with us should they apply and be
found worthy.
In this uncertain day and age when minority groups are used by our
enemies to 'Sow the seeds of distrust and confusion, we should avoid establishing artificial barriers, merely to provide a 'Convenience for a small
group of potential members.
The strength of Masonry is a solid front where all groups, irrespective of background, class, race or other distinction can 'meet, work and
understand one another.
We therefore recommend that the petition for the dispensation above
referred to be denied.
The request for a dispensation was denied.

SPANISH LANGUAGE LODGE
The Grand Master has referred to the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes the petition of sundry brethren praying for a dispensation to open a Lodge of Master Masons in the City of Los Angeles to
be composed of members of Mexkan ancestry and to work exclusively in
the Spanish language.
This subject has been before the Grand Lodge on several occasions,
the last at our 1953 Communication. The matter has been exhaustively
debated and each time it has failed of adoption.
Conditions have not materially changed since the introduction of the
flrst resolution many years ago.
The Grand Lecturer, in 'his report Monday, indicated problems presently existing in the Lodges which are now working in foreign languages
by special permission. The difficulties inherent in preserving our uniform
ritual, in preventing deviation and innovations are almost unsurmountable.

90 DAY NOTICE ON RESOLUTIONS
There has been referred to your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes, recommendation number one of the Grand Master providing
that any proposition to receive Grand Lodge action at an annual Communication must be received in the Grand Secretary's office not later
than ninety days prior to the opening date of Grand Lodge; and provided further, that Grand Lodge could vote to consider any proposition
on the vote of five-sixths of those .present, regardless of when it was
brought in.
Your committee is fully in accord with this recommendation and
recommends its adoption, but suggests that the provision for the fivesixths vote be modified to provide for a two-thirds vote of those present,
regardless of when the proposition is brought in.

REVISION OF FUNERAL SERVICES
Your Committee has had referred to it the Resolution of Past Master
Herbert R. Hargrave. Inspector of the 418th Masonic District, proposing a modificatiqn of the Revised Funeral Service of 1955. The effect of
his resolution simply means that the so-called "committal" would be
used also in cremation or mausoleum services.
The technical amendments proposed would result in the deletion of
paragraph 2, page 17 of the Funeral Service reading, "If the remains
are to be cremated, etc.... " and the rewording of the last two paragraphs on page 21 which would then read as follows:
" ( 11 ) If the entire service has been concluded in the chapel or
lodge room, the officers and brethren need not accompany the remains to the Cemetery, Mausoleum or Crematory, but if Master and Chaplain elect to do so, a simple
prayer may be offered at the place of interment.
If the service is to be conducted at the ·place of interment,
the Master and Chaplain should accompany the remains
to the last resting place. The other brethren should repair
to the place of interment, and with the officers, form an
aisle of brethren from hearse to place of committal, officers nearest the hearse. With Master and Chaplain leading, the casket is conducted to place of <:ommittal. The
officers and brethren turn in and follow the casket as it

310

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

1passes through the aisle. Master and Chaplain take up
positions at head of the casket, the Senior Warden at the
foot. Other brethren, under direction of the Marshal are
grouped formally at any convenient place."
One major objection to use of the committal in the old ceremony,
in case of cremation, was that the language was not appropriate to
a ~rematio~, consequently one of the first changes in the revision by
this Committee last year was to insert the instruction that the committal
paragraph be not used in case of cremation.
However, the language of the "committal" was later revised, and
we think that in its present form it can very appropriately be used at
a cremation or mausoleum service, as well as interment.
The Committee on Ritual sees no objection to the resolution, and
we, accordingly. recommend its adoption.
Adopted.

MASONIC LIBRARY IN LOS ANGELES
Your Committee has had referred to it that portion of the Grand
Masters Report covering the establishment of a Grand Lodge Masonic
Library in Los Angeles.
We feel that such a branch library in Los Angeles could be a welcome addition to the Grand Lodge Library in San Francisco, and could
very properly be supported by Grand Lodge funds. We find, however,
se~eral un.an9"'.'ered questions which render it impossible for your committee to mtelhgently come to a decision at this time. These are:
1. The type of books vlhich comprise the existing library. It has
been intimated that 50% of the volumes are fiction, and 25%
copies of Grand Lodge Proceedings, etc.
2. Whether or not a full-time Librarian is necessary.
3. The ty.p e and ultimate cost of adequate housing.
4. Future expansion of the library, and proposed means of financing.
5. Detailed cost estimates of operating expenses.
6. Availability of funds without increasing rper capita assessment.
The operative Mason does not commence construction of an edifice
without plans and blueprints of the finished structure. We likewise
believe that a project such as this should be covered by adequate
designs upon the trestleboard so that all may know the complete program and its costs.
The proposed new program has such far reaching effects that we
feel forther study should be made before a decision is reached.
We, therefore, recommend that the incoming Grand Master appoint
a special Committee to study all phases of the endeavor and report
back next year.
We have conferred with the Finance Committee, and they have
concurred with this recommendation.
Adopted.

MASONIC TRIAL PROCEDURES
There has been referred to the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes the recommendation of the Grand Master to set up a Committee to study and review Masonic Trial Procedures.
The confusing problem of Masonic Trials to the layman has been a
source of difficulty for many years. Several attempts to clarify our law
and procedures have been made with the result that the whole problem,
while perhaps clear to our attorneys, appears to be a patch work to the
ordinary Master who must struggle through a maze of legal language.
We concur with the recommendation of the Grand Master and suggest that the incoming Grand Master appoint a Special Committee to
study the present law and, if feasable, develop a manual for the use of
the brethren who are charged with the responsibility of carrying out the
provisions of our laws dealing with Masonic Trials.
Adopted.

DEMOLAY SPONSORSI-llP
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had under
review the report of the special committee on DeMolay which was created last year to study and report on the possibility of improving the
present status of DeMolay sponsorship. We had expected that the report would be 1presented directly to Grand Lodge and action taken
thereon. However, the report has been referred to us and we submit the
following:
This is a subject which has engaged this Grand Lodge on several
occasions. An exhaustive study and report was made in 1946 and on
the basis of that report the present Grand Lodge Committee has been
operating.
There is no question that the Order of DeMolay has for its precepts all of the qualities necessary for the development of youth. We
further agree that all Masons should be interested in the welfare of
youth and that the protection and development of our young people
should be our paramount concern.
This duty. however, is a Mason's obligation by reason of his prac1

313

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

tice of the virtue of good citizenship and as a member of the community
rather than through the activity of ·his Masonic Lodge.
Masons should be interested in the work of all organizations dedicated to the interest of youth. Boys and girls alike through Boy Scouts,
Girl Scouts, DeMolay, Rainbow, Jobs Daughters and other movements
deserve attention and support. To single out one organization to the
exclusion of the others of a similar nature is inequitable. It would mean
opening the door to pressure from others who would have similar claims
upon us.
It is almost impossible to assume sponsorship without taking on financial obligation. It is true that the resolution before us prohibits the
use of Lodge funds, but we predict that this will be temporary only and
within a short period a request will be made to eliminate the prohibitions
for the reason that sponsorship assumes all the responsibility of management and control.
A Lodge sponsoring a DeMolay Chapter wound find that in the eyes
of Masonry and the world at large, it was properly chargeable with the
membership admitted and their subsequent action, with no chance to
control the admission or to control the acts and conduct after admission.
In other words, an untoward act would, in the minds of the general public, be directly chargeable to the Lodge in question.
We feel that our present system properly directed and staffed. can
do more for the DeMolay Movement by propaganda methods than by
assuming full and complete responsibility for its operation.
We therefore move the adoption of the following resolution, recommending a no vote.
That every Chartered Lodge shall have the power to sponsor chapters of the Order of DeMolay, such sponsorship to entail the providing
of competent adult leadership and the promotion of interest in the purposes of the Order.
No Lodge shall be permitted to use Lodge funds in connection with
the sponsorship of the Order of DeMolay.
The above resolution was adopted.
An amendment, Section 159.1, designed to provide the law for such
sponsorship failed of adoption. The Grand Master ruled that permission to sponsor Chapters of DeMolay would be the policy of Grand
Lodge.

DEMOLAY PUBLICITY
San Bernardino Lodge No. 348 having sponsored a resolution with

for clarification purposes to Sec. 636 R.D. to permit the printing in
Trestle Boards of information regarding DeMolay and similar Masonic

This Committee reiterates its support of the Grand Lodge rulings
heretofore made against printing information in Trestle Boards regarding the activities of groups other than constituent Lodges of Grand

recognizes that such prohibitions are not intended to and should not prohibit the insertion of news items that could be of interest to Lodge members only and that the Master of a Lodge would not be violating the
letter or spirit of said prohibition by incorporating in his message or
editorial comment such news items of interest to Lodge members.
Referred back to Committees on Jurisprudence and on Policy and

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON RECOGNITION
OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
During the year your Committee has given diligent attention to external Masonic affairs, to petitions for recognition and reports as follows:
NATIONAL GRAND LODGE OP lcEI.AND

This Grand Lodge was erected on July 23, 1951, under the sponsorship of the National Grand Lodge of Denmark. A delegation from the
latter under the leadership of its Grand Master, M. W. Frode Rydgaard, performed the constitution ceremony. Delegations from the National Grand Lodge of Norway and the National Grand Lodge of
Sweden were present. The late M. W. Sveinn Bjornsson, President of
the Republic of Iceland, was the first Grand Master. Present Grand
Master is M. W. Olafur Larusson.

GRAND LoDGE OP THE DOMINICAN REPUBLIC

The petition of this Grand Lodge, located at Cuidad Trujillo, Dominican Republic, was mentioned in our report last year but action
thereon was held in abeyance. Since then we have received documentary
evidence supplied by the Grand Master, Luis A. Brouwer, the Grand
Secretary, Alfredo de la Cuesta M., which convinces us that said Grand
Lodge meets our tests for recognition. A report from Brother Nathan A.
Reid, Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of Panama, confirms our
conviction.
We therefore move that the Grand Lodge of the Dominican Republic
be recognized by the Grand Lodge of California.
Adopted.
GRAND LoDGE VALLE DE MEXICO

Around 1911 this Grand Lodge challenged the regularity of York
Grand Lodge of Mexico and difficulties ensued until 1920 when a Commision from the Gtand Lodge of Texas and our P.G.M. Adams made an
on the spot investigation which resulted in affirmation of the regularity
of said York Grand Lodge and a determination that said Valle de
Mexico was the schismatic body ( 1921 Proc. 387-410). Hostilities between the two bodies continued until March 7, 1945, when an intervisitation compact, Decree No. 445, was consummated.
On the basis of said compact our Grand Lodge continued in amity
with York Grand Lodge and also recognized Valle de Mexico ( 1946
Proc. •p. 181 ) .
On May 21, 1953, Valle de Mexico, without notice to York, issued
a Decree No. 596 annulling said intervisitation compact. Since then the
breach has extended and under date of December 3, 1955, Valle de
Mexico issued and published a Decree No. 659 declaring York Grand
Lodge to be irregular and an invader of its Masonic territory and proscribing amity between the two Grand Lodges their constituent Lodges
and members.
GRAND loDGE OP GUATEMALA

This Grand Lodge was recognized by California in 1923 ( 1923 Proc.
p. 700). The Castilo Armas revolution in 1954, among other things,

316

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

resulted in the supervision of Masonry by the government. Out of this
arose two groups of Masons vying for the control of the Grand Lodge.
The old Grand Lodge is represented by Bianachi, the present Grand
Master. The other group, which under the direction of the Supreme
Council of Scottish Rite organized a new Grand Lodge bearing the same
name as the old one, is represented by Orbaugh as Grand Master. The
new Grand Lodge took possession of the property of the old Grand
Lodge. The old Grand Lodge under Bianchi then brought suit to recover
the property but the Court held that it belonged to the new Grand
Lodge.
In March, 1956, Orbaugh, on behalf of the new Grand Lodge, flied
a petition with the Public Ministry-Consultin g Department seeking determination that the new Grand Lodge was the legal and proper one.
Bianchi group opposed and sought legal determination in favor of the
old Grand Lodge. Based on technical reasons no determination was
made by the Ministry, which suggested that the controversy be submitted
to the courts dealing with penal matters.
As far as we know all regular Grand Lodges still recognize the old
Grand Lodge and not one has recognized the new one.
CONCLUSION

Respecting the Grand Lodge of Valle de Mexico and the Grand
Lodge of Guatemala it must be concluded that Masonic affairs are in a
state of turmoil and confusion induced and aggragated perhaps by influences from sources not apparent. This ·committee recommends no
drastic action at this time. Its purpose is to seek additional information
during the ensuing year with a view to definite action at our next annual
communication. Since California is not excessively distant from the
two troubled spots this Committee respectfully suggests to the incoming
Grand Master that great benefit to Masonry might ensue if a delegate
who can speak Spanish were sent to the two spots in difficulty for a personal investigation on behalf of Grand Lodge. We point out that no
member of this Committee is bilingual.
Respectfully submitted,
JoHN R. MooRE
CHESTER H. WARLOW
ARTHUR M. WARREN

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON JURISPRUDENC E
DECISIONS OP THE GRAND MASTER

To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee reports on decisions of the Grand Master, as follows:
DECISION No. 1

The Grand Master correctly held that a brother may reimburse a
Lodge for expenses which it incurred in a Masonic trial. (Authority,
Sec. 157 Ross Digest.)
Adopted.
DEc1s10N No. 2
It is altogether improper, as the Grand Master ruled, to publish the
names of Candidates, Entered Apprentices or Fellow Crafts in a Lodge
roster. We would add that it is not lawful to publish these names in
any fashion, except, where concurrent jurisdiction is concerned, the
names of applicants for the degrees and for affiliation may be restrictively
published among the Lodges holding concurrent jurisdiction by posting
such names on the bulletin boards of such Lodges during Lodge meetings only. (Secs. 214 and 696 Ross Digest.)
Adopted.
DEc1s10N No. 3

A Lodge unde.l" dispensation is a temporary structure subject to dissolution at the will and pleasure of the Grand Master. It is therefore not
proper for such Lodge to organize a corporation for the purposes indicated in Sec. 151 of Ross Digest. The Grand Master's decision to such
effect is sound.
Adopted.
DEc1s10N No. 4

May an organization, requiring Masonic affiliation as a condition to
membership, hold meetings in a building where liquor is sold over a bar?
The Grand Master correctly answered this question in the negative.
(Secs. 126.1 and 596 Ross Digest.)
Adopted.
DECISION No. 5

A series of questions, relating to jurisdictional boundaries and
waiver of jurisdiction by Lodges, were propounded to the Grand Master
who answered them in accord with Masonic law.
Adopted.

318

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

DECISION No. 6
To the question, May a member of California Lodge residing in
Louisiana join with other Shriners there in soliciting advertising, etc.,
for the Shrine publications without being in violation of our California
Law? The Grand Master responded as follows:
"My answer was, no. Any other answer would imply that a Mason
could disregard the laws of the Grand Lodge under which is own Lodge
is beholden as soon as he crosses a state line or a jurisdictional boundary.
which is certainly not the case. It appears to me that a sojourning brother
has two sets of laws to which he must conform, the laws of the Lodge
to which he belongs including, of course, the Grand Lodge to which it is
beholden, and the laws of the Grand Lodge in whose jurisdiction he re.sides. Because the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge is his place of resi.dence might be more lenient than the laws of his home Grand Lodge,
certainly this does not permit him to apply a new set of rules to regulate
his conduct. This would obviously be a violation of his vows."
The Grand Master's answer is in accord with our law.
(Secs. 127 and 289 Ross Digest.)
Adopted.
DEc1s10N No. 7

The Grand Master defined presiding officer at a Lodge meeting as
the Master or ranking Warden, in the absence of the Master, regardless
of his position in the lodge.-room; and-Held that the presiding officer
must remain in the lodge.-room during the time that the Lodge it at labor
and further that the presiding officer may invite any qualified brother to
assume the Master's chair and confer degrees or transact business.
These acts of the Grand Master are sound. (Sec. 772 Ross Digest.)
Adopted.
DEc1s10N No. 8
The Grand Master held that a Lodge cannot participate in a parade
except with a dispensation from the ·Grand Master, as Ross Digest, Sec.tion No. 124, very dearly indicates. While this Section specifies parad.ing in Masonic clothing in its prohibition, the implication is surely there
that it applies to any Lodge of Masons, regardless of aprons.
He further held that the funds of a Lodge may not be expended for
a parade Boat, inasmuch as our laws specifically state the purposes for
which the funds may be used, and by no stretch of the imagination, can
the term "fraternal intercourse" be interpreted to allow expenditures of
money under this provision for such purpose.
We concur with the Grand Master in this decision. (Secs. 124, 158
and 159 Ross Digest.)
Adopted.
DECISION No. 9

This decision is correct.
Adopted.

The following resolution, prepared at the 105th Annual Communication and carried forward to this Communication as unfinished business,
was presented by the Committee on Jurisprudence with the recommendation that it be adopted.
Resolved: That Ross Digest be amended by inserting the language
quoted below as subparagraph E. under subsection 1. of Sec. 86, and as
subparagraph ( e) under subsection 1. of Sec. 152.1 :
"Investment certificates issued by a building and loan association or
a savings and loan association organized and existing under the laws of
the State of California which is an insured institution as defined by Title
IV of the National Housing Act, and shares issued by any such association which issues no investment certifi·cates and which is an insured institution as defined by said Title IV, and shares issued by any federal
savings and loan association."
Reasons for suggested amendment:
Under our existing law as recently construed by our Grand Master,
neither shares nor certificates issued by state or federal building or savings and loan associations are eligible for investment of Lodge funds, or
Grand Lodge funds.
This amendment would therefore eliminate the discrimination which
now exists against the securities of such state and federal associations.
All federal savings and loan associations are insured institutions.
Since the amendment is limited to securities issued by insured institutions and to the types of securities which are insured, the suggested
amendment is conservative in its character.
Respectfully submitted,
JoHN R. MOORE, Past Master
Meridian Lodge No. 667
The resolution was not adopted.

There have been referred to this Committee, the Report of the Grand

which he recommends that Lodges Under Dispensation, as listed in the
Grand Secretary's report, be not required to pay per capita tax.
We have reviewed the Report of the Grand Treasurer and it has our
entire approval. We have given consideation to the recommendation of
the Grand Secretary relating to Lodges Under Dispensation and it has
our approval.
Adopted.
CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE
There was referred to this Committee, the Report of the California
Masonic Memorial Temple excepting recommendations 1 to 5 both inclusive. Each member of this Committee has received from the auditor
his Report on the Temple Corporation. It has been examined in detail,
discussed in Committee, and has received the approval of all of the
members of the Committee.
MARICOPA MASONIC BUILDING ASSOCIATION
At the 1953 Communication, Grand Lodge adopted the resolution of
the Finance Committee authorizing the Grand Master, the chairman of
the Committee on Finance and the chairman of the Committee on Lodge
Financing to extend such assistance to the brethren of Tehachapi and
Maricopa Lodg.es in their building projects as might be in their judgment decided upon. This generous action was taken to assist these
Lodges in recovering from the disastrous earthquake.
Subsequently, $15,000 was approved and paid to Teha~hapi and
$10,000 to Maricopa. In the last year, an additional $5,000 was requested, approved, and paid to Maricopa.
We. therefore, offer the following resolution:
Resolved, that the action of the Grand Master, the chairman of the
Committee on Finance and the chairman of the Committee on Lodge
Financing, pursuant to instructions by Grand Lodge at the 1953 Annual
Communication, in extending financial assistance to the extent of $5.000
to Maricopa Masonic Building Association, be. and the same is ratified
and approved.
Adopted.

PUBLIC SCHOOLS SCHOLARSHIP AWARD

In his term now ending. the Grand Master announced and made
scholarship awards in connection with Public Schools totaling $2,000.
Your Committee feels that this fund and the overall purpose being served
is of sufficient importance to warrant a separate designation in the budget, and have acted accordingly.
AUDIT OP ACCOUNTS

In accordance with the provision of Ordinances, an audit of all accounts of Grand Lodge for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1956, has been
made. Each member of the Finance Committee has received and examined these audits. It is our opinion that the reports present the correct
condition of the finances of the Grand Lodge. We express appreciation
to Brother Hammond, our Auditor, for the excellent manner in which
the various audits have been completed and for his personal counsel and
cooperation with this Committee.
MASONIC HOMES

Your Committee has reviewed the audit of the accounts of the Masonic Homes of California and the report of the Trustees. We have
consulted the Board to ascertain their estimate of the funds needed to
support the operation of the Homes for the next fiscal year and find that
a renewal of the per capita tax of 50c will be sufficient.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of 50c per capita be levied for the fiscal year
ending June 30, 1957, the proceeds to be paid to the Trustees of the
Masonic Homes.
Adopted.
BUDGET

Before hearing the proposed budget for the current fiscal year, you
will be interested in the results for the previous year. Total income of
Grand Lodge from all sources was $335,035.10. The total amount spent
for all purposes was $309,740.12, leaving a surplus transferred to Capital
account of $25,294.98.
We had estimated in our budget that there would be a surplus of
$33,000. The difference of approximately $8.000 is more than accounted
for by two expenditures referred to in this report which were unforeseen
and not budgeted-$5,000 paid to Maricopa Building Association and

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

329

the approximate expense of $7,700 incurred in connection with the
Groundbreaking Ceremony. Otherwise, actual surplus would have been
in excess of the estimate.
In presenting for your consideration the proopsed budget for the
fiscal year ending June 30, 1957, comments on several items are made
for your enlightenment.
SALARIES

Your Committee has discussed with the Grand Secretary the salaries
of his staff in the Grand Lodge office and the needs for the new fiscal
year. We are including in this item a small increase which will cover
his recommendations.
RETIREMENT PLAN---'GRAND LooGE EMPLOYEES

At the 1955 Annual Communication on the recommendation of this
Committee, Grand Lodge appropriated $4,000 to cover the estimated
cost of placing the employees in the Grand Lodge Office under the Masonic Homes Retirement Pension Plan, effective for these employees
January 1, 1956.
In the past year, we have had compiled the necessary data on employees outside the Grand Lodge office, such as those in the various
Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus, and in the two University
Clubhouses.
Combining these employees with those in the Grand Lodge Office
placed under the Plan last year, we are advised by our Actuaries that
the sum of $15,000 will be required to cover the cost of placing all such
employees of Grand Lodge under the Plan. We have included an appropriation in this amount and recommend its approval. This appropriation is to cover the cost of the employees in the Grand Lodge Office for
the full fiscal year and for the cost of the remaining Grand Lodge employees outside the Grand Lodge Office for the period beginning January 1, 1957, to the end of the fiscal year. For your future guidance, this
Committee wishes you to know that the total cost for a fuU year for all
employees in succeeding years will approximate $22,000. This covers
the cost of current service of employees, but only the minimum payment
required to cover credits earned by all employees prior to the adoption of
this Plan by Grand Lodge.
In order to provide the necessary authority for this action, we offer
the following resolution and move its adoption:
"Whereas, at the 107th Annual Communication, Grand Lodge directed that certain of its employees be placed under the Retirement
Pension Plan now in effect for employees of the Masonic Homes: which
Grand Lodge employees are in addition to those in the Grand Lodge
Office placed under this plan at the 106th Annual Communication,
Now, therefore, be it
Resolved, that the Grand Master and Grand Secretary be authorized

330

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

to do all things necessary to implement the integration of these additional
employees of Grand Lodge into the Masonic Homes Retirement Pension
Plan.
Adopted.

Gentlemen:
We have made an examination of the 1956 Annual Returns of the Constituent Lodge.s of the Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California, reporting on
the membership and on the payments due Grand Lodge in accordance with
the provisions of the Constitution and Ordinances and the action taken by
Grand Lodge at the 1955 annual communication. Our examination was made
!n accordance with generally accepted auditing standards, and accordingly
mcluded such tests of the accounting records and such other auditing procedures as we considered necessary in the circumstances.
The total payments due Grand Lodge, based upon the 1956 annual returns, amount to $983,050.50, as shown by the accompanying statement,
marked Exhibit A. At the date of this report, August 31, 1956, this amount
had been collected in full and transferred to the Grand Treasurer with the
exception of a balance of $3,075.50 arising from errors made in the returns.
This balance was in the process of adjustment and collection at the date of
this report.
Respectfully submitted.,
SKINNER & HAMMOND
Certified Public Accountants

had an aggregate market value of $644,666.01. On August 2, 1955, Grand
Lodge, pursuant to the resolution adopted at the 1954 Communication, sold to
the Masonic Temple Association of California, Inc., for the sum of $254,887 .50
the 33,985 shMes of the capital stock of that association owned by it at July
31, 1955. The shares of the Masonic Temple Association of California, Inc.,
owned by Grand Lodge represented 51.63% of the outstanding stock of that
corporation. The cost of these shares, as shown on the books of Grand Lodge,
was $339,850.00. The loss on the sale of this stock amounting to $84,962.50,
being extraordinary and non-recurring in nature, has been cha·rged directly
to the capital of Grand Lodge, as will be noted by reference to Exhibit A.
During the year Grand Lodge, pursuant to the resolution adopted at the
1955 Communication, transferred to the building fund of the California Masonic Memorial Temple the proceeds of $254,887 .50 from the sale of the stock
of Masonic Temple Association of California, Inc., referred to above.
The 1955 Communication of Grand Lodge approved the including of the
employees of Grand Lodge under the Masonic Homes of California Retirement Income Plan, which became effective January 1, 1955. Pending amendment of the trust agreement and the Retirement Income Plan of the Masonic
Homes of California and the approval by the Internal Revenue Service, the
funds contributed by the participating employees of Grand Lodge have been
retained in the Grand Lodge accounts. The total contributions from January
1 to July 31, 1956, representing 3% of the participating employees' regular
salary and amounting to $874.50, is shown as a liability on Exhibit A. The
past service liability to be funded by Grand Lodge and the present value of
benefits to be provided by future contributions of Grand Lodge have not
been determined pending amendment of the original plan.
On Schedules 4, 5, and 6, of this report, the expenses and appropriations
for the current year are shown in comparison with those for the preceding
fiscal year, and also with the budget for the current year adopted by Grand
Lodge at the 1955 Communication. It may be noted that the total expenses
and appropriations were less than the amount provided in the budget. However, in certain individual categories expenditures exceeded the amount that
had been provided in the budget. Any such expenditures were not paid until
approved by the Grand Master. Supplies purchased during the year for
resale to Lodges and individuals amounted to $16,854.04, and sales of such
supplies amounted to $20,578.41, leaving a net difference of $3,724.37, which
has been added to revenue as shown on Exhibit B. The accounts being on a
cash basis of accounting, the inventory of unsold supplies is not reflected on
the attached financial statements.
The details of all expenditures during the year were examined by us
with the exception of the Grand Master's travel, secretarial, and miscellaneous expense, certain of the expenditures of the Endowment Board, and the
appropriations to Employment Bureaus and to the University Clubhouses.
No vouchers covering such expenses and appropriations have been required
to be filed with Grand Lodge. Our examination disclosed no UlllPRid bills at
July 31, 1956, with the exception of sundry expenses, insignificant in amount.
The publication of the "California Freemason" has continued during the
current year under a resolution adopted at the 1954 Communication of Grand
Lodge. Subscriptions at $1.00 per year were collected and single copies were
sold producing an aggregate revenue of $25,365.18. Of this revenue $19,331.00
represents the prepaid portion of subscriptions at July 31, 1956, and at that
date Grand Lodge was contingently liable in that amount. In the financial
statements herewith, the revenue of $25,365.18, including the prepaid portion
thereof, has been offset against the expense of the Correspondence Committee
amounting to $27,004.27, resulting in a net expense for the Correspondence
Committee for the year of $1,639.09, and an un·expended budget of $4,360.91,
as shown on Schedule 6.

During the year the Masonic Homes Endowment Board and the California Masonic Memorial Temple Committee continued to engage in campaigns to raise money for the Masonic Homes and the new Masonic Memorial
Temple. The funds collected by the Endowment Board are paid to the Endowment Fund of Masonic Homes of California and the funds collected by
the Memorial Temple Committee are paid to the California Masonic
Memorial Temple corporation and are not reflected in the attached statement.
The expense of the Endowment Board and of the Memorial Temple Committee are shown on Schedule 6 of this report.
Under date of October 4, 1955, the officers of California Masonic Memorial Temple signed promissory notes with six San Francisco banks for a
total of $3,000,000.00. Under authorization given at the 1953 Communication,
Grand Lodge became the guarantor of these notes. The Memorial Temple
did not need to draw any funds against these notes between the date they
were signed and July 31, 1956.
In our opinion, the accompanying balance sheet and statement of revenue and eX!pense together with the foregoing comment, present fairly, on
the cash basis of accounting, the financial position of The Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California at July
31, 1956, and the results of its operations for the year then ended in confonnity with generally accepted accounting principles applied on a basis
consistent with that of the preceding year.

September 5, 1956
Masonic Homes of California
Masonic Temple

San Franeisco, California
Gentlemen:
We have examined. the Balance Sheet of
MASONIC HOMES OF CALIFORNI A
(A California Non-Profit Corporation)
as of July 31, 1956, and the related Statement of Revenue and Expense for
the year then ended. In connection therewith we also examined the Balance
Sheets of the Permanent Endowment Fund and the other endowment and
trust funds of the Masonic Homes of California as of July 31, 1956, and their
related statemenrts of revenue for the year then ended. Our examination was
made in accordance with generally accepted auditing stand·a rds, and accordingly included such tests of the accounting records and such other auditing
procedures as we considered necessary in the circumstance s.
The total revenue received by Masonic Homes of California during the
fiscal year ended July 31, 1956, amounted to $690,059.51, as shown on Exhibit
E. Its operating expenses for the year amounted to $783,244.50 resulting in
an excess of operating expense of lji93,184.99. Capital gains from the sales of
securities amounted to $85,300.98, resulting in a final excess of expense over
revenue, including capital gains, of $7 ,884.01, as shown on Exhibit C. Included
in the operating expenses of $783,244.50, is the sum of $58,068.00, covering
the payment in full of the cost of pension benefits based on the past services
of employees covered under the "Masonic Homes of California Retirement
Income Plan," which became effective January 1, 1955. The past service cost
of $58,068.00 is a non-recurrin g expense.
General Fund cash on hand and on deposit in banks at July 31, 1956, as
shown by Exhibit A, amounted to $344,659.30, a decrease of $536,628.72 from
the amount on hand and on deposit at the beginning of the year. The greater
part of this decrease represents cash used to purchase additional securities
as investments.
The total amount of the General Fund invested in securities at July 31,
1956, amounted to $1,812,728.27, as shown on Exhibit A, an increase of $715,431.40 over the amount at the beginning of the year. Securities purchased
are stated on the books and in this report at cost. Securities received as donations are stated at market value when received. or at the nominal value of
$1.00, if the market value was not known.
The amount of $82,766.32 shown as notes and contracts receivable O!l'l
Exhibit A is the result of sales of real estate received by the Masonic Homes
of California by assignment from applicants admitted to the Home at Decoto.
The value of land, buildings, and equipment is shown on Exhibit A, at
$3,150,622.21, the cost when originally purchased. In accordance with the
consistent policy of the Trustees, depreciation of buildings and equipment is
not provided for in the accounts, but replacement s of original items are considered expenses of operations. During the current year additions to the
Decoto Home were $20,081.77 for elevators. Additions to the Covina Home
were $29,121.61 for the superintende nt's residence and $6,969.50 for fences.
The total additions of $56,172.88 were made from funds provided by the Reserves for Special Purposes, as shown on Schedule 4. The buildings and
contents of the Decoto and Covina Homes are insured for fire, with extended
coverage, in the amount of $4,428,500.00. The valuations are reviewed annually for insurance purposes.
The Other Assets of $2,811.48 shown on Exhibit A consist of real estate
and life insurance policies assigned to Masonic Homes of California by residents of the Decoto Home. The individual parcels of real estate and life
insurance policies are each recorded at the nominal value of $1.00 for aceount-

356

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

ability, with the exception that payments by Masonic Homes of Californi~ on
loans obtained by the assignors of such policies are added to the nominal
values. The proceeds from the sale of this real estate and from ~e life insurance policies are credited direct to one of the Reserves for Special Purposes
as directed by the Trustees.
The sundry liabilities of $421.31 shown on Exhibit A include contributions of employees of the Masonic Homes in the amount of $417.31 payable
to Wells Fargo Bank as Trustee under the "Masonic Homes of California
Retirement Income Plan."
The "Masonic Homes of California Retirement Income Plan" was authorized at the 1947 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. This
Plan became effective January 1, 1955. The object of the Plan is to provide a
method whereby Masonic Homes of California and its emplo;vees may make
regular contributions to a trust fund to provide de~nite retirement income
benefits for participating employees who become entitled thereto. ~nder the
terms of the Plan participating employees contribute 3% of their regular
salary, which is deposited by the Masonic Homes with the Wells Fargo Bank
as Trustee and the Masonic Homes may make voluntary contributions to the
trust fund' in order to place the Plan on a sound actuarial basis. During the
current year voluntary contributions under the Plan were made by Masonic
Homes of California in the amounts of $58,068.00 and $22,454.34, and charged
to expense of the current year, as shown on Exhibit E. The payment of $58,068.00, paid in full the estimated cost of benefits under the Plan based upon
the past service of employees, and the payment of $22,454.34, covered the
current service cost for the calendar year 1955, of pensions payable under the
Plan. The current payment of $22,454.34 represented 16.098% of the payroll
for the calendar year 1955 of participating employees under the Plan.
The Trustees of the Masonic Homes have established six special reserves
to which are credited the amounts of donations and bequests which are to be
used for purposes other than direct operating expenses. These reserves, aggregating $1,529,093.00 at July 31, 1956, are shown on the attached Balance
Sheet as "Reserves for Special Purposes." The assets represented by these
reserves are included in the assets of the General Fund, shown on Exhibit A.
The activities of these reserves during the year are shown on Schedule 4.
Endowment and trust funds held by the Masonic Homes of California
amounted to a total of $7,665,685.15 at July 31, 1956, as shown on Exhibit A.
Of these funds $7,118,977.47 was in the Permanent Endowment Fund of
Masonic Homes of California. The Permanent Endowment Fund was increased by $836,428.52 during the current year by donations, bequests, gains
from sale of securities and real estate, and the transfer from the Unappropriated Reserve of $100,000.00. The other endowment and trust funds increased during the year by the aggregate sum of $3,707.66. A description of
each of the endowment funds, together with a Balance Sheet, and, where
appropriate, a statement of the related revenue, is shown on Exhibits F to
N, inclusive.
During the year the Homes discontinued the practice of recording, on its
accounting records, inventories of stores and supplies and livestock and the
amount of such inventories as were recorded on the records at July 31, 1956,
was accordingly charged to Capital, as shown on Exhibit C. Inasmuch as the
accounting records and financial statements of the Homes are generally
maintained on a cash basis of accounting and since the inventories stated on
previous balance sheets of the Homes were not complete inventories and
were in part based upon estimates, we approve of this change in accounting
practice. In all other respects, in our opinion, the accounting principles employed in the preparation of the attached financial statements have been
applied on a basis consistent with that of the preceding year.
In our opinion, subject to the foregoing comments, the accompanying
Balance Sheet, marked Exhibit A, and the related Statement of Revenue and
Expense, marked Exhibit E, together with the balance sheets of the Endowment Funds and the related statements of revenue, present fairly, on the cash
basis of accounting, the financial position of the Masonic Homes of California
and its endowment and trust funds at July 31, 1956, and the results of opera-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

357

tions for the year then ended, in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles.

Gentlemen:
We have e~amined the balance sheet of the
CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE
(A California Non-Profit Conporation)
as of July 31, 1956, and the rela·t ed statement of income and expenses for
the year then ended. Our examination was made in accordance with generally acceI?ted auditing standards, and accordingly included such tests of the
accountmg records and such other auditing procedures as we considered
necessary in the circumstances.
The California Masonic Memorial Temple was incorporated under the
"General Non-Profit Corporation Law" of the State of California on January
6, 1954. Its primary purpose is to hold title to that certain real property
upon which the building to he known as the California Masonic Memorial
Temp!~ is being erected, to collect the income therefrom, and to turn over
the entll'e amount thereof, less expenses, to the Endowment Fund of Masonic
Homes of California, a charitable non-profit corporation.
Conti;-ibutions received durU:g the fiscal year ended July 31, 1956, for
the erection of the new memorial temple amounted to $938,950.68, which
amount has been added to the capital of the Memorial Temple Corporation
as shown on Exhibit A Net income during .the year amounted to $3 377.21'
as shown by Exhibit B. Contributions and net income provided totai fund~
during the year of $942,327.89. Of this amount $497,943.21 was expended
for real estate and construction costs incident to the new temple and the
balance of $444,384.68 was added to the amount on deposit in banks thus
increasing that amount from $1,039,531.06 as at July 31, 1955, to $1,483 B15.74
at July 31, 1956, as shown on Exhibit A

The contributions from individual Masons are collected by the california Masonic Memorial Temple Committee of the Grand Lodge, F. & A. M.
and are turned over immediately on collection to the Memorial Temple
Corporation. The Committee records indicate unpaid contribution pledges
at July 31, 1956, in excess of $100,000.00. Unpaid .pledges are not taken into
account as an asset by the Memorial Temple Corporation until the pledge
is collected by the Committee and turned over to the corporation. The entire amount collected from individual Masons is available for the cost of
erecting the new temple as all the expenses of the Committee have been
paid from funds appropriated out <Jf the revenues of Grand Lodge, F. & A. M.
All of the tenants in the old buildings on the Memorial Temple site at
California and Taylor Streets, San Francisco, vacated the property by
March 31, 1956, in order to make way for the erection of the new temple
building. Subsequent to that date we made a final audit of the records of

During the year the general contract for the erection of the new temple
and a number of special contracts were let. The amounts of the commitments at July 31, 1956, based on executed contracts or on firm bids, are indicated on Schedule 1, together with the amounts paid to July 31, 1956, on
account of completed work. On August 1, 1956, the general contractor,
MacDonald, Young & Nelson, Inc., was paid $67,920.82, representing the
amount due at July 31, 1956, on work completed prior to that date. There
were no other liabilities due and unpaid at July 31, 1956, other than miscellaneous current operation bills of nominal amount.
Under date of October 4, 1955, the officers of California Masonic
Memorial Temple signed promissory notes in favor of the following banks
and in the amounts as shown:

$3,000,000.00

The foregoing promissory notes are secured by a first deed of trust on the
temple site real property and the improvements thereon ·and are also to be
secured by a chattel mortgage on the furnishings and equipment of the new
Temple. Interest at 4% per annum is payable semi-annually on the amounts
actually advanced under said notes. ReP-ayment of the prmcipal advanced
on the notes is to be repaid in annual $20,000.00 instalments to each bank
with final maturity ten years from the date of the notes. The above notes
and the repayment to the banks of advances thereOlll are subject to numerous
provisions set forth in the bank commitment letter. No advances on the
notes had been received on or prior to July 31, 1956.
In our opinion, subject to the foregoing comments, the accompanying
balance sheet and statement of income and expenses present fairly, on the
cash basis of accounting, the financial position of the California Masonic
Memorial Temple at July 3~, 19~6, and the results of its oper~tions .foi: the
year then ended, in conforrmty with generally accepted accountmg prmc1ples
applied on a basis consistent with that of the preceding year.

125 Progress, San Francisco, 1858. Charter revoked Oct. 14, 1870.
130 Unity, San Bernardino, 1859. Charter revoked May 13, 1863.
133 Yosemite, Coulterville, 1859. Consolidated with La Grange No. 99, now
known as Yosemite No. 99, Oct. 16, 1913.
137 Oro Fino, Oro Fino, 1860. Charter surrendered June, 1862.
138 Violet, Spanish Flat, 1880. Charter surrendered Oct. 16, 1879.
142 Colusa, Colusa, 1860. Consolidated with Equality No. 240, as Colusa No.
240, April 1, 1882.
148 San Luis Obispo, San Luis Obispo, 1861. Charter surrendered Dee. 2,

Reviews of the Proceedings of other Grand

sent to each Grand Lodge. This program will be
continued.

terly and each issue will carry additional reviews.
Hence, they do not appear in these Proceedings.
